docs.title: Snowflake Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Snowflake is easy to start with: create a warehouse, load a file, run SQL. It's also easy to get surprising results and surprising bills. A load that quietly keeps 199,997 of 200,000 rows, a FLATTEN that drops a quarter of your customers, a one-day query that reads every partition because of how rows arrived, a join that makes revenue six times too high, a MERGE that inserts the same order twice, administrators who can read raw PII through an innocent role grant, a warehouse bill that's 86% idle time, and a dbt model that passes every test while serving stale numbers: none of these are Snowflake bugs. They follow from how Snowflake actually works, and this course shows each one.

It assumes you know SQL and some Python. It doesn't assume any Snowflake experience.

Level 1 covers the foundations: the three-layer architecture and credits, accounts and clients (Snowflake CLI and Python with key pairs), objects and types, warehouses and billing, loading with stages and COPY, Snowflake SQL, semi-structured JSON, Time Travel and Fail-safe, and zero-copy cloning, ending with a small analytics database. Level 2 is performance and data engineering: micro-partitions and pruning, clustering, the Query Profile, the three caches, Snowpipe, streams, tasks, dynamic tables, unloading and Iceberg, ending with an incremental ELT pipeline. Level 3 is security and governance: roles and privileges, authentication after the end of single-factor passwords, network policies, masking and row access policies, tags, secure views, data sharing, encryption and auditing, ending with a governed multi-team platform. Level 4 is building and operating: UDFs and procedures, Snowpark, Python UDFs, Cortex AI functions, cost management, warehouse scaling, replication and failover, dbt and CI/CD, and migration, ending with a cost-aware platform whose chargeback is tested.

Every lesson has a How It Actually Works section: why a filter on one column can skip 97 of 98 micro-partitions and the same filter on another can't skip any, why a clone costs nothing until it diverges, why a secure view is slower, why a masking rule that names one role also unmasks every role above it, and why per-query cost attribution never adds up to the bill.

Versions and what was actually run

This course was written without access to a Snowflake account, and no output is presented as Snowflake output. Every Snowflake SQL statement was parsed with sqlglot 30.22 (Snowflake dialect) and checked against Snowflake's documentation as of October 2026. Where a result is shown, it comes from something that was really run, and is labelled: the same SQL on the same generated data in DuckDB 1.5.6, Python models of the documented billing and replication rules (with their assumptions stated), Snowflake CLI 3.29.0 and the Python connector for everything that doesn't contact Snowflake, Snowpark 1.53.0 in its local testing mode, dbt-core 1.12.5, and pytest suites for every project. Things that couldn't be run, such as Cortex AI output, real query profiles and failover, are described from the documentation and never shown with invented results.

Snowflake changes quickly, and several features here are new in 2025–2026: mandatory MFA and the end of single-factor passwords, programmatic access tokens, Snowpipe's per-GB pricing, task overlap policies, Cortex AI functions and model access control, Gen2 as the default warehouse, Adaptive Warehouses, Optimized Refresh and RPO Assurance for replication, and dbt Projects on Snowflake. Each lesson says what it was checked against, so you can compare with your account.

docs.text:
Level Focus Modules What you can do after 1 · Snowflake Foundations Architecture, clients, objects, warehouses, loading, SQL, JSON, Time Travel, cloning 10 Build and query a well-organized database and predict its cost 2 · Performance & Data Engineering Pruning, clustering, profiles, caches, Snowpipe, streams, tasks, dynamic tables, Iceberg 10 Make queries read less and keep data fresh incrementally 3 · Security, Governance & Sharing RBAC, authentication, network, masking, tags, secure views, sharing, encryption, auditing 10 Run a shared platform where access is designed, tested and audited 4 · Building, Scaling & Operating UDFs, Snowpark, Cortex AI, cost, scaling, replication, dbt CI/CD, migration 10 Build on Snowflake and keep it fast, recoverable and affordable

Each level has 9 teaching modules plus a hands-on project (module 10), for 40 lessons total.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Use a free trial account. Every exercise fits in Snowflake's free trial. Use your own account, never a shared or production one, and give every warehouse AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 from the start.
  • Run the examples twice. Once as written, and once on your account. Results shown from DuckDB or a model are labelled, and comparing them with what Snowflake does is part of the learning.
  • Watch the meter. Keep an eye on WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY while you work. The cost lessons are easier when you've seen your own numbers.
  • Do the projects. Each one combines its level into something you could adapt for real work, and each comes with tests, including the bugs those tests caught.

docs.title: Level 1 · Snowflake Foundations
docs.text:
Level 1 takes you from "Snowflake is a cloud data warehouse" to building and querying a small, well-organized database. Along the way it covers the decisions that determine your bill and your data quality from day one: how long a warehouse idles after a burst of work, why 199,997 of 200,000 rows load, why a FLATTEN quietly drops a quarter of your customers, why a permanent table rewritten nightly holds nine times its size, and why updating 0.001% of a table can rewrite 39% of it.

What was run, and what wasn't

This course was written without access to a Snowflake account, and no output is presented as Snowflake output. Every SQL statement was parsed with sqlglot's Snowflake dialect and checked against Snowflake's documentation. Results shown for queries come from running the same SQL on the same generated data in DuckDB 1.5.6, and are labelled as such. Cost and storage figures come from small Python models of the documented billing rules, also labelled. Snowflake CLI 3.29.0 and the Python connector were run locally for everything that doesn't contact Snowflake. A free trial account is enough to run every exercise yourself.

Prerequisites: comfortable with SQL (joins, GROUP BY; see the SQL Mastery Path) and basic Python for the client and project lessons.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. How Snowflake Is Built: Storage, Compute & Services — the three layers, why they're separate, credits, the 10% cloud-services rule and editions.
  2. Accounts, Snowsight, Snowflake CLI & Python — account identifiers, session context, Snowflake CLI connections with key-pair auth, and the Python connector.
  3. Databases, Schemas, Tables & Data Types — the upper-case identifier rule, permanent vs transient vs temporary tables, types that matter, and unenforced constraints.
  4. Virtual Warehouses: Sizing, Suspend & Credits — sizes and rates, risky defaults, and a billing model where 160 seconds of work cost up to 4,114 seconds.
  5. Loading Data: Stages, File Formats & COPY INTO — stages, file formats, validation, ON_ERROR, 64-day load metadata and file sizing, on a dataset with planted errors.
  6. Snowflake SQL: Windows, QUALIFY & Extensions — QUALIFY, ranking with ties, running totals, GROUP BY ALL, EXCLUDE, PIVOT, MERGE and ASOF JOIN.
  7. Semi-Structured Data: VARIANT & FLATTEN — paths and casts, SQL NULL vs JSON null, the OUTER flag, and how VARIANT is stored.
  8. Time Travel, UNDROP & Fail-safe — querying and restoring the past, retention by edition, and the storage that history holds.
  9. Zero-Copy Cloning & Environments — clones for dev and test, what gets cloned, and when scattered updates make a clone expensive.
  10. Project — Load & Analyse a Sales Dataset — an end-to-end script, an answer key and an automated checker.

docs.title: After Level 1
docs.text: You can build, load and query a Snowflake database correctly. Level 2 is about doing it fast and continuously: how micro-partitions and pruning decide what a query reads, clustering, the Query Profile, the three caches, and the continuous-data features (Snowpipe, streams, tasks and dynamic tables), ending with an incremental pipeline.

docs.title: 01 · How Snowflake Is Built: Storage, Compute & Services
docs.text:
Snowflake is a cloud data platform: a SQL database for analytics that runs only as a managed service on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud. You never install it, size disks or tune a buffer pool. You also never get to look underneath, which is why the most useful thing to learn first is the shape of the system. Almost every Snowflake behaviour that surprises people (why two teams can query the same table without slowing each other down, why a query can be instant the second time, why an idle warehouse still costs money, why you can undo a DROP TABLE) follows from one design decision: storage, compute and coordination are three separate layers, each scaled and billed on its own.

About this course and what was run

Snowflake has no local edition. Everything runs in a Snowflake account in the cloud, and this course was written without access to one. So no output in this course is presented as coming from Snowflake. Instead:

  • Every SQL statement is written against Snowflake's documented syntax and was parsed with the Snowflake dialect of sqlglot 30.22 to catch syntax mistakes. Statements that sqlglot can only partly parse (such as CREATE STREAM and CREATE TASK) were checked against Snowflake's documentation instead.
  • Where a concept can be shown with real computation (window functions, QUALIFY, JSON flattening, min/max pruning, billing arithmetic), it is shown with DuckDB 1.5.6 or a small Python model on a laptop, and labelled that way. DuckDB isn't Snowflake, so its output format, and sometimes its behaviour, differ.
  • Facts that change over time (prices, credit rates, feature status, deadlines) are taken from Snowflake's documentation as of October 2026, and you should re-check them. Snowflake ships changes every few weeks.

With a free trial account, you can run every statement yourself. The lessons tell you what to look for.

docs.title: The three layers
docs.text:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CLOUD SERVICES: authentication, metadata, query parsing and         │
│ optimization, transactions, access control, result cache            │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
      │                │                  │
┌───────────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌────────────────┐
│ Warehouse │   │ Warehouse  │   │ Warehouse      │  ← COMPUTE: independent clusters,
│ BI_WH (S) │   │ ETL_WH (L) │   │ DS_WH (XS)     │    start/stop/resize at will
└───────────┘   └────────────┘   └────────────────┘
      │                │                  │
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ STORAGE: tables as immutable, compressed, columnar micro-partition │
│ files in the cloud provider's object storage                       │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Storage. When you load data, Snowflake reorganizes it into its own columnar format and writes it as micro-partitions: immutable files of 50–500 MB of uncompressed data each (smaller once compressed), stored in the cloud provider's object storage (S3, Azure Blob or GCS) in Snowflake's account, not yours. You can't see these files directly. For every micro-partition, Snowflake records metadata such as each column's minimum and maximum value and the number of distinct values. That metadata is what lets queries skip most of a table (Level 2 · 01). Because files are never modified in place, an UPDATE writes new micro-partitions and retires old ones. Keeping the retired ones for a while is what makes Time Travel and cloning possible (lessons 08 and 09).

Compute. Queries run on virtual warehouses: clusters of cloud servers that Snowflake provisions for you, in T-shirt sizes from X-Small to 6X-Large. A warehouse holds no data. It reads micro-partitions from storage, caches them on local SSD while it runs, and can be suspended (costing nothing) and resumed in seconds. Different workloads can use different warehouses against the same tables without competing for CPU. A nightly ETL job on a Large warehouse doesn't slow down the BI dashboard on a Small one. That's the central promise of the architecture.

Cloud services. A shared, always-on layer handles everything that isn't scanning data: logins, the metadata catalogue, parsing and optimizing SQL, transaction management, access control, and the result cache, which can return an identical query's results without starting a warehouse at all (Level 2 · 04). Some operations, like SHOW TABLES, COUNT(*) on a whole table, or MIN/MAX of a column, can often be answered from metadata alone.

docs.title: Why separation matters, concretely
docs.text:
Situation Traditional shared-nothing warehouse Snowflake ETL load runs while analysts query Both compete for the same nodes Separate warehouses, no CPU contention Data grows 10× Add nodes and rebalance data Storage grows on its own, and compute is unchanged A big query once a month Size the cluster for the peak Resize a warehouse for that query, then shrink it Nobody is querying at night Cluster still runs (and bills) Warehouses suspend, so compute costs nothing A new team needs the same data Copy data to their cluster Point their warehouse at the same tables

What separation doesn't remove is contention for the same warehouse. Twenty analysts sharing one Small warehouse queue behind each other. Level 4 · 06 covers multi-cluster warehouses, which add clusters as queries queue.

docs.title: How you pay: credits
docs.text:
Compute is billed in credits. A running warehouse consumes credits per second (with a 60-second minimum each time it starts) at a rate that doubles with each size step. That's 1 credit per hour for X-Small, 2 for Small, 4 for Medium, and so on up to 512 for 6X-Large, for standard "Gen1" warehouses (Lesson 04 has the table). The dollar price of a credit depends on your edition, cloud, region and contract, so this course talks in credits.

Other charges:

  • Storage: a monthly rate per terabyte, on the compressed size, including data kept for Time Travel and Fail-safe (lesson 08). It's usually small compared with compute.
  • Cloud services: charged only for the part of a day's cloud-services usage that exceeds 10% of that day's warehouse usage. In most accounts that's nothing. Workloads with huge numbers of tiny queries, or heavy use of metadata commands, can exceed it.
  • Serverless features (Snowpipe, automatic clustering, search optimization, serverless tasks and others) run on Snowflake-managed compute, each with its own rate. They don't count toward the 10% cloud-services allowance.
  • Data transfer out of the region or cloud.

Level 4 · 05 shows how to see where credits go and how to cap them.

docs.title: Editions
docs.text:
The edition decides which features you get (and the credit price). From Snowflake's documentation:

Feature Standard Enterprise Business Critical Virtual Private Snowflake Time Travel retention 1 day up to 90 days up to 90 days up to 90 days Multi-cluster warehouses — ✓ ✓ ✓ Materialized views, column-level security (masking) — ✓ ✓ ✓ Tri-Secret Secure (customer-managed key) — — ✓ ✓ Private connectivity (PrivateLink) — — ✓ ✓ Failover and failback between accounts — — ✓ ✓ Isolated environment (dedicated metadata store and compute) — — — ✓

Several lessons depend on Enterprise features (masking policies, 90-day Time Travel, multi-cluster warehouses), and they say so. A trial account typically lets you choose an edition.

docs.title: Where Snowflake fits
docs.text:
Snowflake is built for analytics: large scans, aggregations and joins over historical data, many concurrent readers, and batch or micro-batch loading. It's a poor fit as the primary database behind an application that does thousands of single-row inserts and updates per second. Use PostgreSQL (see the PostgreSQL Mastery Path) or similar, and load Snowflake from it. (Snowflake does offer hybrid tables for row-oriented workloads. They're out of scope here.)

This course assumes you know SQL. If JOIN, GROUP BY and window functions are new to you, start with the SQL Mastery Path. Python appears in the Snowpark and connector lessons, and the Python Mastery Path covers what you need.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
When you submit a query, the cloud services layer authenticates you, checks your role's privileges, parses and optimizes the SQL, and consults the metadata for every micro-partition of every table involved. Using each partition's min/max values, it eliminates partitions that can't contain matching rows, often the vast majority. Only then does it hand a plan, plus the list of surviving micro-partition files, to a warehouse. The warehouse's nodes fetch those files from object storage (or their local SSD cache if they've read them recently), decompress only the columns the query needs, execute the plan in parallel, and return results through the services layer, which also stores them in the result cache for 24 hours.

A write follows the same path in reverse. The warehouse produces new micro-partition files, and the services layer commits the change by atomically updating the metadata to point at the new files instead of the old ones. Nothing is overwritten. The old files remain referenced by Time Travel until their retention expires, then by Fail-safe, and are deleted afterwards. That copy-on-write design is why writes are transactional, why many readers never block writers, and why "undo" features cost only storage.

Because warehouses are stateless with respect to data, a warehouse can be suspended between queries, resized between statements, or given extra clusters, and the data doesn't move. The trade-off is that every warehouse start begins with a cold local cache. Lesson 04 and Level 2 · 04 show what that costs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• One warehouse for everything. You lose the isolation that separation provides. Give ETL, BI and data science their own warehouses.
  • Treating Snowflake like an OLTP database. Single-row inserts in a loop are slow and expensive. Load in batches.
  • Thinking storage is the bill. Compute (warehouses running) usually dominates. An idle-but-running warehouse is the classic waste.
  • Assuming every feature exists in every edition. Masking policies and long Time Travel need Enterprise or higher.
  • Expecting to tune the database the old way. There are no indexes or vacuum to manage. The levers are data layout (clustering), warehouse sizing and query design.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Sign up for a Snowflake trial in a region near you, and note your account's edition, cloud and region (Snowsight shows them in the account menu, or run SELECT CURRENT_ACCOUNT(), CURRENT_REGION();).
  2. Draw the three-layer diagram for a company with a nightly load, a BI tool used by 50 people during office hours, and two data scientists. Which warehouses would you create, what size, and when would each be running?
  3. Using the credit table in this lesson, work out the credits per day for a Medium warehouse that runs 9 hours a day on weekdays, and a Large one that runs 1 hour each night. Which costs more per month?
  4. List three Snowflake features this course will rely on that need Enterprise Edition or above, and check whether your trial account has them.

docs.title: 02 · Accounts, Snowsight, Snowflake CLI & Python
docs.text: Before writing any SQL you need three things: an account to connect to, a client to connect with, and an understanding of the session context (role, warehouse, database, schema) that every statement runs in. Most "permission denied" and "no active warehouse" errors new users hit come from the last one.

docs.title: Accounts and identifiers
docs.text:
A Snowflake account lives in one cloud region and belongs to an organization. The preferred way to name an account is the organization-based identifier:

<orgname>-<account_name>              e.g.  myorg-analytics
https://<orgname>-<account_name>.snowflakecomputing.com

Older material uses the account locator form (xy12345.eu-west-1), which still works but ties the identifier to a region. Use the orgname-accountname form in new configuration. Once connected you can check where you are:

SELECT CURRENT_ORGANIZATION_NAME(), CURRENT_ACCOUNT_NAME(), CURRENT_REGION(), CURRENT_ACCOUNT();

docs.title: Snowsight
docs.text: Snowsight is the web interface: SQL worksheets, Python notebooks, dashboards, data browsing, query history with the Query Profile (Level 2 · 03), cost views and administration. A worksheet has its own role, warehouse, database and schema selectors at the top, which set the session context for the statements in it. When a query fails in a worksheet, check those four selectors first.

docs.title: Session context
docs.text:
Every statement runs with a current role, warehouse, database and schema:

USE ROLE SYSADMIN;
USE WAREHOUSE learn_wh;
USE DATABASE learn_db;
USE SCHEMA public;

SELECT CURRENT_ROLE(), CURRENT_WAREHOUSE(), CURRENT_DATABASE(), CURRENT_SCHEMA();
  • Role decides what you're allowed to do (Level 3 · 01). Your user has a default role, and you can switch to any role granted to you. The same user can see different objects under different roles.
  • Warehouse is the compute that runs queries. Without one, anything that scans data fails with an error saying no active warehouse is selected. Metadata operations and result-cache hits don't need one.
  • Database and schema resolve unqualified names. orders means learn_db.public.orders here. Fully qualified names (database.schema.object) work regardless of context, and scripts that run unattended should use them.

docs.title: Snowflake CLI
docs.text:
Snowflake's own documentation now calls SnowSQL "a legacy command-line client". It's still supported (version 1.5.x until 16 April 2028), but new features go only into Snowflake CLI, the snow command. Install it with pip (or pipx, or Homebrew):

pip install snowflake-cli
snow --version

Snowflake CLI version: 3.29.0

The top-level commands show how wide its scope is: running SQL, managing stages and objects, Snowpark functions, Streamlit apps, notebooks, dbt projects, Git repositories and more (excerpt of real snow --help output):

│ connection     Manages connections to Snowflake.                             │
│ cortex         Provides access to Snowflake Cortex.                          │
│ dbt            Manages dbt on Snowflake projects.                            │
│ git            Manages git repositories in Snowflake.                        │
│ object         Manages Snowflake objects like warehouses and stages          │
│ snowpark       Manages procedures and functions.                             │
│ sql            Executes SQL statements against Snowflake interactively or    │
│                from a query, file, or standard input.                        │
│ stage          Manages stages.                                               │
│ streamlit      Manages a Streamlit app in Snowflake.                         │

docs.title: A connection with key-pair authentication
docs.text:
Snowflake is phasing out single-factor password sign-ins: humans need multi-factor authentication, and scripts and service users should use key pairs, OAuth, programmatic access tokens or workload identity federation (Level 3 · 02 has the details and dates). Key-pair authentication is the simplest to set up from a laptop. Generate an RSA key pair:

openssl genrsa 2048 | openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -inform PEM -out rsa_key.p8 -nocrypt
openssl rsa -in rsa_key.p8 -pubout -out rsa_key.pub

(-nocrypt leaves the private key unencrypted, which is fine for a lab. In production, encrypt it, or better, keep it in a secret manager.) Register the public key on your user, pasting the base64 body without the -----BEGIN/END----- lines:

ALTER USER ana SET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY = 'MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKC...';
DESC USER ana;   -- the RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_FP property shows the key's SHA-256 fingerprint

You can compute that fingerprint locally and compare it with DESC USER. The two should match:

openssl rsa -pubin -in rsa_key.pub -outform DER | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl enc -base64

SHA256:xWy4qmg9a9Y2zY8a0g/qRNp2QGRbDv7emETjmB0BSSU=

(That's the fingerprint of the throwaway key generated for this lesson.) Then add a named connection. With --no-interactive nothing is asked, and nothing is sent to Snowflake yet:

snow connection add --connection-name trial --account myorg-myaccount --user ANA \
  --authenticator SNOWFLAKE_JWT --private-key-file ~/keys/rsa_key.p8 \
  --warehouse LEARN_WH --database LEARN_DB --schema PUBLIC --role SYSADMIN --no-interactive

Wrote new connection trial to …/config.toml

The configuration it wrote:

[connections.trial]
account = "myorg-myaccount"
user = "ANA"
database = "LEARN_DB"
schema = "PUBLIC"
warehouse = "LEARN_WH"
role = "SYSADMIN"
authenticator = "SNOWFLAKE_JWT"
private_key_file = "~/keys/rsa_key.p8"

From here, snow connection test -c trial checks the connection, and snow sql -c trial -q "SELECT CURRENT_USER()" runs a query. (Those two contact Snowflake, so they weren't run for this course.) The same config file is read by the Python connector and Snowpark, so one place defines how all your tools connect. You can see the connector reading it without any network call by asking for a connection name that doesn't exist:

import snowflake.connector
try:
    snowflake.connector.connect(connection_name="prod")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, str(e))

Error Invalid connection_name 'prod', known ones are ['trial']

The connector looks in the directory given by the SNOWFLAKE_HOME environment variable (here pointed at the lab directory) or in its default per-user config directory (~/.snowflake on many setups). With the file readable by other users (chmod 644), the same call still worked but printed a warning, Bad owner or permissions on …. chmod 600 the file, and keep it out of version control.

docs.title: Connecting from Python
docs.text:
The Snowflake Connector for Python follows Python's DB-API. Installed versions used for this lesson: snowflake-connector-python 4.7.5 (pulled in alongside Snowflake CLI 3.29.0).

import snowflake.connector

conn = snowflake.connector.connect(
    connection_name="trial",          # reads [connections.trial] from the config file
)
try:
    cur = conn.cursor()
    cur.execute("SELECT CURRENT_USER(), CURRENT_ROLE(), CURRENT_WAREHOUSE()")
    print(cur.fetchone())

    # bind parameters: never build SQL with f-strings from user input
    cur.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE region = %(region)s", {"region": "EU"})
    print(cur.fetchone()[0])
    print("query id:", cur.sfqid)     # look it up in Snowsight's query history
finally:
    conn.close()

A few facts confirmed by inspecting the installed package:

snowflake-connector-python 4.7.5
write_pandas exists: True
DictCursor exists: True
paramstyle default: pyformat
  • The default parameter style is pyformat (%(name)s and %s), with values escaped on the client side. Server-side binding with ? or :1 is available by setting snowflake.connector.paramstyle = "qmark" (or "numeric") before connecting.
  • snowflake.connector.pandas_tools.write_pandas(conn, df, "TABLE_NAME") bulk-loads a DataFrame by staging it as Parquet and running COPY INTO, which is far faster than row-by-row INSERTs.
  • cur.sfqid is the query ID. Log it with your application's errors so you can find the query in Snowflake's history.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A client connects over HTTPS to <account>.snowflakecomputing.com, which is the cloud services layer. With key-pair authentication, the client signs a short-lived JSON Web Token with your private key. Snowflake verifies the signature against the public key registered on your user, so the private key never leaves your machine. On success the client receives a session token and attaches it to every request. The session holds your current role, warehouse, database, schema and parameters (time zone, statement timeout and so on), which is why USE statements affect later statements in the same session but not other sessions.

Queries are submitted as requests. Small results come back inline. Large results are written by Snowflake to internal storage as compressed chunks, and the client downloads them in parallel directly from object storage, which is why fetching millions of rows is much faster than the request round trip alone would suggest. Every statement gets a query ID that ties together the client call, the query history, the Query Profile and the access history (Level 3 · 09).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No warehouse in the session, often because the user's default warehouse isn't set or the role can't use it.
  • Relying on context in scripts. Fully qualify names in jobs, so a changed default doesn't send writes to the wrong schema.
  • Passwords in code or config committed to Git. Use key pairs or tokens, and keep config.toml private.
  • Building SQL with f-strings. Use bind parameters.
  • Starting new work on SnowSQL. It's legacy. Use Snowflake CLI.
  • Using the account locator in new config. The orgname-accountname identifier is region-independent.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. In a trial account, create a user for scripts, register a key pair, and verify that the fingerprint from DESC USER matches the one you computed with openssl.
  2. Configure two named connections (one with SYSADMIN, one with a read-only role you'll create in Level 3) and run the same SELECT CURRENT_ROLE() through each with snow sql -c.
  3. Write a Python function that runs a parameterized query and returns rows as dicts (DictCursor), and logs the query ID on error. Find a failing query in Snowsight's history using that ID.
  4. Run SHOW PARAMETERS IN SESSION; and find three parameters that would change query results or behaviour (for example, the time zone).

docs.title: 03 · Databases, Schemas, Tables & Data Types
docs.text: Snowflake's objects nest in a fixed hierarchy, and most of the rules you'll trip over at the start are about names, table kinds and types. Three of them catch nearly everyone: unquoted identifiers are stored in upper case, primary keys are not enforced, and there are three timestamp types that behave differently.

docs.title: The hierarchy
docs.text:
Organization
└── Account
    ├── Users, Roles, Warehouses, Integrations, Network policies   (account-level objects)
    └── Database
        └── Schema
            ├── Tables, Views, Materialized views, Dynamic tables
            ├── Stages, File formats, Pipes, Streams, Tasks
            ├── Sequences, Functions (UDFs), Procedures
            └── Policies (masking, row access), Tags

A fully qualified name has three parts: database.schema.object. Warehouses, users and roles live at the account level and have one-part names.

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS learn_db COMMENT = 'Snowflake Mastery Path labs';
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.analytics WITH MANAGED ACCESS;

WITH MANAGED ACCESS makes the schema owner (not each object's owner) control grants inside it. That's a good default for shared schemas (Level 3 · 01).

docs.title: Identifiers: the upper-case rule
docs.text:
Unquoted identifiers are case-insensitive and stored in upper case. Quoted identifiers are case-sensitive and stored exactly as written:

CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.Customers (id INT);          -- stored as CUSTOMERS
SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.customers;                   -- works: resolves to CUSTOMERS
CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw."orderItems" (id INT);       -- stored as orderItems
SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.orderItems;                  -- fails: looks for ORDERITEMS
SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw."orderItems";                -- works

This bites most often when tools create tables with quoted lower-case or mixed-case names (some loaders and DataFrame writers do), and then every query needs quotes. Prefer unquoted snake_case names and let them become upper case. The QUOTED_IDENTIFIERS_IGNORE_CASE parameter changes this behaviour account-wide, and it's best decided before any objects exist.

docs.title: Three kinds of table
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.orders_history (order_id NUMBER, amount NUMBER(12,2));      -- permanent
CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE learn_db.raw.orders_staging (order_id NUMBER, amount NUMBER(12,2));
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE session_scratch (order_id NUMBER, amount NUMBER(12,2));
Permanent Transient Temporary Lives until dropped dropped the session ends Visible to anyone with privileges anyone with privileges only the creating session Time Travel up to 90 days (Enterprise+), 1 on Standard 0 or 1 day 0 or 1 day Fail-safe (7 days) yes no no

Transient tables exist to save storage on data you can rebuild: staging tables, intermediate ETL results, scratch tables. A permanent table that you rewrite completely every hour keeps every old version in Time Travel and then in Fail-safe, and you pay storage for all of it (lesson 08). Transient databases and schemas make everything created in them transient by default.

docs.title: Data types worth knowing
docs.text:
Type Notes NUMBER(p, s) Exact decimal. INT, INTEGER, BIGINT are all aliases for NUMBER(38,0). Use it for money. FLOAT / DOUBLE 64-bit binary floating point. Fine for measurements, wrong for money. VARCHAR(n) Default length 16,777,216 characters, maximum 128 MB. The declared length has no storage or performance cost, so don't agonize over it. BINARY Default 8 MB, maximum 64 MB. BOOLEAN TRUE / FALSE / NULL. DATE, TIME As expected. TIMESTAMP_NTZ "No time zone": wall-clock time, no zone stored or applied. TIMESTAMP_LTZ Stored as UTC, displayed in the session's TIMEZONE. TIMESTAMP_TZ Stores the time and its UTC offset. VARIANT, OBJECT, ARRAY Semi-structured data (lesson 07). A single value can be up to 128 MB. GEOGRAPHY, GEOMETRY Spatial types. VECTOR(FLOAT, n) Fixed-length embedding vectors (Level 4 · 04).

Plain TIMESTAMP is an alias whose meaning is set by the TIMESTAMP_TYPE_MAPPING parameter (TIMESTAMP_NTZ by default). That means two accounts with different settings interpret the same DDL differently. Name the specific type in DDL. The usual choice is TIMESTAMP_NTZ holding UTC for event times, or TIMESTAMP_TZ when the original offset matters.

docs.title: Why NUMBER for money: a demonstration
docs.text:
Snowflake's FLOAT is IEEE-754 binary floating point, like Python's float and most databases' DOUBLE. The rounding it produces can be shown on any engine. Here's DuckDB 1.5.6 locally (not Snowflake), summing 0.1 a million times:

-- DuckDB 1.5.6 (local), not Snowflake
SELECT SUM(0.1::DOUBLE) AS sum_double, SUM(0.1::DECIMAL(38,2)) AS sum_decimal
FROM range(1000000);

┌────────────────────┬───────────────┐
│     sum_double     │  sum_decimal  │
├────────────────────┼───────────────┤
│ 100000.00000000087 │     100000.00 │
└────────────────────┴───────────────┘

In Snowflake, the same principle applies to FLOAT versus NUMBER(38,2). Exact output digits may differ, because the order of floating-point additions in a parallel engine isn't fixed. That's a second reason not to use floats for anything that must reconcile.

docs.title: Constraints: declared, not enforced
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.customers (
    customer_id NUMBER(38,0) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
    email       VARCHAR NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    country     VARCHAR(2),
    created_at  TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()::TIMESTAMP_NTZ
);

On standard Snowflake tables, only NOT NULL is enforced. PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE and FOREIGN KEY are accepted and recorded as metadata, and BI tools and the optimizer can read them, but inserting two rows with the same customer_id succeeds. (Hybrid tables do enforce them. They're a separate, row-oriented table type not covered here.) Two consequences:

  • Deduplication is your job. Load pipelines must use MERGE or QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() = 1 (lesson 06), not rely on the table to reject duplicates.
  • Declaring constraints is still worthwhile. It documents intent, and some tools use it for joins and lineage. Add RELY only if you guarantee the data really satisfies them, because it lets the optimizer trust them (for example, to eliminate unnecessary joins).

docs.title: Sequences and identity columns
docs.text:
CREATE SEQUENCE learn_db.raw.order_seq START = 1 INCREMENT = 1;

CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.orders (
    order_id    NUMBER(38,0) DEFAULT learn_db.raw.order_seq.NEXTVAL,
    customer_id NUMBER(38,0) NOT NULL,
    amount      NUMBER(12,2) NOT NULL,
    ordered_at  TIMESTAMP_NTZ NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.events (
    event_id NUMBER(38,0) IDENTITY(1,1),
    payload  VARIANT
);

Sequence values are unique and increasing, but not gap-free, and under concurrency they aren't necessarily in commit order. Never use them as a count, or as proof of ordering.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
All of these objects are metadata in the cloud services layer. Creating a database or schema writes catalogue entries and touches no storage. A table is a catalogue entry plus a list of the micro-partition files that hold its data, and that list is what changes on every commit. The differences between permanent, transient and temporary tables are differences in how long retired micro-partitions are kept (Time Travel and Fail-safe) and in who can see the catalogue entry (temporary tables are scoped to a session).

Types matter for storage because data is stored per column, compressed with encodings chosen per micro-partition. Values of an exact NUMBER type are stored as integers scaled by the declared scale, and Snowflake picks a compact physical width for the values actually present, which is why NUMBER(38,0) costs no more than a "smaller" integer type. Strings are stored at their actual length, which is why VARCHAR's declared maximum costs nothing. Constraints other than NOT NULL would require checking every write against existing data across many micro-partitions, which is expensive in a scan-oriented, append-optimized engine. That's why they're informational.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Quoted mixed-case identifiers from tools, forcing quotes forever. Standardize on unquoted names.
  • Trusting PRIMARY KEY to prevent duplicates. It doesn't.
  • Using plain TIMESTAMP in DDL and getting NTZ in one account and LTZ in another. Name the type.
  • Storing local wall-clock times without a zone in TIMESTAMP_NTZ, and then being unable to compare across regions. Store UTC.
  • Permanent tables for disposable data. You pay Fail-safe storage on every rewrite. Use transient tables.
  • FLOAT for money. Use NUMBER(p, s).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create Customers, "Customers" and "customers" in one schema. How many tables exist? Write the SELECT that reads each one.
  2. Insert two rows with the same primary key into learn_db.raw.customers, then write a query that finds all duplicated keys, and a QUALIFY query that keeps only the newest row per key.
  3. Set your session TIMEZONE to America/New_York, insert CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() into columns of each timestamp type, change the session time zone to Asia/Kolkata, and select them again. Which values changed?
  4. Create a transient schema and a table inside it, then check SHOW TABLES for its kind and retention_time.

docs.title: 04 · Virtual Warehouses: Sizing, Suspend & Credits
docs.text: A virtual warehouse is where your money goes. Storage is cheap and cloud services are usually free (lesson 01), but every second a warehouse runs costs credits, whether it's working or idle. Getting warehouses right is mostly about two settings, size and auto-suspend, and one habit: a warehouse per workload.

docs.title: Creating a warehouse
docs.text:
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS learn_wh
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE
  STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 900
  COMMENT = 'Labs for the Snowflake Mastery Path';

The defaults, from Snowflake's CREATE WAREHOUSE and parameter reference, show why it's worth setting these explicitly:

Property Default Why you might change it WAREHOUSE_SIZE XSMALL start small, then size from evidence AUTO_SUSPEND 600 seconds 10 idle minutes are billed after every burst of work AUTO_RESUME TRUE keep it on, so queries start the warehouse INITIALLY_SUSPENDED FALSE otherwise creating the warehouse starts billing immediately STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS 172800 (2 days) a runaway query can run for two days STATEMENT_QUEUED_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS 0 (no timeout) queued queries wait forever MAX_CONCURRENCY_LEVEL 8 how many queries run at once before others queue

A two-day statement timeout on an X-Large warehouse is 768 credits for one forgotten cross join. Set a timeout that matches the workload on every warehouse, or at least on the account and the warehouses users can reach.

docs.title: Sizes and credits
docs.text:
For standard (Gen1) warehouses, from Snowflake's documentation:

Size Credits/hour Size Credits/hour X-Small 1 2X-Large 32 Small 2 3X-Large 64 Medium 4 4X-Large 128 Large 8 5X-Large 256 X-Large 16 6X-Large 512

Each size has twice the compute of the one below and costs twice as much per hour. Billing is per second, with a 60-second minimum each time the warehouse starts (resumes).

Gen2 standard warehouses run on newer hardware, consume more credits per hour than Gen1 (third-party guides cite about 1.35× on AWS and 1.25× on Azure; the authoritative rates are in Snowflake's Service Consumption Table), and aim to finish work faster. The Gen1/Gen2 situation is changing. In October 2026 Snowflake's warehouse overview page said Gen2 "isn't the default for new standard warehouses", while the CREATE WAREHOUSE reference lists a GENERATION property defaulting to '2', the Gen2 page says new standard warehouses default to Gen2 unless it isn't available in your region, and the default RESOURCE_CONSTRAINT depends on your region and when your organization was created. After creating a warehouse, check what you actually got:

SHOW WAREHOUSES LIKE 'LEARN_WH';

The output includes the size, state, auto-suspend, and generation or resource constraint columns. Level 4 · 06 compares the generations and the newer warehouse types.

docs.title: Why doubling the size often costs nothing extra
docs.text:
For a query that parallelizes well (a big scan and aggregation), a warehouse twice the size finishes in roughly half the time, at twice the rate, so it costs about the same and you get the answer sooner. That's the most counter-intuitive and useful fact about Snowflake sizing. It breaks down when:

  • the query is small. An X-Small already finishes in a second or two, and a bigger warehouse just costs more for the same 60-second minimum;
  • the work doesn't parallelize (one huge sort, a skewed join key, a single-threaded UDF);
  • the query is waiting on something else, such as a lock, queueing, or a slow external function.

So size per workload, by testing. Run the real job at two sizes and compare elapsed time and credits in the query history (Level 4 · 05). If doubling the size halves the time, keep the bigger one. If it doesn't, go back down.

docs.title: Auto-suspend: the setting that matters most
docs.text:
How long a warehouse keeps running after its last query is pure cost. Here is a model of the billing rules documented above, applied to two workloads (Python, run locally; a model, not measurements from a Snowflake account):

CREDITS_PER_HOUR = {"XSMALL": 1, "SMALL": 2, "MEDIUM": 4, "LARGE": 8, "XLARGE": 16}

def billed_seconds(queries, auto_suspend):
    """queries: list of (start_second, duration_seconds), sorted. Returns (billed_seconds, resumes)."""
    billed, resumes = 0, 0
    run_start = run_end = None          # current running interval of the warehouse
    for start, dur in queries:
        if run_end is not None and start <= run_end + auto_suspend:
            run_end = max(run_end, start + dur)         # still running (or within idle window)
        else:
            if run_start is not None:
                billed += max(60, (run_end + auto_suspend) - run_start)
            run_start, run_end = start, start + dur; resumes += 1
    billed += max(60, (run_end + auto_suspend) - run_start)
    return billed, resumes

dashboard = [(i * 90, 4) for i in range(40)]      # 40 queries of 4 s, one every 90 s
batch = [(i * 300, 300) for i in range(6)]        # 6 queries of 5 min, back to back

for name, wl in (("dashboard: 40 x 4 s queries, one every 90 s", dashboard),
                 ("batch: 6 x 5 min queries back to back", batch)):
    busy = sum(d for _, d in wl)
    print(name, f"(busy time {busy} s)")
    for susp in (60, 300, 600):
        secs, resumes = billed_seconds(wl, susp)
        print(f"   AUTO_SUSPEND={susp:>3}s  billed {secs:>5} s  resumes {resumes:>2}  "
              f"XSMALL {secs/3600*1:.3f} cr   MEDIUM {secs/3600*4:.3f} cr")

dashboard: 40 x 4 s queries, one every 90 s (busy time 160 s)
   AUTO_SUSPEND= 60s  billed  2560 s  resumes 40  XSMALL 0.711 cr   MEDIUM 2.844 cr
   AUTO_SUSPEND=300s  billed  3814 s  resumes  1  XSMALL 1.059 cr   MEDIUM 4.238 cr
   AUTO_SUSPEND=600s  billed  4114 s  resumes  1  XSMALL 1.143 cr   MEDIUM 4.571 cr
batch: 6 x 5 min queries back to back (busy time 1800 s)
   AUTO_SUSPEND= 60s  billed  1860 s  resumes  1  XSMALL 0.517 cr   MEDIUM 2.067 cr
   AUTO_SUSPEND=300s  billed  2100 s  resumes  1  XSMALL 0.583 cr   MEDIUM 2.333 cr
   AUTO_SUSPEND=600s  billed  2400 s  resumes  1  XSMALL 0.667 cr   MEDIUM 2.667 cr

The dashboard did 160 seconds of work and was billed for 2,560 to 4,114 seconds: 16 to 26 times its busy time, depending only on auto-suspend. With the default 600 seconds, it never suspended during the hour. With 60 seconds it suspended after every query and paid the 60-second minimum 40 times, which was still the cheapest option here.

The trade-off the model doesn't show is the cache. A suspended warehouse loses its local SSD cache of table data, so the first queries after a resume read everything from object storage again (Level 2 · 04). For dashboards hitting the same tables, a few minutes of auto-suspend can pay for itself in speed. For ad-hoc and batch work, 60 seconds is a good default. Note too that Snowflake checks for idleness periodically, so actual suspension can happen somewhat later than the exact setting.

docs.title: Resizing, suspending, monitoring
docs.text:
ALTER WAREHOUSE learn_wh SET WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM';   -- running queries finish on the old size
ALTER WAREHOUSE learn_wh SUSPEND;
ALTER WAREHOUSE learn_wh RESUME IF SUSPENDED;
ALTER WAREHOUSE learn_wh SET AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 900;

SHOW WAREHOUSES;
SELECT * FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY(DATEADD('day', -7, CURRENT_DATE())));

Resizing takes effect for new queries. Queries already running finish on the existing compute, and queued queries pick up the new size. A larger size is a good tool for one heavy job: resize, run it, resize back.

docs.title: One warehouse per workload
docs.text:
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS etl_wh WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'LARGE'  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS bi_wh  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL'  AUTO_SUSPEND = 300 INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS ds_wh  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;

Separate warehouses give each workload its own performance (the ETL load can't slow the dashboards), its own cost line in the bill, its own timeout and auto-suspend, and its own access control (Level 3 · 01: grant USAGE on bi_wh only to the BI role).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A warehouse is a set of compute nodes that Snowflake provisions from the cloud provider when the warehouse starts or resumes, drawn from pools Snowflake keeps warm, which is why resuming usually takes seconds rather than minutes. Each size step doubles the node resources. A query's plan is split into parallel work over the micro-partitions it must scan, so more nodes means more partitions processed at once, which is the source of "twice the size, half the time" for scan-heavy queries.

Each node has local SSD used as a cache of recently read micro-partition data (the "warehouse cache"). It survives between queries while the warehouse runs and is lost when it suspends. Up to MAX_CONCURRENCY_LEVEL queries share the nodes at once. When the warehouse is saturated, new queries queue, and how long they wait is reported separately in the query history, which is the signal for multi-cluster scaling (Level 4 · 06). Billing meters the time nodes are allocated to your warehouse, per second after the first minute, regardless of how busy they are.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Leaving AUTO_SUSPEND at the default 600 seconds for bursty workloads. The idle tail can cost more than the work.
  • No statement timeout. The default lets a query run for two days.
  • Sizing up "to be safe". Measure instead. Small queries gain nothing from a bigger warehouse.
  • Never sizing up for heavy jobs, out of fear of the rate, when twice the size can cost the same and finish twice as fast.
  • One shared warehouse for ETL, BI and ad-hoc work. That means contention and no cost attribution.
  • Creating warehouses without INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE, which starts billing at creation.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Extend the billing model with a "resume cost" assumption: the first query after each resume takes 3 seconds longer (cold cache). Does AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 still win for the dashboard workload? At what gap between queries does a longer auto-suspend become cheaper?
  2. In a trial account, run the same heavy aggregation over SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF100.LINEITEM on X-Small, Small and Medium (disable the result cache with ALTER SESSION SET USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE). Record elapsed time and compute credits for each from the query history. Does doubling the size halve the time?
  3. Create etl_wh, bi_wh and ds_wh as above with appropriate timeouts, and write the SHOW WAREHOUSES query (with RESULT_SCAN) that lists each warehouse's size, auto-suspend and state.
  4. Check your trial account's warehouses for the generation they were created with, and find the current Gen2 credit multiplier for your cloud in Snowflake's Service Consumption Table.

docs.title: 05 · Loading Data: Stages, File Formats & COPY INTO
docs.text: Almost all data enters Snowflake the same way: files land in a stage (a location in cloud storage), and COPY INTO reads them into a table in parallel. Row-by-row INSERTs from an application are the slow, expensive exception. This lesson loads a synthetic sales dataset with three planted errors, and shows how to find them before they reach your table.

docs.title: The dataset
docs.text:
The course uses one generated dataset throughout Level 1. Run the generator yourself and you'll get the same files, because it's seeded:

"""Generate the course's synthetic sales dataset: orders (CSV, gzip, 4 files) and customers (JSON lines)."""
import csv, gzip, json, random, datetime as dt
random.seed(2026)
COUNTRIES = ["PT", "ES", "FR", "DE", "IN", "US", "BR", "GB"]
customers = []
for cid in range(1, 5001):
    customers.append({"customer_id": cid, "name": f"Customer {cid}", "country": random.choice(COUNTRIES),
                      "signup": (dt.date(2024, 1, 1) + dt.timedelta(days=random.randrange(700))).isoformat(),
                      "contact": {"email": f"c{cid}@example.com", "phone": None if cid % 7 == 0 else f"+1-555-{cid:04d}"},
                      "tags": random.sample(["vip", "newsletter", "b2b", "mobile", "returning"], k=random.randint(0, 3))})
with open("customers.json", "w") as f:
    for c in customers: f.write(json.dumps(c) + "\n")
start = dt.datetime(2026, 1, 1)
rows = []
for oid in range(1, 200_001):
    ts = start + dt.timedelta(seconds=random.randrange(270 * 86400))
    qty = random.choice([1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 5])
    price = round(random.uniform(3, 250), 2)
    rows.append([oid, random.randint(1, 5000), ts.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), random.choice(["web", "store", "app"]),
                 f"SKU-{random.randint(1, 800):04d}", qty, f"{price:.2f}", random.choice(["paid", "paid", "paid", "refunded", "cancelled"])])
rows.sort(key=lambda r: r[2])
# three deliberately broken rows
rows[1000][5] = "two"                         # non-numeric quantity
rows[50000][2] = "2026-02-30 10:00:00"        # impossible date
rows[150000] = rows[150000][:6]               # missing columns
header = ["order_id", "customer_id", "ordered_at", "channel", "sku", "quantity", "unit_price", "status"]
for part in range(4):
    chunk = rows[part * 50_000:(part + 1) * 50_000]
    with gzip.open(f"orders_part{part}.csv.gz", "wt", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f); w.writerow(header); w.writerows(chunk)
print("written")

866022 orders_part0.csv.gz
866020 orders_part1.csv.gz
865836 orders_part2.csv.gz
866416 orders_part3.csv.gz
894302 customers.json

order_id,customer_id,ordered_at,channel,sku,quantity,unit_price,status
107572,573,2026-01-01 00:02:42,app,SKU-0492,1,167.53,paid
42731,4234,2026-01-01 00:05:22,store,SKU-0746,1,170.83,cancelled

Four gzip files of about 0.87 MB each (3.06 MB uncompressed) hold 200,000 orders. Three rows are broken on purpose: a quantity of two, the date 2026-02-30, and a row missing its last two columns.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
A stage is where files wait to be loaded:

Stage Reference Use User stage @~ your own scratch files Table stage @%orders files for one table only Named internal stage @learn_db.raw.landing files uploaded from clients, managed by Snowflake Named external stage @learn_db.raw.s3_landing files in your own S3/GCS/Azure bucket 
CREATE STAGE IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.landing
  DIRECTORY = (ENABLE = TRUE)
  COMMENT = 'Files uploaded with PUT for the Level 1 labs';

For external stages, use a storage integration (an account-level object that holds a cloud IAM role Snowflake assumes), never credentials pasted into the stage:

CREATE STORAGE INTEGRATION s3_landing_int
  TYPE = EXTERNAL_STAGE
  STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
  ENABLED = TRUE
  STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-landing'
  STORAGE_ALLOWED_LOCATIONS = ('s3://my-company-landing/orders/');

CREATE STAGE learn_db.raw.s3_landing
  URL = 's3://my-company-landing/orders/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_landing_int;

(Creating the integration then requires adding Snowflake's IAM user to the role's trust policy on the AWS side. DESC INTEGRATION s3_landing_int shows the values to use.)

docs.title: File formats
docs.text:
A file format describes how to parse files, and defining it once as an object keeps every load consistent:

CREATE FILE FORMAT IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.csv_gz
  TYPE = CSV
  COMPRESSION = GZIP
  SKIP_HEADER = 1
  FIELD_DELIMITER = ','
  FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"'
  NULL_IF = ('', 'NULL')
  EMPTY_FIELD_AS_NULL = TRUE
  ERROR_ON_COLUMN_COUNT_MISMATCH = TRUE;

CREATE FILE FORMAT IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.json_lines
  TYPE = JSON
  STRIP_OUTER_ARRAY = FALSE;

docs.title: Uploading with PUT
docs.text:
PUT uploads local files to an internal stage. It runs from a client (Snowflake CLI, a driver), not from a Snowsight worksheet:

snow stage copy "./orders_part*.csv.gz" @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/ -c trial
snow sql -c trial -q "LIST @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/"

snow stage copy --help notes that a local glob pattern "has to be enclosed in quotes", hence the quotes. The equivalent SQL from a driver is PUT file://./orders_part*.csv.gz @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/ AUTO_COMPRESS = FALSE. The files are already gzipped, and AUTO_COMPRESS = FALSE stops the client from compressing them again.

docs.title: Validate before you load
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.orders (
    order_id     NUMBER(38,0),
    customer_id  NUMBER(38,0),
    ordered_at   TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
    channel      VARCHAR,
    sku          VARCHAR,
    quantity     NUMBER(10,0),
    unit_price   NUMBER(10,2),
    status       VARCHAR
);

COPY INTO learn_db.raw.orders
  FROM @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/
  FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.csv_gz')
  VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ALL_ERRORS;

VALIDATION_MODE parses the files and returns the errors without loading anything. Each error row names the file, line, column and the problem. For this dataset, you should see exactly the three planted problems: a numeric conversion failure for two, a timestamp conversion failure for 2026-02-30, and a column-count mismatch. (RETURN_ERRORS returns errors only from the first file that has any. RETURN_ALL_ERRORS also includes files partially loaded by an earlier ON_ERROR = CONTINUE run.)

You can check what to expect without a Snowflake account. Here's DuckDB 1.5.6 locally (not Snowflake), with its reject table, typing the same columns:

-- DuckDB 1.5.6 (local), not Snowflake
CREATE TABLE orders AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('orders_part*.csv.gz', header=true, store_rejects=true,
  columns={'order_id':'BIGINT','customer_id':'BIGINT','ordered_at':'TIMESTAMP','channel':'VARCHAR','sku':'VARCHAR',
           'quantity':'INTEGER','unit_price':'DECIMAL(10,2)','status':'VARCHAR'});
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_loaded FROM orders;
SELECT DISTINCT line, column_name, error_type, left(csv_line, 58) AS csv_line FROM reject_errors ORDER BY csv_line;

rows_loaded: 199997

│   1002 │ quantity    │ CAST            │ 36809,2098,2026-01-02 10:09:16,app,SKU-0500,two,64.20,pai │
│      2 │ status      │ MISSING COLUMNS │ 119204,411,2026-07-21 23:35:33,web,SKU-0362,3             │
│      2 │ unit_price  │ MISSING COLUMNS │ 119204,411,2026-07-21 23:35:33,web,SKU-0362,3             │
│      2 │ ordered_at  │ CAST            │ 58910,3983,2026-02-30 10:00:00,store,SKU-0256,1,76.57,canc│

(Trimmed from DuckDB's box output.) Three bad rows, 199,997 good ones. One DuckDB detail is worth knowing for testing this way: an earlier attempt that only ran SELECT COUNT(*) over the files reported 199,999 rows. The engine skipped converting columns it didn't need, so the two conversion errors were never hit. Validate by loading the typed columns.

docs.title: Load with an error policy
docs.text:
COPY INTO learn_db.raw.orders
  FROM @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/
  FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.csv_gz')
  ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';

ON_ERROR decides what bad rows do:

Value Effect ABORT_STATEMENT default for COPY: the first error stops the load and nothing is loaded CONTINUE load good rows, skip bad ones (reports one error per file in the result) SKIP_FILE skip any file containing an error (default for Snowpipe) SKIP_FILE_10, 'SKIP_FILE_10%' skip a file once its errors reach a count or exceed a percentage

With the default, this dataset loads nothing: the first planted error aborts the statement. With CONTINUE you'd expect 199,997 rows loaded, with ROWS_PARSED exceeding ROWS_LOADED by the bad rows in the affected files. That expectation comes from the data, as validated above. It's not output from a Snowflake run. COPY returns one result row per file (status, rows parsed, rows loaded, first error), and the VALIDATE table function retrieves all errors from a previous COPY by its query ID:

SELECT * FROM TABLE(VALIDATE(learn_db.raw.orders, JOB_ID => '_last'));

SKIP_FILE is the safer choice when a file is a unit of meaning (one day's export): either all of it loads or none. The docs warn that SKIP_FILE buffers each whole file and is slower than CONTINUE or ABORT_STATEMENT.

docs.title: Running the same COPY twice
docs.text:
COPY INTO learn_db.raw.orders FROM @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/
  FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.csv_gz') ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';

The second run loads nothing, because every file is skipped as already loaded. COPY keeps load metadata per table, recording which files (by name and checksum) it has loaded, and skips them. That metadata expires after 64 days. After that, a file whose load status is unknown is skipped by default, unless you set LOAD_UNCERTAIN_FILES = TRUE. FORCE = TRUE reloads everything and duplicates rows. Use it only after truncating.

docs.title: Transforming during load, and loading by column name
docs.text:
COPY can select, reorder and cast columns from the staged files:

COPY INTO learn_db.raw.orders (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status)
FROM (
    SELECT $1::NUMBER, $2::NUMBER, TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP_NTZ($3), LOWER($4), $5,
           TRY_TO_NUMBER($6), $7::NUMBER(10,2), $8
    FROM @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/
)
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.csv_gz');

TRY_TO_* functions return NULL instead of failing, so two and 2026-02-30 become NULLs you can find later rather than errors. That's useful, and dangerous if nobody looks. For Parquet, Avro and ORC, MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE maps file columns to table columns by name, and INFER_SCHEMA can generate the table definition:

CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.events
  USING TEMPLATE (
    SELECT ARRAY_AGG(OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*))
    FROM TABLE(INFER_SCHEMA(LOCATION => '@learn_db.raw.landing/events/', FILE_FORMAT => 'learn_db.raw.parquet_fmt'))
  );

docs.title: Sizing files
docs.text: Snowflake recommends files of roughly 100–250 MB compressed (or larger) for bulk loading. Files are the unit of parallelism: one file is processed by one thread, so one huge file can't use the whole warehouse, and millions of tiny files spend more time on per-file overhead than on data. The 0.87 MB files here are far below that, which is fine for a lab but would waste credits at scale. Batch small outputs before loading.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
COPY INTO runs on your warehouse. Snowflake lists the files in the stage path, filters out those recorded in the table's load metadata, and distributes the remaining files across the warehouse's threads. Each thread decompresses and parses its file, applies the file format and any transformation, and writes rows into new micro-partitions. The whole COPY is one transaction. Under ABORT_STATEMENT an error means no micro-partitions are committed. Under CONTINUE, the good rows from all files are committed together. Afterwards, the load metadata records each file's name, size, checksum and status, which is how a repeated COPY knows to skip them, and why that protection only lasts as long as the metadata (64 days).

PUT never touches a warehouse. The client encrypts (and optionally compresses) the files and uploads them straight to the stage's cloud storage. An external stage with a storage integration means Snowflake reads your bucket by assuming the IAM role you granted it, so no keys are stored in Snowflake.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Relying on the default ABORT_STATEMENT in a pipeline and discovering a single bad row has blocked a whole day's load. Choose ON_ERROR deliberately and monitor errors.
  • ON_ERROR = CONTINUE without monitoring the difference between rows parsed and loaded.
  • TRY_TO_* conversions that silently turn bad data into NULLs. Count them after loading.
  • FORCE = TRUE to "fix" a load, which duplicates every previously loaded row.
  • Credentials in stage definitions. Use storage integrations.
  • Thousands of tiny files, or one 20 GB file. Aim for 100–250 MB compressed.
  • Testing a load with COUNT(*) only. As DuckDB showed, unused columns may never be converted. Validate typed loads.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Generate the dataset, upload it to an internal stage, and run COPY … VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ALL_ERRORS. Compare the three errors Snowflake reports with the DuckDB result above.
  2. Load with ON_ERROR = 'SKIP_FILE' and record which file(s) were skipped and how many rows that cost. Then reload the skipped files with ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE', using the FILES = (...) option to target them.
  3. Load the same files with the TRY_TO_* transformation, then write a query that finds every row where a conversion produced NULL.
  4. Load customers.json into a table with a single VARIANT column (lesson 07 queries it).

docs.title: 06 · Snowflake SQL: Windows, QUALIFY & Extensions
docs.text:
Snowflake speaks standard ANSI SQL with a set of extensions that make analytical queries shorter and clearer. This lesson covers the ones you'll use weekly, on the orders and customers loaded in lesson 05. It assumes you know joins and GROUP BY. The SQL Mastery Path covers those.

Where the results come from

The statements below are Snowflake SQL. Their results were produced by running the same queries on the same generated data in DuckDB 1.5.6 on a laptop, because DuckDB implements these extensions (QUALIFY, GROUP BY ALL, EXCLUDE, PIVOT, ASOF JOIN) with the same semantics. The numbers are what Snowflake should return for this dataset. Formatting, column types and the naming of PIVOT columns differ. Where the dialects differ, the lesson says so.

docs.title: QUALIFY: filter on a window function
docs.text:
The classic "latest row per key" query normally needs a subquery. QUALIFY filters on window functions directly, the way HAVING filters on aggregates:

SELECT customer_id, order_id, ordered_at, unit_price * quantity AS amount
FROM learn_db.raw.orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at DESC) = 1
ORDER BY customer_id
LIMIT 3;

customer_id | order_id | ordered_at          | amount
          1 |    79422 | 2026-09-10 05:34:43 | 428.58
          2 |   171272 | 2026-08-19 08:41:43 | 634.02
          3 |   194457 | 2026-09-25 21:42:12 | 847.80

The evaluation order is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window functions → QUALIFY → ORDER BY → LIMIT. This is the standard way to deduplicate in Snowflake, which matters because primary keys aren't enforced (lesson 03):

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE learn_db.raw.orders_dedup AS
SELECT *
FROM learn_db.raw.orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY ordered_at DESC) = 1;

docs.title: Ranking, with ties
docs.text:
"Top 3 SKUs by units per channel":

SELECT channel, sku, SUM(quantity) AS units,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY channel ORDER BY SUM(quantity) DESC) AS rnk
FROM learn_db.raw.orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY channel, sku
QUALIFY rnk <= 3
ORDER BY channel, rnk;

channel | sku      | units | rnk
app     | SKU-0699 |   183 |   1
app     | SKU-0411 |   172 |   2
app     | SKU-0491 |   170 |   3
store   | SKU-0662 |   159 |   1
store   | SKU-0349 |   155 |   2
store   | SKU-0663 |   154 |   3
web     | SKU-0697 |   162 |   1
web     | SKU-0630 |   161 |   2
web     | SKU-0635 |   161 |   2

Look at web: two SKUs tied at 161 units, both are rank 2, and there's no rank 3. RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK doesn't, and ROW_NUMBER breaks ties arbitrarily (add tie-breaker columns to its ORDER BY if the result must be stable). The window function can rank an aggregate (SUM(quantity)) because windows are evaluated after GROUP BY.

docs.title: Running totals and period comparisons
docs.text:
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at) AS month,
       SUM(unit_price * quantity) AS revenue,
       SUM(SUM(unit_price * quantity)) OVER (ORDER BY DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at)) AS running_revenue,
       LAG(SUM(unit_price * quantity)) OVER (ORDER BY DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at)) AS prev_month
FROM learn_db.raw.orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;

month               | revenue    | running_revenue
2026-01-01 00:00:00 | 3733367.04 |      3733367.04
2026-02-01 00:00:00 | 3447838.33 |      7181205.37
2026-03-01 00:00:00 | 3731570.31 |     10912775.68
2026-04-01 00:00:00 | 3660444.72 |     14573220.40

(First four months shown. The DuckDB run didn't include the LAG column.) A window with ORDER BY and no frame clause uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, i.e. a running total. Write the frame explicitly (ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for a 3-month moving sum) whenever it matters.

docs.title: Shorter queries: GROUP BY ALL, EXCLUDE, RENAME, REPLACE
docs.text:
SELECT channel, status, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(unit_price * quantity) AS revenue
FROM learn_db.raw.orders
GROUP BY ALL
ORDER BY channel, status;

channel | status    | orders | revenue
app     | cancelled |  13458 |  3641501.90
app     | paid      |  40061 | 10892006.16
app     | refunded  |  13269 |  3525570.92
store   | cancelled |  13339 |  3596972.63
store   | paid      |  39918 | 10765993.11
...

GROUP BY ALL groups by every non-aggregate expression in the SELECT list, so you can't forget one. SELECT * gets modifiers to drop, rename or replace columns without listing all the others:

SELECT * EXCLUDE (sku, status) FROM learn_db.raw.orders ORDER BY order_id LIMIT 2;
SELECT * RENAME (ordered_at AS order_ts) FROM learn_db.raw.orders LIMIT 2;
SELECT * REPLACE (ROUND(unit_price, 0) AS unit_price) FROM learn_db.raw.orders LIMIT 2;

order_id | customer_id | ordered_at          | channel | quantity | unit_price
       1 |        1186 | 2026-05-20 21:41:10 | store   |        1 |     165.36
       2 |         953 | 2026-01-15 03:00:49 | store   |        2 |      29.36

(Output of the EXCLUDE query.)

docs.title: PIVOT and UNPIVOT
docs.text:
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT channel, status, quantity FROM learn_db.raw.orders)
PIVOT (SUM(quantity) FOR status IN ('paid', 'refunded', 'cancelled')) AS p (channel, paid, refunded, cancelled)
ORDER BY channel;

channel | paid  | refunded | cancelled
app     | 85856 |    28041 |     28870
store   | 85700 |    28890 |     28475
web     | 85537 |    28721 |     28288

In Snowflake, pivoted columns are named after the values including their quotes ('paid'), which is awkward to reference. The column alias list after AS p (...) gives them clean names. PIVOT … IN (ANY ORDER BY status) pivots on whatever values exist, without listing them. UNPIVOT reverses the operation.

docs.title: Conditional and safe expressions
docs.text:
SELECT order_id,
       IFF(quantity >= 3, 'bulk', 'single')                AS order_kind,
       ZEROIFNULL(quantity) * unit_price                   AS amount,
       TRY_TO_NUMBER('two')                                AS bad_number,     -- NULL, not an error
       TRY_TO_DATE('2026-02-30')                           AS bad_date,       -- NULL
       sku ILIKE 'sku-00%'                                 AS low_sku,
       channel LIKE ANY ('web', 'app')                     AS online,
       DIV0(unit_price, 0)                                 AS safe_div        -- 0 instead of division error
FROM learn_db.raw.orders
LIMIT 5;

The TRY_ family (TRY_TO_NUMBER, TRY_TO_DATE, TRY_CAST, …) is the query-time version of the error handling from lesson 05. ILIKE is case-insensitive LIKE, and LIKE ANY/ILIKE ANY match against several patterns.

docs.title: MERGE: upserts
docs.text:
Loading changed records into a table is a MERGE:

MERGE INTO learn_db.analytics.customers AS t
USING learn_db.raw.customer_updates AS s
  ON t.customer_id = s.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_deleted THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.name = s.name, t.country = s.country, t.updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND NOT s.is_deleted THEN
  INSERT (customer_id, name, country, updated_at) VALUES (s.customer_id, s.name, s.country, s.updated_at);

If the source has two rows for the same key, the result is ambiguous. Snowflake's ERROR_ON_NONDETERMINISTIC_MERGE parameter (on by default) makes such a merge fail instead of updating the row unpredictably. Deduplicate the source with QUALIFY first.

docs.title: ASOF JOIN: "the latest value at that time"
docs.text:
Matching each order to the price in effect when it was placed is an inequality join that's painful in standard SQL. ASOF JOIN does it directly:

SELECT o.order_id, o.ordered_at, o.sku, p.list_price
FROM learn_db.raw.orders o
ASOF JOIN learn_db.raw.price_changes p
  MATCH_CONDITION (o.ordered_at >= p.effective_at)
  ON o.sku = p.sku;

For each order, it picks the price row with the latest effective_at that is not after ordered_at, for the same SKU.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.orders SAMPLE (1);                -- about 1% of rows
SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.orders SAMPLE SYSTEM (1) SEED (7); -- about 1% of micro-partitions, repeatable

Row sampling (BERNOULLI, the default) reads everything and keeps each row with the given probability. SYSTEM (block) sampling picks whole micro-partitions, so it reads less but is clumpier.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
QUALIFY, GROUP BY ALL and the SELECT * modifiers are rewrites done by the compiler in the cloud services layer: QUALIFY becomes a filter applied after the window-function step, GROUP BY ALL expands to the explicit expression list, EXCLUDE expands to the remaining column list. They cost nothing at runtime.

Window functions are executed by partitioning rows by the PARTITION BY key across the warehouse's workers, sorting each partition by the ORDER BY key, then streaming through the sorted rows computing running values. A window over a very skewed key (one customer with half the orders) lands mostly on one worker, which is a common cause of slow window queries (Level 2 · 03). MERGE is a join between target and source, followed by rewriting the micro-partitions that contain matched rows (immutable files again, lesson 01), so it's much cheaper when matched rows are concentrated in few micro-partitions (Level 2 · 01–02).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• ROW_NUMBER without a tie-breaker for deduplication, giving different "latest" rows on different runs.
  • Confusing RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER when there are ties, like the web channel above.
  • Relying on the default window frame. Write ROWS BETWEEN … when you mean a fixed number of rows.
  • MERGE from a source with duplicate keys. Deduplicate first.
  • Pivoted column names with quotes in them. Alias them.
  • TRY_ functions hiding data problems. Count the NULLs they produce.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a query that returns, for each customer, their first and latest paid order and the number of days between them, in one pass with window functions.
  2. Compute a 7-day moving average of daily paid revenue using an explicit ROWS frame. Then explain how the result would differ with RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '6 days' PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW if some days had no orders.
  3. Create a customer_updates table with an update, a new customer, a deletion, and two updates for one customer, and run the MERGE above. What happens? Fix it with QUALIFY.
  4. Build a small price_changes table (three SKUs, a few price changes each) and use ASOF JOIN to compute revenue at list price. Check three orders by hand.

docs.title: 07 · Semi-Structured Data: VARIANT & FLATTEN
docs.text: Snowflake stores JSON (and Avro, Parquet, ORC and XML) in a column of type VARIANT and lets you query it with path expressions, without defining a schema first. That makes it easy to land raw API responses and event payloads and model them later. It also hides a few traps. An INNER-style FLATTEN silently drops rows with empty arrays, JSON null isn't SQL NULL, and a field with nulls in it is stored less efficiently. Each of these is shown here on the customers.json file from lesson 05.

docs.title: Loading JSON into a VARIANT
docs.text:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.customers_json (
    v          VARIANT,
    file_name  VARCHAR,
    loaded_at  TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()::TIMESTAMP_NTZ
);

COPY INTO learn_db.raw.customers_json (v, file_name)
FROM (SELECT $1, METADATA$FILENAME FROM @learn_db.raw.landing/customers/)
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.json_lines');

Each line of the file becomes one row with the whole object in v. METADATA$FILENAME records which file each row came from, which is invaluable when you trace a bad record later. A record looks like this:

{"customer_id": 1, "name": "Customer 1", "country": "ES", "signup": "2024-11-23",
 "contact": {"email": "c1@example.com", "phone": "+1-555-0001"}, "tags": []}

docs.title: Paths and casts
docs.text:
SELECT v:customer_id::NUMBER          AS customer_id,
       v:name::VARCHAR                AS name,
       v:contact.email::VARCHAR       AS email,
       v:contact.phone::VARCHAR       AS phone,
       v['country']::VARCHAR          AS country,
       v:tags[0]::VARCHAR             AS first_tag,
       TO_DATE(v:signup::VARCHAR)     AS signup_date
FROM learn_db.raw.customers_json
LIMIT 5;
  • : steps into the top level, and . steps further (v:contact.email). Bracket notation (v['country']) handles keys with spaces or special characters.
  • Field names are case-sensitive: v:Name and v:name are different paths.
  • Without ::type, a path returns a VARIANT, displayed with JSON quotes ("Customer 1"). Always cast to the type you mean, both for display and for correct comparisons and joins.
  • A path that doesn't exist returns NULL, not an error. That's convenient, and it means typos produce silent NULLs.

docs.title: SQL NULL vs JSON null
docs.text:
The file has two kinds of "no phone number": a key whose value is null (every 7th customer, 714 of them) and, in other datasets, a key that's missing entirely. Snowflake's documentation distinguishes:

  • SQL NULL: the value is missing (also what a non-existent path returns).
  • JSON null ("VARIANT NULL"): a JSON null value, stored as a VARIANT holding null.
SELECT COUNT(*)                                    AS customers,
       COUNT_IF(v:contact.phone IS NULL)           AS sql_null_phone,      -- JSON nulls are NOT SQL NULL
       COUNT_IF(IS_NULL_VALUE(v:contact.phone))    AS json_null_phone,
       COUNT_IF(v:contact.phone::VARCHAR IS NULL)  AS null_after_cast
FROM learn_db.raw.customers_json;

For this file you'd expect sql_null_phone = 0 (every record has the key), json_null_phone = 714, and null_after_cast = 714, because casting a JSON null to a string produces SQL NULL. Those expected values come from the file contents (714 records with "phone": null), not from a Snowflake run. If JSON nulls mean nothing special in your data, the file format option STRIP_NULL_VALUES = TRUE removes them at load time, and that also helps storage, as explained below.

docs.title: FLATTEN: arrays into rows
docs.text:
tags is an array. To count customers per tag, turn each array element into a row with LATERAL FLATTEN:

SELECT t.value::VARCHAR AS tag, COUNT(*) AS customers
FROM learn_db.raw.customers_json c,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => c.v:tags) t
GROUP BY tag
ORDER BY customers DESC;

FLATTEN returns the columns SEQ, KEY, PATH, INDEX, VALUE and THIS. VALUE is the element, INDEX its position. Run on the same file in DuckDB (with UNNEST, DuckDB's equivalent; not Snowflake):

tag        | customers
vip        |      1524
returning  |      1523
b2b        |      1500
newsletter |      1494
mobile     |      1464

Now count customers after flattening:

rows_after_inner_unnest | customers_kept
                   7505 |           3737

There are 5,000 customers, but only 3,737 survive the flatten: the 1,263 customers with an empty tags array vanished, because an element-less array produces no rows, exactly like an inner join. Snowflake's FLATTEN behaves the same way by default. To keep them, use OUTER => TRUE, which emits one row with NULLs for empty arrays:
