SELECT c.v:customer_id::NUMBER AS customer_id, t.value::VARCHAR AS tag
FROM learn_db.raw.customers_json c,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => c.v:tags, OUTER => TRUE) t;

This is the most common silent-data-loss bug in semi-structured pipelines. A report built on the inner flatten undercounts customers by 25% and nothing errors.

FLATTEN also walks objects (KEY holds the field name) and, with RECURSIVE => TRUE, entire nested structures. That helps you discover what fields a messy payload actually contains:

SELECT DISTINCT f.path, TYPEOF(f.value) AS type
FROM learn_db.raw.customers_json c,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => c.v, RECURSIVE => TRUE) f
ORDER BY f.path;

docs.title: Building JSON
docs.text:
SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT('id', o.customer_id, 'country', c.v:country::VARCHAR) AS obj,
       ARRAY_AGG(o.order_id) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY o.order_id)        AS order_ids
FROM learn_db.raw.orders o
JOIN learn_db.raw.customers_json c ON c.v:customer_id::NUMBER = o.customer_id
GROUP BY o.customer_id, c.v:country::VARCHAR;

OBJECT_CONSTRUCT drops keys whose values are SQL NULL. OBJECT_CONSTRUCT_KEEP_NULL keeps them as JSON nulls. PARSE_JSON turns a string into a VARIANT, and TO_JSON does the reverse.

docs.title: From raw to modelled
docs.text:
The usual pattern is to land raw JSON in a VARIANT column, then expose a typed view (or table) for everyone else:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW learn_db.analytics.customers AS
SELECT v:customer_id::NUMBER       AS customer_id,
       v:name::VARCHAR             AS name,
       v:country::VARCHAR          AS country,
       TO_DATE(v:signup::VARCHAR)  AS signup_date,
       v:contact.email::VARCHAR    AS email,
       v:contact.phone::VARCHAR    AS phone,
       v:tags                      AS tags,
       file_name, loaded_at
FROM learn_db.raw.customers_json;

New fields in the payload don't break the load, and the view decides what's exposed and how it's typed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A VARIANT isn't stored as a text blob. When you load semi-structured data, Snowflake inspects the elements and extracts frequently occurring, consistently typed fields into their own hidden columns inside each micro-partition, stored and compressed like ordinary columns, with min/max metadata for pruning. The rest is kept in a single parsed binary structure. Querying v:country on a well-behaved payload therefore reads only the extracted country subcolumn, nearly as cheaply as a real column.

Snowflake's documentation lists the conditions that prevent extraction. One is that an element containing even a single JSON null isn't extracted. So contact.phone in this dataset, with 714 nulls, would stay inside the generic structure, and a filter on it can't use subcolumn statistics. Elements with mixed types (sometimes a string, sometimes a number) are also not extracted, and by default extraction is limited to 200 elements per partition per table. That's the technical reason behind the advice to strip nulls and keep types consistent, and to promote fields you filter on often into real columns.

FLATTEN is a table function applied once per input row (that's what LATERAL expresses): it returns zero or more rows per input, and the outer query joins each input row to its output rows. Zero output rows for an empty array means the input row disappears, unless OUTER => TRUE asks for a placeholder row.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting OUTER => TRUE, which dropped 1,263 of 5,000 customers here.
  • Comparing uncast VARIANTs (v:country = 'PT' works by coercion, but joins and GROUP BY on uncast values behave unexpectedly). Cast with ::.
  • Treating JSON null as SQL NULL. IS NULL is false for it. Use IS_NULL_VALUE, cast first, or strip nulls at load time.
  • Case mistakes in paths. v:Country silently returns NULL.
  • Leaving hot filter fields inside VARIANT with nulls or mixed types, which blocks subcolumn extraction and pruning.
  • Exposing raw VARIANT to analysts. Publish a typed view.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Load customers.json and run the null-counting query. Do your three counts match the expected 0 / 714 / 714? Reload with STRIP_NULL_VALUES = TRUE and run it again.
  2. Run the tag count with and without OUTER => TRUE, then write a query that counts customers per tag including a '(none)' bucket for customers without tags.
  3. Use the recursive FLATTEN query to list every path in the payload and its types. Add a record where customer_id is a string ("42") and run it again.
  4. Create the analytics.customers view and join it to raw.orders to find paid revenue per country.

docs.title: 08 · Time Travel, UNDROP & Fail-safe
docs.text: Because Snowflake never modifies micro-partitions in place (lesson 01), the previous versions of your data still exist for a while after every UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE or DROP. Time Travel lets you query and restore those versions yourself. Fail-safe keeps them for a further 7 days, recoverable only by Snowflake Support. Both are excellent insurance, and both have a storage cost that's easy to multiply without noticing.

docs.title: Querying the past
docs.text:
-- the table as it was 5 minutes ago
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM learn_db.raw.orders AT(OFFSET => -60*5);

-- as of a specific time
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM learn_db.raw.orders AT(TIMESTAMP => '2026-10-13 09:00:00'::TIMESTAMP_LTZ);

-- just before a particular statement ran (use its query ID from the history)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM learn_db.raw.orders BEFORE(STATEMENT => '01b2c3d4-0000-1234-0000-000000000abc');
  • OFFSET is in seconds relative to now, so negative means "ago".
  • TIMESTAMP is a point in time. Cast it explicitly (TIMESTAMP_LTZ), or the session's time zone and the default timestamp mapping can shift it by hours.
  • BEFORE(STATEMENT => …) is the precise tool after an accident: "the table just before that DELETE".

A request beyond the retention period fails with an error rather than returning partial data.

docs.title: Recovering from mistakes
docs.text:
Here's a realistic accident: a DELETE with the wrong condition. First, find the statement:

DELETE FROM learn_db.raw.orders WHERE status = 'paid';     -- meant: status = 'cancelled'

SELECT query_id, query_text, start_time
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.QUERY_HISTORY())
WHERE query_text ILIKE 'DELETE FROM learn_db.raw.orders%'
ORDER BY start_time DESC
LIMIT 1;

Then put the deleted rows back, without touching anything changed since:

INSERT INTO learn_db.raw.orders
SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.orders BEFORE(STATEMENT => '<query_id of the DELETE>')
WHERE status = 'paid';

Or restore the whole table to that point by cloning it, and swap it in:

CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.orders_restored CLONE learn_db.raw.orders
  BEFORE(STATEMENT => '<query_id of the DELETE>');
ALTER TABLE learn_db.raw.orders SWAP WITH learn_db.raw.orders_restored;

SWAP WITH exchanges the two tables in one metadata operation, so readers never see a missing table.

docs.title: UNDROP
docs.text:
DROP TABLE learn_db.raw.orders;
UNDROP TABLE learn_db.raw.orders;

SHOW TABLES HISTORY LIKE 'ORDERS' IN SCHEMA learn_db.raw;   -- includes dropped versions and when

UNDROP works for tables, schemas and databases (and, per the docs, several other object types, such as dynamic tables and Iceberg tables) within the retention period. It fails if an object with the same name already exists, so rename the new one first. That's common when someone dropped a table and then recreated it empty. Dropping a schema or database and UNDROPping it restores everything inside.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
Standard Edition Enterprise and higher Default retention 1 day 1 day Maximum, permanent objects 1 day 90 days Transient and temporary objects 0 or 1 day 0 or 1 day Fail-safe after retention 7 days (permanent only) 7 days (permanent only) 
ALTER TABLE learn_db.raw.orders SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 30;   -- Enterprise+
ALTER DATABASE learn_db SET DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 7;             -- inherited by new children
SHOW TABLES LIKE 'ORDERS' IN SCHEMA learn_db.raw;                        -- retention_time column

Retention is set at the account, database, schema or table level, and child objects inherit unless they set their own. An account administrator can also set MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS, which puts a floor under everything: the effective retention is the larger of the two. That's a good guardrail against someone setting 0 on a production table.

docs.title: Fail-safe is not a backup you control
docs.text: After Time Travel retention ends, data from permanent tables moves into Fail-safe for 7 days. You can't query it, clone it or restore it yourself. Only Snowflake Support can attempt recovery, as a best-effort service for disasters. Transient and temporary tables have no Fail-safe. Plan your recovery on Time Travel (and replication, Level 4 · 07), and think of Fail-safe as a last resort you hope never to need, but still pay storage for.

docs.title: The storage cost of history
docs.text:
Time Travel and Fail-safe store retired micro-partitions, and you pay for them like active data. A table that's rewritten often retires a lot. This model computes what a 100 GB table holds if it's fully rewritten once a day (for example CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE … AS SELECT or INSERT OVERWRITE in a nightly job). It's Python run locally, following the documented retention rules, not a measurement:

SIZE_GB = 100          # compressed size of the table
def held(retention_days, failsafe_days):
    # each daily rewrite retires one full copy; copies live retention + failsafe days after being retired
    return SIZE_GB * (1 + retention_days + failsafe_days)

table kind                             retention fail-safe  GB held x active
permanent, Standard default                    1         7      900        9
permanent, 30-day retention                   30         7     3800       38
permanent, 90-day retention                   90         7     9800       98
transient, 1-day retention                     1         0      200        2
transient, 0-day retention                     0         0      100        1

A permanent table rewritten daily holds 9× its size even at the default 1-day retention, because of Fail-safe. Set 90-day retention "to be safe" on it, and it holds 98×. The same table as transient holds 2× or 1×. Real tables usually change only part of their micro-partitions per day, so the multiplier is lower, but the shape is right. For tables you can rebuild from their sources, such as staging tables, intermediate ETL tables and anything recreated nightly, use transient tables and short retention, and keep long retention for the tables that are the system of record.

You can see where storage goes:

SELECT table_catalog, table_schema, table_name,
       active_bytes / POWER(1024, 3)      AS active_gb,
       time_travel_bytes / POWER(1024, 3) AS time_travel_gb,
       failsafe_bytes / POWER(1024, 3)    AS failsafe_gb
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS
WHERE deleted IS NULL OR deleted = FALSE
ORDER BY time_travel_bytes + failsafe_bytes DESC
LIMIT 20;

(ACCOUNT_USAGE views lag real time, by minutes to a few hours depending on the view. Level 3 · 09 covers them.)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every committed change produces a new table version: a new list of micro-partition files, recorded in the metadata with a timestamp. Files that a new version no longer references aren't deleted. They're marked as retired at that time. A Time Travel query (AT, BEFORE) simply asks the metadata for the file list that was current at the requested moment and scans those files, so querying the past costs the same as querying the present, plus any storage that was kept. UNDROP restores the dropped object's metadata entry, and its files are still there.

When a retired file's age exceeds the retention period, it moves out of the Time Travel window into Fail-safe, where it's still stored, but no longer reachable through SQL. After 7 more days it's permanently deleted. TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS reports bytes in each of the three states. A clone (lesson 09) adds a twist: a retired file still referenced by another table's current version isn't "history" for that table, so the accounting follows the file's owner.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Long retention on frequently rewritten tables. It multiplies storage, as the model shows.
  • Permanent tables for staging and scratch data. You pay 7 days of Fail-safe on every rewrite.
  • Relying on Fail-safe as a backup. You can't access it yourself.
  • Time Travel with an ambiguous timestamp literal. Cast to TIMESTAMP_LTZ or use OFFSET/STATEMENT.
  • UNDROP after recreating the table under the same name. Rename the new one first.
  • Retention 0 on important tables "to save money". Use MIN_DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS as a guardrail.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Delete all paid orders, then restore exactly those rows with BEFORE(STATEMENT => …), and check that the row count matches the original.
  2. Drop the orders table, create a new empty orders, then get the original back with UNDROP (rename the empty one first). Use SHOW TABLES HISTORY to see both.
  3. Extend the storage model so that only 10% of the table's micro-partitions change per day. What does a permanent table with 30-day retention hold now?
  4. Run the TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS query in a trial account after a few days of exercises and find the table with the largest Time Travel bytes. Should it be transient?

docs.title: 09 · Zero-Copy Cloning & Environments
docs.text: CREATE … CLONE makes a full, independent, writable copy of a table, schema or entire database in seconds, regardless of size, without copying any data. It's one of the features that most changes how teams work: every developer can have a copy of production to test against, every CI run can get a fresh database, and every risky migration can be rehearsed on a clone first. This lesson covers how to use it, the rules about what gets cloned, and the case where a clone quietly stops being free.

docs.title: Cloning
docs.text:
-- a table
CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.orders_dev CLONE learn_db.raw.orders;

-- a whole database, for a developer
CREATE DATABASE learn_db_dev_ana CLONE learn_db;

-- a database as it was yesterday at 06:00 (Time Travel + clone)
CREATE DATABASE learn_db_audit CLONE learn_db
  AT(TIMESTAMP => '2026-10-12 06:00:00'::TIMESTAMP_LTZ);

-- keep the grants of the source table (all except OWNERSHIP)
CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.orders_copy CLONE learn_db.raw.orders COPY GRANTS;

The clone is immediately usable and fully independent: changes to it don't affect the source, and changes to the source after the clone don't appear in it. Combining CLONE with AT/BEFORE gives you a point-in-time copy, which is the standard way to rehearse a recovery (lesson 08) or reproduce yesterday's report exactly.

docs.title: What comes along, and what doesn't
docs.text:
From Snowflake's cloning documentation:

Object in a cloned database/schema Behaviour Tables, views, sequences, file formats cloned Grants on child objects cloned; grants on the database/schema container itself are not External named stages cloned (they point at the same bucket) Internal named stages cloned only with INCLUDE INTERNAL STAGES; table stages are cloned empty Pipes pipes on external stages are cloned; pipes on internal stages are not Streams cloned, but unconsumed records in them are inaccessible in the clone Tasks, alerts cloned suspended Tables with automatic clustering clustering is suspended on the clone (ALTER TABLE … RESUME RECLUSTER)

Two of these matter in practice:

  • Tasks start suspended, which is what you want. A cloned dev database must not start running production jobs. But it also means a cloned pipeline doesn't "just run": resume what you need deliberately.
  • External stages and pipes still point at production storage. A cloned pipe on an external stage, if resumed, loads production's files into your dev tables. Review and repoint these before resuming anything.

docs.title: A dev/test workflow
docs.text:
-- every morning (or per pull request), a fresh copy of production for development
CREATE OR REPLACE DATABASE analytics_dev CLONE analytics_prod;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE analytics_dev TO ROLE developer;           -- container grants aren't cloned

-- a migration rehearsal
CREATE OR REPLACE DATABASE analytics_migration_test CLONE analytics_prod;
-- run the migration scripts against analytics_migration_test, then run the tests, then:
DROP DATABASE analytics_migration_test;

Pair it with masking policies (Level 3 · 04) so developers on a clone of production don't see personal data they shouldn't. Policies are attached to columns and travel with the clone.

docs.title: When a clone stops being free
docs.text:
A clone shares the source's micro-partitions. Storage is only consumed for micro-partitions that one side rewrites after the clone. Since micro-partitions are immutable, changing even one row in a micro-partition rewrites the whole micro-partition. So the question is how many micro-partitions a change touches, and that depends on how the changed rows are distributed, not on how many there are.

This model (Python, run locally, not a Snowflake measurement) takes a ~1 TB table of 1,000,000,000 rows in 20,000 micro-partitions of 50,000 rows, and computes how much of it a single UPDATE in the clone rewrites:

P, ROWS_PER_P, GB_PER_P = 20_000, 50_000, 0.05
def partitions_touched(rows_updated, scattered):
    if scattered:      # updated rows spread uniformly at random over the table
        return P * (1 - (1 - 1 / P) ** rows_updated)
    return min(P, -(-rows_updated // ROWS_PER_P))     # updated rows packed together (e.g. one recent date)

  rows updated % of table | clustered: parts      GB | scattered: parts      GB
        10,000     0.001% |                1     0.1 |            7,870   393.5
       100,000     0.010% |                2     0.1 |           19,865   993.3
     1,000,000     0.100% |               20     1.0 |           20,000  1000.0
    10,000,000     1.000% |              200    10.0 |           20,000  1000.0

Updating 0.001% of rows, if they're scattered across the table (say "set is_test = TRUE for these 10,000 customer IDs"), rewrites about 39% of the table. Updating 0.01% rewrites essentially all of it. The clone now owns close to a full copy, and so does the source's Time Travel history. The same 10,000 rows packed together (one day's orders, when the table is ordered by date) touch a single micro-partition.

The same arithmetic governs every UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE in Snowflake, clone or not. It's the cost of the change, the Time Travel storage it generates, and the work automatic clustering has to redo. Level 2 · 01–02 builds on it: keeping related rows together in micro-partitions is what makes both queries and changes cheap.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A table's identity in the metadata is, essentially, a list of micro-partition files. CLONE creates a new metadata entry whose list points at the same files, which is why it takes the same time for 1 KB and 100 TB. From then on the two tables evolve independently. A write to either one creates new files referenced only by that table, and the retired files remain referenced by the other table's current version (and by Time Travel). A file is deleted only when nothing references it anymore. That includes no table version within its retention, and no clone.

That's also why storage accounting can surprise you. If you drop the source table while a clone still uses its files, those files don't disappear. They remain, now billed to the table that still needs them. TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS reports this through its RETAINED_FOR_CLONE_BYTES column.

Cloning a database or schema clones each child object the same way, plus the container metadata. Objects that point outside Snowflake (external stages, pipes on them) are cloned as pointers to the same external resources, which is why they need review.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting container grants. The cloned database has none of the source database's grants.
  • Resuming cloned pipes or tasks without repointing them. Dev loads production files, or dev jobs write somewhere shared.
  • Scattered updates on a clone (anonymizing a column in place, flagging random rows), which turns a free clone into a full copy. Prefer views, or masking policies for anonymization.
  • Keeping old clones forever. As the source changes, the clone holds onto partitions the source has retired. Drop clones you no longer need.
  • Expecting stream contents to carry over. Unconsumed stream records aren't accessible in the clone.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Clone learn_db to learn_db_dev, then compare SHOW GRANTS ON DATABASE for both, and SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE for a table in each.
  2. Create a clone of raw.orders, update 1,000 random rows in it (WHERE UNIFORM(0, 199, RANDOM()) = 0 approximates 0.5%), and check the clone's ACTIVE_BYTES in TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS the next day. With only four small files' worth of data, how many micro-partitions does the table even have? (SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION reports the total.)
  3. Extend the model: the 10,000 scattered rows are updated every day for 30 days in the source table (not a clone), with 30-day Time Travel. How much Time Travel storage results?
  4. Write a script (SQL or Snowflake CLI) that recreates a developer database from production every morning and grants it to the developer role, and run it twice. Does the second run disturb anything?

docs.title: 10 · Project — Load & Analyse a Sales Dataset
docs.text:
This project puts Level 1 together. Starting from an empty account, you'll create a warehouse, a database and schemas; stage, validate and load the orders CSVs and the customers JSON from lesson 05; build typed, deduplicated views; answer eight questions; and check your answers automatically against a key.

How this project was verified without a Snowflake account

The SQL script was parsed statement by statement with sqlglot's Snowflake dialect (23 of 23 statements parsed into full syntax trees). The answer key was computed by loading the same generated files into DuckDB 1.5.6 with the same error handling (the three planted bad rows rejected). The checker script was tested by running it against that DuckDB database through a small fake snowflake.connector. When you run the project in Snowflake, your numbers should match the key. If they don't, the checker tells you which question to investigate.

docs.title: The script
docs.text:
project.sql. Run it top to bottom in a Snowsight worksheet (or snow sql -c trial -f project.sql), after uploading the files as described in step 2's comments:

-- Level 1 project: load and analyse the sales dataset.
-- Run as a role that can create databases and warehouses (SYSADMIN in a trial account).

-- 1. Compute and storage containers ------------------------------------------------------
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS learn_wh
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE
  STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 900;
USE WAREHOUSE learn_wh;

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab.raw;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab.analytics;

-- 2. Stage and file formats --------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE STAGE IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab.raw.landing;
CREATE FILE FORMAT IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab.raw.csv_gz
  TYPE = CSV COMPRESSION = GZIP SKIP_HEADER = 1 FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"'
  NULL_IF = ('', 'NULL') ERROR_ON_COLUMN_COUNT_MISMATCH = TRUE;
CREATE FILE FORMAT IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab.raw.json_lines TYPE = JSON;

-- upload from your machine first:
--   snow stage copy "./orders_part*.csv.gz" @sales_lab.raw.landing/orders/ -c trial
--   snow stage copy ./customers.json @sales_lab.raw.landing/customers/ -c trial

-- 3. Raw tables ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab.raw.orders (
    order_id NUMBER(38,0), customer_id NUMBER(38,0), ordered_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ, channel VARCHAR,
    sku VARCHAR, quantity NUMBER(10,0), unit_price NUMBER(10,2), status VARCHAR,
    file_name VARCHAR, loaded_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()::TIMESTAMP_NTZ
);
CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_lab.raw.customers_json (
    v VARIANT, file_name VARCHAR, loaded_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()::TIMESTAMP_NTZ
);

-- 4. Validate, then load ---------------------------------------------------------------------
COPY INTO sales_lab.raw.orders (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status)
  FROM @sales_lab.raw.landing/orders/
  FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'sales_lab.raw.csv_gz')
  VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ALL_ERRORS;                     -- expect exactly 3 errors

COPY INTO sales_lab.raw.orders (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status, file_name)
  FROM (SELECT $1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8, METADATA$FILENAME FROM @sales_lab.raw.landing/orders/)
  FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'sales_lab.raw.csv_gz')
  ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';

COPY INTO sales_lab.raw.customers_json (v, file_name)
  FROM (SELECT $1, METADATA$FILENAME FROM @sales_lab.raw.landing/customers/)
  FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'sales_lab.raw.json_lines');

-- 5. Modelled layer ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW sales_lab.analytics.customers AS
SELECT v:customer_id::NUMBER AS customer_id, v:name::VARCHAR AS name, v:country::VARCHAR AS country,
       TO_DATE(v:signup::VARCHAR) AS signup_date, v:contact.email::VARCHAR AS email,
       v:contact.phone::VARCHAR AS phone, v:tags AS tags
FROM sales_lab.raw.customers_json;

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW sales_lab.analytics.orders AS
SELECT order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price,
       quantity * unit_price AS amount, status
FROM sales_lab.raw.orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY loaded_at DESC) = 1;

-- 6. Checks and analysis (compare with the answer key) ---------------------------------------
-- Q1 rows loaded
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_loaded FROM sales_lab.raw.orders;
-- Q2 monthly paid revenue
SELECT TO_CHAR(DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at), 'YYYY-MM') AS month, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
-- Q3 refund rate by channel
SELECT channel, ROUND(AVG(IFF(status = 'refunded', 1, 0)), 4) AS refund_rate
FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
-- Q4 top 3 countries by paid revenue
SELECT c.country, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders o JOIN sales_lab.analytics.customers c USING (customer_id)
WHERE o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 3;
-- Q5 customers without any orders
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers_without_orders
FROM sales_lab.analytics.customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id);
-- Q6 customers with paid orders in 6 or more distinct months
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers_active_6plus_months FROM (
  SELECT customer_id FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders WHERE status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at)) >= 6);
-- Q7 duplicate order ids in the raw table
SELECT COUNT(*) AS duplicate_order_ids FROM (
  SELECT order_id FROM sales_lab.raw.orders GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1);
-- Q8 JSON nulls in contact.phone
SELECT COUNT_IF(IS_NULL_VALUE(v:contact.phone)) AS null_phone FROM sales_lab.raw.customers_json;

Design choices worth noticing:

  • Transient raw tables. Raw data can be reloaded from the stage, so it doesn't need 7 days of Fail-safe (lesson 08).
  • Validate before loading. VALIDATION_MODE = RETURN_ALL_ERRORS should report exactly the three planted errors. Then ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE' loads everything else.
  • Lineage columns. METADATA$FILENAME and loaded_at let you trace every row to a file and a load.
  • Views as the contract. The analytics views cast VARIANT paths to real types and deduplicate with QUALIFY, so analysts never touch raw JSON or duplicate rows.
  • One small warehouse with a 60-second auto-suspend and a 15-minute statement timeout (lesson 04).

docs.title: The checker
docs.text:
check_answers.py runs the same eight questions through the Python connector and compares them with the key:

"""Run the project's check queries in Snowflake and compare them with answer_key.json.
Usage: python check_answers.py <connection name from config.toml>"""
import json, sys
import snowflake.connector

KEY = json.load(open("answer_key.json"))
Q = {
 "rows_loaded": "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_lab.raw.orders",
 "monthly_paid_revenue": """SELECT TO_CHAR(DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at), 'YYYY-MM'), SUM(amount)
     FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""",
 "refund_rate_by_channel": """SELECT channel, ROUND(AVG(IFF(status = 'refunded', 1, 0)), 4)
     FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1""",
 "top3_countries_paid_revenue": """SELECT c.country, SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
     FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders o JOIN sales_lab.analytics.customers c USING (customer_id)
     WHERE o.status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 3""",
 "customers_without_orders": """SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales_lab.analytics.customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS
     (SELECT 1 FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)""",
 "customers_active_6plus_months": """SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT customer_id FROM sales_lab.analytics.orders
     WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT DATE_TRUNC('month', ordered_at)) >= 6)""",
 "duplicate_order_ids": """SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT order_id FROM sales_lab.raw.orders
     GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1)""",
 "null_phone": "SELECT COUNT_IF(IS_NULL_VALUE(v:contact.phone)) FROM sales_lab.raw.customers_json",
}

def normalize(rows):
    out = [[float(x) if isinstance(x, (int, float)) or type(x).__name__ == "Decimal" else x for x in r] for r in rows]
    return out[0][0] if len(out) == 1 and len(out[0]) == 1 else out

with snowflake.connector.connect(connection_name=sys.argv[1]) as conn:
    cur = conn.cursor()
    failures = 0
    for name, sql in Q.items():
        got = normalize(cur.execute(sql).fetchall())
        want = KEY[name]
        ok = got == want if not isinstance(want, list) else [list(map(lambda v: float(v) if isinstance(v, (int, float)) else v, w)) for w in want] == got
        failures += not ok
        print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {name}" + ("" if ok else f"\n      expected {want}\n      got      {got}"))
    print(f"\n{len(Q) - failures}/{len(Q)} checks match the answer key")

python check_answers.py trial        # 'trial' is the connection name from lesson 02

docs.title: Testing the checker without Snowflake
docs.text:
A checker that has never run is a guess, so it was exercised against the DuckDB copy of the data. A fake snowflake.connector module translates each query from Snowflake SQL to DuckDB SQL with sqlglot and runs it:

Argument 'format' is not supported for expression 'ToChar' when targeting DuckDB.
PASS  rows_loaded
FAIL  monthly_paid_revenue
      expected [['2026-01', 3733367.04], ['2026-02', 3447838.33], ...]
      got      [['2026-01-01 00:00:00', 3733367.04], ['2026-02-01 00:00:00', 3447838.33], ...]
PASS  refund_rate_by_channel
PASS  top3_countries_paid_revenue
PASS  customers_without_orders
PASS  customers_active_6plus_months
PASS  duplicate_order_ids
PASS  null_phone

7/8 checks match the answer key

Seven checks pass. The one failure is the test double's limitation, not the query's: sqlglot couldn't translate Snowflake's TO_CHAR(…, 'YYYY-MM') format to DuckDB (it printed a warning), so the months came back as full timestamps. The revenue values match exactly. In Snowflake, TO_CHAR with that format returns 2026-01. This is a useful reminder that a translated test proves the logic, not every function's exact output. The real run is in Snowflake.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Everything you built is metadata plus files. The warehouse is a compute definition that runs only during the COPY statements and queries. The COPY statements turned 3 MB of CSV and 0.9 MB of JSON into micro-partitions (only a handful at this size). The views are stored queries that the optimizer expands into every query that uses them, so QUALIFY deduplication and the VARIANT casts run each time a view is read. For a 200,000-row table that's trivial. For a billion rows you'd materialize the cleaned data instead, as Level 2 does with streams, tasks and dynamic tables.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Skipping validation and discovering bad rows in a dashboard.
  • Comparing a partial month with full months.
  • Running the load twice with FORCE = TRUE. The duplicate check will catch it.
  • Leaving the warehouse with the default 10-minute auto-suspend for a lab you use for five minutes a day.
  • Querying raw VARIANT in reports instead of the typed view.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the whole project in a trial account and get 8/8 from the checker. Record the credits used by learn_wh in Snowsight's cost view.
  2. Add a question to the key and the checker: average order value per channel for paid orders. Compute the expected value yourself before running it in Snowflake.
  3. Make the load idempotent end to end: running project.sql twice should leave every check passing. What needs to change, if anything?
  4. Clone sales_lab to sales_lab_dev, delete all refunded orders in the clone, and show that the production checker still passes while a checker pointed at the clone fails the refund-rate question.

docs.title: Level 2 · Performance & Data Engineering
docs.text:
Level 2 is about two things: making queries read less, and keeping data up to date continuously without reprocessing everything. Both come down to how Snowflake stores data in micro-partitions. Along the way you'll see a one-day query read 1 of 98 partitions or all 98 depending only on row order, a text clustering key that can't tell any SKUs apart, a join that silently made revenue six times too high, a warehouse that would wake 288 times a day to merge nothing, and a MERGE that inserted the same order twice.

What was run

As in Level 1, nothing here was run on Snowflake. Pruning, clustering layouts and partitioned exports were demonstrated for real with Parquet row-group statistics in DuckDB 1.5.6, which work on the same min/max principle. The project's MERGE logic was tested locally against seven batches of changes. Costs are small models of the documented billing rules, with their assumptions stated. All Snowflake SQL was syntax-checked and verified against the October 2026 documentation, including several features that changed in 2025–2026 (Snowpipe's per-GB pricing, task overlap policies, dynamic table refresh modes).

Prerequisites: Level 1.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Micro-Partitions & Pruning — min/max metadata, pruning shown with real Parquet statistics, overlap and depth, and filters that can and can't prune.
  2. Clustering Keys & Automatic Clustering — choosing keys and their order, the text-prefix trap, the cost trade-off, sort-on-load and search optimization.
  3. Query Profile & Performance Tuning — queuing, exploding joins, UNION, spilling and pruning, and a workflow to find the queries worth tuning.
  4. The Three Caches — result, warehouse and metadata caches, their exact rules, and the auto-suspend trade-off modelled.
  5. Continuous Loading with Snowpipe — auto-ingest pipes, per-GB billing, the 14-day re-staging trap and Snowpipe Streaming.
  6. Streams: Change Data Capture — net-change semantics, consuming with DML, transactions, staleness and the CHANGES clause.
  7. Tasks & Task Graphs — schedules, stream-gated and triggered tasks, serverless compute, graphs with finalizers, and failure handling.
  8. Dynamic Tables — declarative pipelines, target lag, refresh modes and the silent fallback to full refresh.
  9. Unloading, External Tables & Iceberg — partitioned unloads, external tables over your files, and Snowflake-managed vs externally managed Iceberg tables.
  10. Project — An Incremental ELT Pipeline — stream, deduplicating MERGE task and incremental dynamic table, with the merge logic tested against full rebuilds.

docs.title: After Level 2
docs.text: You can build fast queries and continuous pipelines. Level 3 is about who may see and do what: roles and privileges, authentication, network controls, masking and row access policies, tags, secure views, data sharing, encryption, and auditing with account usage and access history, ending with a governed multi-team platform.

docs.title: 01 · Micro-Partitions & Pruning
docs.text: Snowflake has no indexes. The single biggest factor in how much data a query reads, and therefore how long it runs and what it costs, is pruning: skipping micro-partitions that can't contain matching rows, using the minimum and maximum values Snowflake records for every column of every micro-partition. Pruning is automatic, but whether it works depends on something you control: how rows are grouped into micro-partitions, which mostly means the order the data arrived in.

docs.title: What Snowflake records per micro-partition
docs.text:
From Snowflake's documentation, each micro-partition holds 50–500 MB of uncompressed data, stored by column, and its metadata includes:

  • the range of values (min and max) of each column,
  • the number of distinct values,
  • other properties used for optimization.

When a query has a filter like WHERE ordered_at BETWEEN '2026-03-15' AND '2026-03-16', the cloud services layer compares the filter with every micro-partition's ordered_at range before a warehouse reads anything, and drops those whose range can't overlap. Only the survivors are scanned, and of those, only the referenced columns.

docs.title: A real demonstration with Parquet
docs.text:
Parquet files work the same way: rows are grouped into row groups, and each row group stores min/max statistics per column. That makes them a faithful, runnable stand-in for micro-partitions. This experiment (DuckDB 1.5.6 and Python, locally, not Snowflake) writes the 200,000 orders from Level 1 twice: once in time order, as they'd arrive from an application, and once shuffled, as they might after an unordered bulk load or many scattered updates:

import duckdb
con = duckdb.connect("../data/sales.duckdb")
ROWS_PER_GROUP = 2000            # 100 "micro-partitions"
con.sql(f"COPY (SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY ordered_at) TO 'orders_by_time.parquet' (ROW_GROUP_SIZE {ROWS_PER_GROUP})")
con.sql(f"COPY (SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY hash(order_id)) TO 'orders_shuffled.parquet' (ROW_GROUP_SIZE {ROWS_PER_GROUP})")

DuckDB rounded the row-group size to its internal vector size, giving 98 row groups of up to 2,048 rows. Their ordered_at ranges look like this:

orders_by_time.parquet                                  orders_shuffled.parquet
row_group │ stats_min           │ stats_max            row_group │ stats_min           │ stats_max
        0 │ 2026-01-01 00:02:42 │ 2026-01-03 20:07:00          0 │ 2026-01-01 00:43:58 │ 2026-09-27 21:06:39
        1 │ 2026-01-03 20:08:02 │ 2026-01-06 16:31:03          1 │ 2026-01-01 07:26:32 │ 2026-09-27 22:42:14
        2 │ 2026-01-06 16:33:40 │ 2026-01-09 12:51:36          2 │ 2026-01-01 01:30:33 │ 2026-09-27 19:16:20

In time order, each row group covers about three days. Shuffled, every row group covers the entire nine months. Now apply the pruning rule (skip a group if its [min, max] can't overlap the filter) to three filters:

def would_scan(path, col, lo, hi):
    conv = int if col == "customer_id" else str      # compare numbers as numbers, ISO timestamps as text
    groups = [(g, conv(mn), conv(mx)) for g, mn, mx in stats(path, col)]
    lo, hi = conv(lo), conv(hi)
    keep = [g for g in groups if not (g[2] < lo or g[1] > hi)]       # skip if [min,max] misses [lo,hi]
    return len(keep), len(groups)

orders_by_time.parquet
   one day   (ordered_at on 2026-03-15)   scans   1 of 98 row groups
   one month (ordered_at in 2026-06)      scans  12 of 98 row groups
   one customer (customer_id = 4242)      scans  98 of 98 row groups
orders_shuffled.parquet
   one day   (ordered_at on 2026-03-15)   scans  98 of 98 row groups
   one month (ordered_at in 2026-06)      scans  98 of 98 row groups
   one customer (customer_id = 4242)      scans  98 of 98 row groups

The same data, the same query: one day reads 1% of the table in time order and 100% shuffled. And no layout helps every column. Customer 4242's orders are spread across the whole year, so a customer filter scans everything in both layouts.

(An earlier version of this script compared customer_id statistics as text, and "pruned" groups where '4242' sorted outside a string range like '1003'…'4999'. It reported 84 of 98 for one layout, which was wrong. Pruning on numbers has to compare numbers. The engine does this correctly. Hand-written analyses have to as well.)

docs.title: Measuring it: overlap and depth
docs.text:
Snowflake describes how well a table is laid out for a column with two numbers, both computed from micro-partition ranges:

  • overlaps: how many other micro-partitions a micro-partition's range overlaps;
  • depth: how many micro-partitions contain a given value. A depth of 1 means a value lives in exactly one micro-partition.

Computing these from our row groups' ordered_at ranges (averaged over every partition, and over every boundary value for depth, our approximation of Snowflake's metric):

orders_by_time.parquet     partitions 98  average_overlaps   0.00  average_depth   1.00
orders_shuffled.parquet    partitions 98  average_overlaps  97.00  average_depth  49.50

In Snowflake you get these numbers, for real micro-partitions, from:

SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('learn_db.raw.orders', '(ordered_at)');
SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_DEPTH('learn_db.raw.orders', '(ordered_at)');

The first returns JSON with the total partition count, average_overlaps, average_depth and a histogram of depths. Snowflake's docs note that depth isn't an absolute score: query performance is the real test. The direction is clear, though: closer to 1 is better for filters on that column.

docs.title: Seeing pruning in Snowflake
docs.text:
For any query, the Query Profile in Snowsight (Level 2 · 03) shows, on the TableScan operator, Partitions scanned and Partitions total. The same numbers are in the query history:

SELECT query_id, query_text, partitions_scanned, partitions_total,
       ROUND(100 * partitions_scanned / NULLIF(partitions_total, 0), 1) AS pct_scanned,
       bytes_scanned, total_elapsed_time
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE warehouse_name = 'LEARN_WH'
  AND start_time > DATEADD('day', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY bytes_scanned DESC
LIMIT 20;

A frequently run query with a selective filter and pct_scanned near 100 is the clearest sign that the table's layout doesn't match how it's queried.

docs.title: Writing filters that can prune
docs.text:
Pruning needs a predicate that can be compared with the column's min/max:

-- prunes: plain range on the column
SELECT SUM(quantity * unit_price) FROM learn_db.raw.orders
WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-03-15' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-16';

-- may not prune: the column is hidden inside an arbitrary expression
SELECT SUM(quantity * unit_price) FROM learn_db.raw.orders
WHERE TO_CHAR(ordered_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD') = '2026-03-15';

-- doesn't prune (per Snowflake's docs): the bound comes from a subquery, even if it returns a constant
SELECT SUM(quantity * unit_price) FROM learn_db.raw.orders
WHERE ordered_at >= (SELECT MAX(report_date) FROM learn_db.analytics.report_runs);

Snowflake can prune through some simple expressions (casts, date truncation), but not arbitrary ones, and it can't use a bound it doesn't know at compile time. The reliable habits are to filter the raw column with range predicates, and when the bound comes from data, look it up first and pass it in as a literal or a session variable.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Pruning happens at compile time, in the cloud services layer, using metadata only. For each table in the query, the optimizer walks the micro-partition list (which can hold millions of entries for large tables) and evaluates each predicate against each partition's min/max statistics. A partition is kept if the predicate might be true for some value in its range, and dropped if it's provably false for all of them. The warehouse receives only the surviving file list. That's why pruning reduces both I/O and the number of files to fetch, and why it works the same on a cold or warm warehouse.

Snowflake can also prune at runtime in joins: after building a hash table from the smaller side of a join, it can derive a range of join-key values and skip probe-side partitions outside it. But compile-time pruning on filters is the part you can design for.

Micro-partitions are formed in the order rows are written. Rows loaded together land together, so a table loaded daily, in time order, is naturally well clustered by time, exactly like orders_by_time.parquet. What destroys that layout is loading data in random order, or rewriting it with operations that reshuffle rows. The next lesson covers how to restore or enforce a layout with clustering keys.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming an index exists. There are none. Layout plus pruning is the mechanism.
  • Wrapping the filter column in functions (TO_CHAR(ts) = …, YEAR(ts) = 2026 on hot paths). Filter on the column with ranges.
  • Filter bounds from subqueries, which don't prune.
  • Judging a table by row count. Look at partitions_scanned / partitions_total for the real queries.
  • Expecting good pruning on every column. Only the column(s) the data is ordered by (or naturally correlated with) prune well.
  • Loading historical backfills in random order, then wondering why recent-day queries scan everything.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the Parquet experiment with row groups of 500 and 8,000 rows. How do the "one day" and "one month" scan counts change, and why?
  2. Write a third layout ordered by customer_id and rerun the three filters. Which query improves, and which gets worse?
  3. In Snowflake, load the orders once in file order and once shuffled (INSERT INTO … SELECT … ORDER BY RANDOM()), at a larger scale (SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10.ORDERS works). Compare SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION and partitions_scanned for a one-day filter.
  4. Rewrite the subquery-bound query so it prunes, using SET max_date = (SELECT …); followed by WHERE ordered_at >= $max_date.

docs.title: 02 · Clustering Keys & Automatic Clustering
docs.text: The last lesson showed that pruning depends on how rows are grouped into micro-partitions: a one-day filter read 1 of 98 partitions when the data was in time order and 98 of 98 when it wasn't. A clustering key tells Snowflake which grouping you want, and Automatic Clustering keeps it that way in the background as data changes, for a price. This lesson covers when that price is worth paying, how to choose the key, and the cheaper alternatives.

docs.title: No layout serves every filter
docs.text:
The same 200,000 orders written in four orders (98 row groups each, real Parquet min/max statistics, DuckDB locally), with the number of row groups three filters must scan:

layout                                    day   customer    channel
no order (shuffled)                     98/98      98/98      98/98
CLUSTER BY (ordered_at)                  1/98      98/98      98/98
CLUSTER BY (customer_id)                98/98       1/98      98/98
CLUSTER BY (channel, ordered_at)         6/98      98/98      33/98
  • Ordering by ordered_at makes date filters nearly free and does nothing for customers.
  • Ordering by customer_id is the mirror image.
  • (channel, ordered_at) serves both channel filters (33/98, one-third of the data for one of three channels) and date filters (6/98: for each channel, the rows of one day sit together) reasonably well. Neither is as good as a dedicated layout.

So clustering is a choice about which queries matter most. Look at the filters in your heaviest, most frequent queries (Level 2 · 03 shows how to find them) before choosing.

docs.title: Defining a clustering key
docs.text:
ALTER TABLE learn_db.raw.orders CLUSTER BY (TO_DATE(ordered_at), channel);

-- or at creation
CREATE TABLE learn_db.raw.events (event_ts TIMESTAMP_NTZ, event_type VARCHAR, user_id NUMBER, payload VARIANT)
  CLUSTER BY (TO_DATE(event_ts), event_type);

SHOW TABLES LIKE 'ORDERS' IN SCHEMA learn_db.raw;     -- cluster_by and automatic_clustering columns
SELECT SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION('learn_db.raw.orders');

Snowflake's documented guidance for choosing keys:

  • At most 3 or 4 columns or expressions. More tends to cost more than it gains.
  • Order columns from lowest to highest cardinality. A high-cardinality column first makes the later columns nearly useless, just as customer_id before ordered_at would scatter dates.
  • Avoid the extremes of cardinality. A boolean barely prunes. A nanosecond timestamp or a unique ID is expensive to keep clustered. Use an expression that reduces cardinality: TO_DATE(event_ts) instead of event_ts, or TRUNC(id, -6) for numeric IDs.
  • Prefer columns used in selective filters, then columns used in joins.

docs.title: The text-prefix trap
docs.text:
Snowflake's documentation adds a detail that's easy to miss: when clustering on a text column, the clustering metadata tracks only the first several bytes, typically 5 or 6. Our SKUs look like SKU-0417, so their first 5 bytes are SKU-0 for every row. To clustering, they're all the same value.

This model (Parquet locally, not Snowflake) shows what bounds truncated to a prefix would mean for skipping data on a table ordered by sku, filtering for one SKU:

full-length      min/max: scans  1 of 98 row groups for sku = 'SKU-0417'
6-byte prefix    min/max: scans 13 of 98 row groups for sku = 'SKU-0417'
5-byte prefix    min/max: scans 98 of 98 row groups for sku = 'SKU-0417'

With a 5-byte prefix, every group looks identical and nothing can be told apart. The docs' statement concerns the clustering metadata (what Automatic Clustering and the depth calculation see). Whether query-time pruning uses longer bounds isn't specified there, so treat the model as an illustration of the clustering side. The practical rule is the same either way: don't cluster on text whose distinguishing characters come after a common prefix. Cluster on an expression that puts the distinguishing part first, such as TRY_TO_NUMBER(SUBSTR(sku, 5)), or on a numeric surrogate key.

docs.title: Automatic Clustering: what it does and costs
docs.text:
Once a table has a key, Automatic Clustering monitors it and, when enough new or changed micro-partitions overlap, rewrites them in key order in the background. It's a serverless feature: it doesn't use your warehouses, it's billed in credits at its own rate (in the Service Consumption Table), and it also creates new micro-partitions, which means more Time Travel and Fail-safe storage for the retired ones.

ALTER TABLE learn_db.raw.orders SUSPEND RECLUSTER;    -- pause background work
ALTER TABLE learn_db.raw.orders RESUME RECLUSTER;

SELECT start_time, end_time, credits_used, num_bytes_reclustered, num_rows_reclustered
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.AUTOMATIC_CLUSTERING_HISTORY
WHERE table_name = 'ORDERS'
ORDER BY start_time DESC;

Snowflake's own guidance is that clustering keys "are not intended for all tables". It's optimal when you need the fastest response regardless of cost, or when the query savings outweigh the clustering credits. In practice the good candidates are:

  • large tables (many thousands of micro-partitions, typically terabytes, since small tables are scanned quickly anyway);
  • queried frequently with selective filters on the key;
  • that change in ways that degrade natural order (late-arriving data, updates and merges scattered across history).

A table that's appended in time order and queried by time is already well clustered by time. Adding a time clustering key mostly adds cost.

docs.title: Cheaper alternatives
docs.text:
Sort on load. If the data arrives in batches, order each batch by the columns you filter on. Micro-partitions are formed in write order (lesson 01), so a sorted insert produces clustered micro-partitions at no extra cost:

INSERT INTO learn_db.raw.orders
SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.orders_staging
ORDER BY TO_DATE(ordered_at), channel;

For a one-time fix of a badly ordered table, rewrite it sorted with CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE … AS SELECT … ORDER BY … (watch the Time Travel storage from lesson 08).

Search optimization for point lookups. The customer = 4242 filter can't be served by a time-ordered layout. The search optimization service (Enterprise Edition) builds a separate persistent access structure for selective equality and some other predicates (point lookups, IN lists, substring and semi-structured searches), so such queries skip micro-partitions without changing the table's order:

ALTER TABLE learn_db.raw.orders ADD SEARCH OPTIMIZATION ON EQUALITY(customer_id, sku);
DESCRIBE SEARCH OPTIMIZATION ON learn_db.raw.orders;

It's also serverless and billed for building, maintaining and storing the structure. A common design for large fact tables is a time clustering key (or natural time order) for range scans, plus search optimization on the ID columns used in lookups.

Materialized views (Enterprise) can keep a differently clustered copy of a subset for a specific query pattern, at the cost of storage and maintenance.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Automatic Clustering doesn't sort the entire table. It continuously evaluates the clustering state from micro-partition metadata (overlap and depth for the key), selects sets of micro-partitions whose key ranges overlap heavily, and rewrites just those, merging and sorting their rows into new micro-partitions with narrow ranges. New data is clustered incrementally the same way. It aims for "good enough" clustering that improves pruning, not a perfect global sort, because a perfect sort of a constantly changing large table would be far too expensive. When micro-partitions reach a state where their ranges no longer overlap, they're in what the docs call a constant state and aren't reclustered again.

Every rewrite is a normal DML-style change: new micro-partitions, retired old ones, Time Travel and Fail-safe on the retired ones. That's why clustering a table that receives scattered updates (lesson 09's model) can cost both reclustering credits and storage. The scattered changes keep breaking the order, and the service keeps restoring it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Clustering small tables. They scan quickly anyway, so you pay for nothing.
  • Clustering on a high-cardinality raw column (timestamps, IDs). Use an expression that reduces cardinality.
  • High cardinality first in a multi-column key.
  • Text keys with a long common prefix. Clustering tracks only the first 5–6 bytes.
  • Adding a time key to an append-only, time-ordered table. It's already clustered.
  • Never checking AUTOMATIC_CLUSTERING_HISTORY. Clustering credits can quietly exceed what queries save.
  • Using clustering for point lookups. Search optimization is the tool for that.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add CLUSTER BY (customer_id, ordered_at) to the layout experiment in this order and in the reverse order, and fill in the table for both. Which order serves the day filter better, and why?
  2. In Snowflake, create a 50-million-row table from SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10.LINEITEM in random order, record SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION on l_shipdate, add CLUSTER BY (l_shipdate), and check again over the next hours together with AUTOMATIC_CLUSTERING_HISTORY credits.
  3. Instead of a clustering key, rebuild the same table with ORDER BY l_shipdate and compare partitions_scanned for a one-week filter with the automatically clustered version. Which was cheaper overall?
  4. Design the physical layout for a 20 TB events table queried mostly by event_date ranges, often filtered by tenant_id (2,000 tenants), and occasionally by event_id lookups. Which key, in which order, plus which other feature?

docs.title: 03 · Query Profile & Performance Tuning
docs.text: When a Snowflake query is slow, guessing is expensive: a bigger warehouse doubles the rate whether or not it helps. Snowflake records what every query actually did, operator by operator, in the Query Profile and the query history. This lesson is a field guide to reading them, organized around the problems Snowflake's documentation itself lists as the most common: exploding joins, UNION without ALL, queries too large for memory (spilling), and inefficient pruning. Queuing is added because it looks like slowness but isn't.

docs.title: Where to look
docs.text:
Snowsight → Monitoring → Query History → a query → Query Profile shows the execution plan as a tree of operators (TableScan, Filter, Join, Aggregate, Sort, WindowFunction, Result…), the percentage of time spent in each, rows flowing along each edge, and panes for Most Expensive Nodes, Statistics and Query Insights. The same per-operator data is available in SQL:

SELECT operator_id, operator_type, operator_statistics, execution_time_breakdown
FROM TABLE(GET_QUERY_OPERATOR_STATS(LAST_QUERY_ID()));

And for many queries at once, ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY (latency up to 45 minutes, 365 days of history) has the summary columns you'll use most:

SELECT query_id, warehouse_name, warehouse_size,
       total_elapsed_time / 1000            AS elapsed_s,
       compilation_time / 1000              AS compile_s,
       queued_overload_time / 1000          AS queued_s,
       partitions_scanned, partitions_total,
       bytes_scanned / POWER(1024, 3)       AS gb_scanned,
       percentage_scanned_from_cache,
       bytes_spilled_to_local_storage  / POWER(1024, 3) AS gb_spilled_local,
       bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage / POWER(1024, 3) AS gb_spilled_remote,
       rows_produced
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE start_time > DATEADD('day', -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
  AND warehouse_name IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY total_elapsed_time DESC
LIMIT 50;

Read a slow query's numbers in this order. Each points to a different fix.

docs.title: 1. Was it slow, or was it waiting?
docs.text: queued_overload_time is time spent waiting for the warehouse, because it was already running as many queries as it could. A query that ran for 2 seconds after queuing for 40 isn't slow. The warehouse is oversubscribed. The fix is concurrency (a multi-cluster warehouse, or splitting workloads across warehouses, Level 4 · 06), not a bigger size. queued_provisioning_time is time waiting for the warehouse to start or resize. compilation_time that's large relative to execution points at very complex SQL (huge IN lists, deeply nested views) or a lot of metadata, as with tables with very many micro-partitions and no pruning.

docs.title: 2. Exploding joins
docs.text:
A join whose output is far larger than its inputs usually means a missing or incomplete join condition. This is reproduced on the course data: joining orders to a price history on sku alone, forgetting that each SKU has six price rows over time (DuckDB 1.5.6 locally, not Snowflake):

price_rows: 4800   skus: 800

join on sku only (missing the time condition)    -> 1,199,982 rows
ASOF join: price in effect at order time         ->   199,997 rows

revenue_wrong: 287,444,874
revenue_asof:   47,902,749

The join multiplied every order by six, and the revenue figure was six times too high. Nothing failed, and the result looks plausible unless someone checks. In the Query Profile, this shows as a Join operator producing far more rows than it consumes, often with most of the query's time spent in it. Fix the condition (here, ASOF JOIN … MATCH_CONDITION from Level 1 · 06, or a BETWEEN effective_at AND next_effective_at range join), or deduplicate the right-hand side to one row per key before joining. A cheap habit that catches this early: compare COUNT(*) before and after a join you expect to be one-to-one.

docs.title: 3. UNION without ALL
docs.text: UNION removes duplicates, which means a full aggregation over both inputs. UNION ALL just concatenates. In the profile, UNION appears as a UnionAll operator with an extra Aggregate above it. If the inputs can't overlap (two different months, two regions) or duplicates don't matter, write UNION ALL.

docs.title: 4. Spilling: the query didn't fit in memory
docs.text:
Large sorts, aggregations with many groups, window functions over big partitions, and joins with a large build side need memory. When they run out, Snowflake spills intermediate data to the warehouse's local SSD (bytes spilled to local storage) and, if that's not enough, to remote storage (bytes spilled to remote storage). Remote spilling is dramatically slower.

Fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Reduce the data before the expensive step: filter earlier, select fewer columns, aggregate before joining.
  2. Process in smaller batches (per day, per region).
  3. Use a larger warehouse for that query. More nodes means more memory and local disk. This is the case where sizing up genuinely pays: a query that spilled remotely on a Medium can run several times faster on a Large and cost less.
  4. For memory-hungry Snowpark/ML work, a Snowpark-optimized warehouse (more memory per node).

docs.title: 5. Inefficient pruning
docs.text: partitions_scanned close to partitions_total for a query with a selective filter means the filter couldn't skip data (lessons 01–02). Check that the filter is on the raw column with a range predicate, not hidden in a function or a subquery. If the filter is fine, the table's layout doesn't match the query, and clustering or sort-on-load fixes it. percentage_scanned_from_cache tells you how much came from the warehouse's SSD cache rather than remote storage (lesson 04).

docs.title: A tuning workflow
docs.text:
1. Find what matters. Rank recurring queries by total elapsed time or credits over a week, not the single slowest run:
SELECT query_parameterized_hash,
       ANY_VALUE(query_text)                 AS example,
       COUNT(*)                              AS runs,
       SUM(total_elapsed_time) / 1000 / 3600 AS total_hours,
       AVG(partitions_scanned / NULLIF(partitions_total, 0)) AS avg_scan_ratio,
       SUM(bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage) / POWER(1024, 3) AS gb_spilled_remote
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE start_time > DATEADD('day', -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY query_parameterized_hash
ORDER BY total_hours DESC
LIMIT 20;

query_parameterized_hash groups queries that differ only in literal values, so the dashboard query run 5,000 times with different dates counts as one workload. 2. Open the Query Profile of a representative run and identify the most expensive operator. 3. Match the symptom to one of the five problems above and apply its fix. 4. Re-measure with USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE, so the result cache doesn't make it look instant (lesson 04).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A query compiles in the cloud services layer into a plan of operators, and pruning is decided there (lesson 01). The warehouse executes the plan in parallel: every node processes a share of the micro-partitions, and operators like joins and aggregations exchange rows between nodes by hashing the join or grouping key, so that matching rows meet on the same node. That exchange is why a skewed key (one customer with a huge share of the rows) overloads one node while others idle. It shows up as one slow operator with a long tail in the profile's per-node statistics.

Each operator has a memory budget on its node. When a hash table or sort buffer outgrows it, the operator writes partitions of its data to local SSD and processes them in passes, and when local disk is full, to remote object storage. That's the spilling the profile reports. The fix is either less data per node (filter or batch) or more nodes and memory (a larger warehouse). The per-operator row counts you see in the profile are the actual rows produced at runtime, which is what makes exploding joins easy to spot after the fact.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sizing up without reading the profile. It doubles the cost of a queued, exploding or badly pruned query and fixes none of them.
  • Tuning the slowest single query instead of the workload that consumes the most time in aggregate.
  • Joins that aren't one-to-one when you assume they are. Check row counts.
  • UNION by habit.
  • Benchmarking with the result cache on. The second run looks instant.
  • Ignoring remote spilling. It's the clearest signal that a larger warehouse (or smaller batches) will pay off.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. In a trial account, write the exploding join against SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF1 deliberately (join LINEITEM to PARTSUPP on partkey only), open its Query Profile and find the Join operator's input and output row counts. Then fix it by adding suppkey.
  2. Force spilling: run a COUNT(DISTINCT …) over a large sample table grouped by a high-cardinality key on an X-Small warehouse, then on a Medium. Compare bytes spilled, elapsed time and credits.
  3. Run the workload query above in your account and pick the top workload. Which of the five problems does its profile show?
  4. Rewrite a UNION query from your own work as UNION ALL where it's safe, and compare the two profiles.

docs.title: 04 · The Three Caches
docs.text: The second run of a Snowflake query is often dramatically faster than the first, sometimes instant, and sometimes it uses no warehouse at all. Three different caches are responsible, each with its own rules. Knowing them explains confusing benchmarks ("my tuning made it 100× faster", when it really just hit the result cache), and it informs one real cost decision: how long to keep a warehouse running.

docs.title: 1. The result cache (cloud services)
docs.text:
When a query finishes, its result is persisted. An identical query can be answered from that result without running anything, often without a warehouse at all. From Snowflake's documentation:

  • Results are kept for 24 hours. Each reuse resets the 24 hours, up to a maximum of 31 days from the first run.
  • Reuse requires the same query text (case and whitespace included), and that:
  • the underlying table data hasn't changed (including micro-partition changes from reclustering);
  • the query uses no non-reusable functions (UUID_STRING, RANDOM, RANDSTR, external functions) and reads no hybrid tables;
  • the role has the required privileges on everything the query reads;
  • result-affecting configuration hasn't changed.
  • Meeting these conditions doesn't guarantee reuse.
  • The USE_CACHED_RESULT parameter (default TRUE) turns it off per session, user or account.
SELECT channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price) FROM learn_db.raw.orders GROUP BY channel;   -- runs on the warehouse
SELECT channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price) FROM learn_db.raw.orders GROUP BY channel;   -- answered from the result cache
select channel, sum(quantity * unit_price) from learn_db.raw.orders group by channel;   -- different text: runs again

ALTER SESSION SET USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE;     -- always do this before benchmarking

In the Query Profile, a cache hit shows a single QUERY RESULT REUSE node. Two practical uses:

  • Dashboards. Many users opening the same dashboard run identical SQL, and after the first, it's free until the data changes. That's a strong reason to generate dashboard SQL consistently.
  • Post-processing. RESULT_SCAN turns any recent result, including the output of SHOW, DESCRIBE or CALL, into a table you can query:
SHOW WAREHOUSES;
SELECT "name", "size", "auto_suspend", "state"
FROM TABLE(RESULT_SCAN(LAST_QUERY_ID()))
WHERE "auto_suspend" IS NULL OR "auto_suspend" > 300;

(Columns from SHOW output are lower-case and must be quoted.) Snowflake also documents a pipe operator ->> that chains a command into a follow-up query without displaying the first result.

docs.title: 2. The warehouse cache (local SSD)
docs.text:
Each warehouse node keeps micro-partition data it has read (only the columns read) on local SSD. A later query on the same warehouse that needs the same data reads it locally instead of from remote object storage. The Query Profile and QUERY_HISTORY.PERCENTAGE_SCANNED_FROM_CACHE report how much came from cache. Its rules are simpler and harsher:

  • It belongs to one warehouse. Another warehouse reading the same table starts cold.
  • It's lost when the warehouse suspends. Resizing also changes the set of nodes, and newly added nodes start cold.
  • It holds data, not results, so it helps different queries that touch the same micro-partitions.

docs.title: 3. The metadata cache
docs.text:
Snowflake knows each micro-partition's row count and per-column min/max (lesson 01). Queries that can be answered from that alone, such as COUNT(*) of a whole table or MIN/MAX of a column without filters, plus SHOW and DESCRIBE commands, may be served by cloud services without scanning data and without a running warehouse.

SELECT COUNT(*), MIN(ordered_at), MAX(ordered_at) FROM learn_db.raw.orders;   -- often metadata-only

docs.title: The real decision: auto-suspend vs a warm cache
docs.text:
Lesson 04 of Level 1 showed that short auto-suspend saves credits. The warehouse cache adds the other side: every resume starts cold. This model (Python locally) makes the trade-off concrete with stated assumptions, not measurements. A dashboard query takes 3 s warm and 12 s cold, queries arrive at a fixed interval for one hour, and billing follows the documented rules:

WARM, COLD = 3, 12
def simulate(gap, auto_suspend, hours=1):
    t, billed, run_start, run_end, resumes, latency = 0, 0, None, None, 0, []
    while t < hours * 3600:
        warm = run_end is not None and t <= run_end + auto_suspend
        dur = WARM if warm else COLD
        if warm:
            run_end = max(run_end, t + dur)
        else:
            if run_start is not None:
                billed += max(60, run_end + auto_suspend - run_start)
            run_start, run_end, resumes = t, t + dur, resumes + 1
        latency.append(dur); t += gap
    billed += max(60, run_end + auto_suspend - run_start)
    return billed, resumes, sum(latency) / len(latency)

 gap between queries AUTO_SUSPEND  billed s  resumes  avg latency s
                  60           60      3603        1            3.1
                  60          300      3843        1            3.1
                 120           60      2160       30           12.0
                 120          300      3783        1            3.3
                 300           60       864       12           12.0
                 300          300      3603        1            3.8
  • Queries every minute: the warehouse never gets a chance to suspend either way, so a short auto-suspend costs nothing in latency.
  • Every 2 minutes: a 60-second suspend saves 43% of the billed time (2,160 vs 3,783 s), but every query runs cold, at 12 s instead of 3.3 s average.
  • Every 5 minutes: 60 s suspend bills 864 s against 3,603 s, about a quarter of the cost, with all queries cold.

Neither setting is right in general. For an interactive dashboard where users notice 12 seconds, the longer suspend buys 4× faster responses at roughly double the cost. For a scheduled job nobody watches, take the cheap setting. And if the dashboard SQL is consistent, the result cache may answer most opens for free anyway, which can make the question moot.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The result cache lives in the cloud services layer, not on a warehouse, which is why it survives warehouse suspends and works across warehouses for users with the right privileges. A result is keyed on the exact query text plus the context that affects results. Before reuse, cloud services checks that the tables' current versions are the ones the result was computed from. Any committed change, even one that doesn't touch the rows in the result, creates a new table version and invalidates it. Results are stored like query output for large results: as files in Snowflake-managed storage that clients download directly.

The warehouse cache is ordinary local SSD on the compute nodes, organized by micro-partition file and column. Since micro-partitions are immutable, a cached file can never be stale: either the query still needs that exact file, or the table now references a different one. That's why the cache needs no invalidation logic, and why suspending (returning the nodes) is the only thing that empties it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Benchmarking with the result cache on. The second run is a cache hit, not a faster query.
  • Generating dashboard SQL with varying whitespace, aliases or literal order, which defeats result reuse.
  • RANDOM() or UUID_STRING() in dashboard queries, which are never reusable.
  • Sharing one warehouse between unrelated workloads to "share the cache". They evict each other's data and compete for CPU. Separate warehouses still win.
  • Setting auto-suspend by rule of thumb. Decide from query arrival gaps and what users will tolerate.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. In a trial account, run an aggregation over SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10.LINEITEM three times: normally, again (look for the result-reuse node), and again with USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE (look at the percentage scanned from cache). Then suspend and resume the warehouse and run it a fourth time.
  2. Make the second run miss the result cache by changing only the letter case of a keyword. Then make it miss by inserting one row into an unrelated part of the table.
  3. Use SHOW TABLES with RESULT_SCAN to list the five largest tables in a database by "bytes".
  4. Change the model's assumptions to match your own warehouse (measure warm and cold times for a real dashboard query) and find the auto-suspend that minimizes cost while keeping average latency under your target.

docs.title: 05 · Continuous Loading with Snowpipe
docs.text: Lesson 05 of Level 1 loaded files with COPY INTO on a warehouse you control. That's ideal for big, scheduled batches. For data that trickles in all day (files every few minutes from an application, a CDC tool or a partner's export), a warehouse that resumes every five minutes to load a few megabytes wastes most of what it bills. Snowpipe runs the same COPY logic on Snowflake-managed serverless compute whenever new files appear, and bills by the gigabyte.

docs.title: A pipe is a saved COPY
docs.text:
CREATE PIPE IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.orders_pipe
  AUTO_INGEST = TRUE
  COMMENT = 'Loads order files as they land in s3://my-company-landing/orders/'
AS
COPY INTO learn_db.raw.orders (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status, file_name)
FROM (SELECT $1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8, METADATA$FILENAME FROM @learn_db.raw.s3_landing/orders/)
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.csv_gz');

The pipe holds a COPY INTO statement, and Snowpipe runs it for each new file. There are two ways for it to learn about new files:

  • AUTO_INGEST = TRUE: the cloud provider sends an event notification when a file lands, for example an S3 event notification to the SQS queue Snowflake creates for the pipe. For S3, SHOW PIPES shows that queue's ARN in the notification_channel column, and you configure the bucket to send ObjectCreated events to it. On GCS and Azure, you create a notification integration instead.
  • REST API: your application calls Snowpipe's insertFiles endpoint with the file names after uploading them, which is useful for internal stages or when you control the writer.

To load files already in the stage when the pipe was created (Snowpipe only reacts to new events), run once:

ALTER PIPE learn_db.raw.orders_pipe REFRESH;     -- queues files staged in the last 7 days

docs.title: How Snowpipe differs from bulk COPY
docs.text:
From Snowflake's documentation:

Bulk COPY INTO Snowpipe Trigger you run it (or a task does) file events or REST calls Compute your warehouse serverless Typical latency as often as you run it typically within a minute of Snowpipe learning about a file Billing warehouse time 0.0037 credits per GB (all editions since 8 December 2025) Default ON_ERROR ABORT_STATEMENT SKIP_FILE Transaction one per COPY statement per file (files may be combined or split across transactions) Load metadata per table, 64 days per pipe, 14 days

Billing is on the file's uncompressed size for text formats (CSV, JSON, XML) and the stored size for binary formats (Parquet, Avro, ORC). A 1 GB gzip CSV that's 5 GB uncompressed is billed as 5 GB.

docs.title: The cost difference for trickle data
docs.text:
A model of the documented rates (Python, locally). It assumes each small scheduled COPY takes 10 seconds on an X-Small with a 60-second auto-suspend, so each run bills 70 seconds:

SNOWPIPE_PER_GB = 0.0037
def snowpipe(gb_per_day): return gb_per_day * SNOWPIPE_PER_GB
def scheduled_copy(runs_per_day, seconds_per_run=10, auto_suspend=60, credits_per_hour=1):
    return runs_per_day * max(60, seconds_per_run + auto_suspend) / 3600 * credits_per_hour

 uncompressed GB/day  Snowpipe cr/day |  COPY every 5 min  COPY every hour
                   1           0.0037 |             5.600            0.467
                   3           0.0111 |             5.600            0.467
                  10           0.0370 |             5.600            0.467
                  30           0.1110 |             5.600            0.467

For trickle volumes, running a warehouse every five minutes costs hundreds of times more than Snowpipe: 5.6 credits a day of mostly idle minimums against cents. Even hourly loads cost more until volumes reach well over 100 GB/day. For large daily batches, compare against measured warehouse load time for your own files. Load speed depends heavily on file format, size and transformation, so it isn't modelled here.

docs.title: The 14-day trap: re-staging a corrected file
docs.text:
Snowflake's documentation is explicit:

Each pipe keeps load metadata, which is a record of the files that it processed in the last 14 days … Snowpipe ignores any staged file whose path and name match a file in this record, even if the file was modified … Because Snowpipe also records files that failed to load, it ignores a corrected file that you stage again with …

…the same name. Picture the realistic incident: a file fails to load (SKIP_FILE, because of one bad row), someone fixes the row and uploads the file again under the same name, and Snowpipe silently ignores it for 14 days. The fix is a new file name (add a version or timestamp suffix), or a one-off manual COPY INTO of that file on a warehouse. ALTER PIPE … REFRESH won't help, because the name is already recorded.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
SELECT SYSTEM$PIPE_STATUS('learn_db.raw.orders_pipe');      -- execution state, pending file count, last errors

SELECT file_name, status, row_count, row_parsed, first_error_message, last_load_time
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COPY_HISTORY(
       TABLE_NAME => 'learn_db.raw.orders',
       START_TIME => DATEADD('hour', -24, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())))
ORDER BY last_load_time DESC;

SELECT start_time, end_time, credits_used, bytes_billed, bytes_inserted, files_inserted
