FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.PIPE_USAGE_HISTORY
WHERE pipe_name = 'ORDERS_PIPE'
ORDER BY start_time DESC;

Alert on files with a Load failed status. Under SKIP_FILE, a bad file is skipped without stopping anything else, so nobody notices unless something is watching. Pausing for maintenance:

ALTER PIPE learn_db.raw.orders_pipe SET PIPE_EXECUTION_PAUSED = TRUE;
ALTER PIPE learn_db.raw.orders_pipe SET PIPE_EXECUTION_PAUSED = FALSE;

docs.title: Snowpipe Streaming
docs.text: When data arrives as rows, not files (Kafka topics, application events, CDC streams), writing small files just to have Snowpipe read them adds latency and cost. Snowpipe Streaming lets a client (the Snowflake Kafka connector, or your own code using Snowflake's ingest SDK) write rows directly into tables. Snowflake's documentation describes its high-performance architecture as delivering up to 20 GB/s per table and ingest-to-queryable latency as low as 5 seconds, with ordered, exactly-once ingestion through named channels and offset tokens. The per-GB rate above covers it too. Streaming wasn't exercised for this course, so check the current SDK and connector documentation before designing around it.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
With auto-ingest, the cloud provider publishes an event per new object to a queue owned by Snowflake. Snowpipe consumes those events, filters them against the pipe's stage path and its 14-day load metadata, and puts the remaining files in a per-pipe ingestion queue. Snowflake-managed compute picks up queued files, runs the pipe's COPY logic on them (possibly combining small files or splitting large ones), and commits the rows. Because it's not one statement over a known file list, there's no single transaction: files appear in the table as they're processed, in no guaranteed order. That's why downstream processing usually uses streams (next lesson) rather than assuming a load "finished".

Billing per GB means file count and file size no longer change what you pay directly, but they still affect latency and efficiency. Snowflake's general advice of roughly 100–250 MB compressed files, or new files about once a minute for continuous sources, still applies.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• A warehouse waking every few minutes for small loads. That's Snowpipe's job.
  • Re-staging a fixed file under the same name and waiting for it to load. It won't, for 14 days.
  • Not monitoring SKIP_FILE failures. They're silent by design.
  • Expecting ordering across files. Process downstream by content (timestamps, sequence numbers), not arrival.
  • Forgetting REFRESH for files that were staged before the pipe existed.
  • Credentials in stages instead of storage integrations.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. In a trial account with an S3 bucket (or Azure/GCS equivalent), create the stage, integration and auto-ingest pipe. Upload the four order files one at a time and watch them appear with COPY_HISTORY.
  2. Upload a version of orders_part2.csv.gz with a broken row. Confirm it's skipped, fix it, upload it again with the same name, and observe that nothing happens. Then load it properly.
  3. Using your actual daily volume and the model above, at what volume would an hourly scheduled COPY on an X-Small become cheaper than Snowpipe? Measure the real COPY time for one of your files rather than using the 10-second assumption.
  4. Write a monitoring query that returns every file loaded with errors, or skipped, in the last 24 hours across all pipes in a database.

docs.title: 06 · Streams: Change Data Capture
docs.text: Incremental pipelines need to answer one question efficiently: what changed since I last looked? Reprocessing a whole table every hour doesn't scale, and timestamp columns miss updates and deletes. A stream is a Snowflake object that tracks changes to a table (or view) from a point called its offset, and returns exactly those changes when you query it. Streams are the building block for incremental MERGEs, and with tasks (next lesson), for complete pipelines.

docs.title: Creating and reading a stream
docs.text:
CREATE STREAM IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.orders_changes ON TABLE learn_db.raw.orders;

SELECT *, METADATA$ACTION, METADATA$ISUPDATE, METADATA$ROW_ID
FROM learn_db.raw.orders_changes;

A stream has the source table's columns plus three metadata columns:

  • METADATA$ACTION: INSERT or DELETE.
  • METADATA$ISUPDATE: TRUE when the record is part of an UPDATE. An update appears as a pair: a DELETE of the old row and an INSERT of the new one, both with ISUPDATE = TRUE.
  • METADATA$ROW_ID: a stable identifier for the row, used to match those pairs.

SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('learn_db.raw.orders_changes') returns whether there's anything to process, cheaply. Tasks use it to skip runs (lesson 07).

docs.title: Net changes, not a log
docs.text:
A stream returns the difference between two table versions: the version at its offset and the current one. It isn't a log of every statement. From Snowflake's documented semantics, here's what a standard stream would return for some sequences of changes between two consumptions:

Changes since the offset Stream contents INSERT row 1 one INSERT row, ISUPDATE = FALSE UPDATE existing row 2 DELETE (old values) + INSERT (new values), both ISUPDATE = TRUE INSERT row 3, then UPDATE it one INSERT with the final values, ISUPDATE = FALSE (it's a new row as far as the delta is concerned) INSERT row 4, then DELETE it nothing UPDATE row 5 three times one DELETE/INSERT pair: original values → latest values DELETE existing row 6 one DELETE row

That's exactly what you need to bring a downstream table up to date, and exactly what you don't get if you want an audit trail of every intermediate value. For that, write changes to a history table as they happen, or query history with Time Travel.

docs.title: Consuming a stream: the offset advances only on DML
docs.text:
The rule that matters most: querying a stream doesn't move its offset. The offset advances only when the stream is read by a DML statement (INSERT, MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE TABLE AS …) that commits. Then the changes are considered consumed.

MERGE INTO learn_db.analytics.orders_clean AS t
USING (
    SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.orders_changes
    WHERE NOT (METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE' AND METADATA$ISUPDATE)      -- drop the "before" half of updates
) AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE
WHEN MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN UPDATE SET
     t.customer_id = s.customer_id, t.ordered_at = s.ordered_at, t.channel = s.channel, t.sku = s.sku,
     t.quantity = s.quantity, t.unit_price = s.unit_price, t.status = s.status
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN INSERT
     (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status)
     VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.ordered_at, s.channel, s.sku, s.quantity, s.unit_price, s.status);

Filtering out the DELETE half of update pairs leaves, per row, either an INSERT (new or updated row: upsert it) or a genuine DELETE (remove it). That's the standard CDC merge. If the raw table can receive duplicates for the same order_id in one batch, deduplicate inside the USING subquery with QUALIFY (Level 1 · 06), or the merge will fail as nondeterministic.

When several statements must see the same changes (for example, write to two target tables), wrap them in an explicit transaction. Within it, the stream has repeatable read semantics, so every statement sees the same records, and the offset advances once, at COMMIT:

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO learn_db.analytics.order_events SELECT order_id, METADATA$ACTION, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() FROM learn_db.raw.orders_changes;
MERGE INTO learn_db.analytics.orders_clean AS t USING learn_db.raw.orders_changes AS s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
  WHEN MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE' AND NOT s.METADATA$ISUPDATE THEN DELETE;
COMMIT;

Without the transaction, the first statement would consume the changes and the second would see an empty stream.

docs.title: Stream types
docs.text:
Type Records Use Standard (default) inserts, updates, deletes (net) general CDC, merges APPEND_ONLY = TRUE inserts only append-only sources such as event logs, raw loads, which is cheaper to compute INSERT_ONLY = TRUE inserts only external tables and externally managed Iceberg tables 
CREATE STREAM learn_db.raw.orders_appends ON TABLE learn_db.raw.orders APPEND_ONLY = TRUE;

For a raw table that's only ever loaded by COPY/Snowpipe, an append-only stream is the natural choice. One table can have many streams, each with its own offset, so several independent consumers can each process all changes at their own pace.

docs.title: Staleness
docs.text:
A stream depends on the source table's history (Time Travel, lesson 08). If its offset falls outside the source's retention period, it becomes stale: the unconsumed changes are gone, and it must be recreated. To give streams slack, Snowflake temporarily extends a table's retention for an unconsumed stream, up to MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS (default 14 days). Snowflake's documentation gives examples of how often a stream must be consumed:

DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS consume at least every 14 0 14 days 1 14 14 days 0 90 90 days 
SHOW STREAMS IN SCHEMA learn_db.raw;      -- the stale and stale_after columns
DESCRIBE STREAM learn_db.raw.orders_changes;

A pipeline that pauses for a long holiday, or a dev stream nobody consumes, goes stale. Monitor stale_after.

docs.title: The CHANGES clause: read-only change queries
docs.text:
To look at changes between two points without creating a stream or moving any offset, query the table with CHANGES (change tracking must be enabled on the table, which creating a stream does automatically):

ALTER TABLE learn_db.raw.orders SET CHANGE_TRACKING = TRUE;

SELECT *
FROM learn_db.raw.orders
  CHANGES (INFORMATION => DEFAULT)
  AT (OFFSET => -60*60);          -- net changes during the last hour

INFORMATION => APPEND_ONLY restricts it to inserts. This is good for audits, debugging and ad-hoc reconciliation, and not a replacement for a stream in a pipeline (nothing tracks what you've processed).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A stream stores no data. It stores an offset: a reference to a table version. When you query it, Snowflake compares the table's micro-partitions at the offset version with those at the current version. Micro-partitions present in both are unchanged and skipped. Those added or removed between the versions are read, and with the hidden row-level change-tracking columns that enabling change tracking adds to the table, Snowflake computes the net inserts and deletes per row. That's why the result is a net delta, why it costs more when changes are scattered across many micro-partitions (lesson 09's model again), and why an append-only stream, which only has to read added micro-partitions, is cheaper.

Consuming a stream in a committed DML transaction records the table version the statement read as the new offset. Querying it alone doesn't commit anything, so nothing moves. And since the offset is just a version reference, the stream depends on that version still being retained: when Time Travel no longer covers it, there's nothing to compare against, and the stream is stale.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting a SELECT to consume the stream. Only committed DML moves the offset.
  • Two statements reading the same stream without a transaction. The second one sees nothing.
  • Forgetting the DELETE half of update pairs in a merge, which deletes rows that were only updated.
  • Expecting every intermediate change. Streams return net changes between offsets.
  • Letting streams go stale in rarely run pipelines or dev environments.
  • Standard streams on append-only tables. Use APPEND_ONLY = TRUE.
  • Short retention plus MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 0, which leaves no slack for a delayed consumer.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create a stream on raw.orders, then insert a row, update an existing row, insert-then-delete another, and update a fourth row twice. Query the stream and compare it with the table in this lesson.
  2. Run the CDC MERGE and confirm the stream is empty afterwards. Then show that a plain SELECT from the stream doesn't empty it.
  3. Write the two-statement transaction above without BEGIN/COMMIT, and show that the second statement processes nothing.
  4. Create a stream on a table with DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 0 and MAX_DATA_EXTENSION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 0, change the table, and inspect stale_after in SHOW STREAMS. What happens?

docs.title: 07 · Tasks & Task Graphs
docs.text: A task runs a SQL statement (or a call to a stored procedure) on a schedule or when new data arrives, inside Snowflake, with no external scheduler. Combined with streams (lesson 06), tasks give you incremental pipelines: a stream collects changes, and a task merges them downstream. This lesson covers how tasks are scheduled, where their compute comes from, how to chain them into graphs, and how to keep them from failing silently or burning credits doing nothing.

docs.title: A first task
docs.text:
CREATE TASK IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.merge_orders
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('learn_db.raw.orders_changes')
AS
  MERGE INTO learn_db.analytics.orders_clean AS t
  USING (SELECT * FROM learn_db.raw.orders_changes
         WHERE NOT (METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE' AND METADATA$ISUPDATE)) AS s
  ON t.order_id = s.order_id
  WHEN MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'DELETE' THEN DELETE
  WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET t.status = s.status, t.quantity = s.quantity, t.unit_price = s.unit_price
  WHEN NOT MATCHED AND s.METADATA$ACTION = 'INSERT' THEN INSERT (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status)
       VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.ordered_at, s.channel, s.sku, s.quantity, s.unit_price, s.status);

ALTER TASK learn_db.raw.merge_orders RESUME;     -- tasks are created SUSPENDED
EXECUTE TASK learn_db.raw.merge_orders;          -- run once now, e.g. to test

Three details:

  • Tasks are created suspended. Nothing runs until ALTER TASK … RESUME, and forgetting that is the most common reason a "scheduled" pipeline never ran.
  • SCHEDULE is either an interval ('5 MINUTE', '1 HOUR', and in seconds where supported) or a cron expression with a time zone: 'USING CRON 0 6 * * MON-FRI Europe/Lisbon'. Always give a time zone in cron schedules.
  • WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA(…) is evaluated by cloud services before starting compute. If the stream is empty, the run is skipped and no warehouse resumes. Without it, this task would wake etl_wh 288 times a day. At the 60-second minimum on an X-Small that's 288 × 60 s = 4.8 hours, or 4.8 credits a day, to merge nothing most of the time.

docs.title: Triggered tasks: run when data arrives
docs.text:
Leave out the SCHEDULE and keep the WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA(…) condition, and the task becomes a triggered task that runs when the stream has data, instead of polling on a timer:

CREATE TASK learn_db.raw.merge_orders_triggered
  TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL = '5 MINUTE'
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('learn_db.raw.orders_changes')
AS
  INSERT INTO learn_db.analytics.order_events (order_id, action, seen_at)
  SELECT order_id, METADATA$ACTION, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() FROM learn_db.raw.orders_changes;

This one has no WAREHOUSE, so it's also serverless, and for serverless triggered tasks Snowflake requires a TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL. USER_TASK_MINIMUM_TRIGGER_INTERVAL_IN_SECONDS limits how often a triggered task may fire.

docs.title: Where the compute comes from
docs.text:
User-managed warehouse Serverless Declared by WAREHOUSE = etl_wh omitting WAREHOUSE (optionally USER_TASK_MANAGED_INITIAL_WAREHOUSE_SIZE) Sizing you choose Snowflake predicts from recent runs, up to the equivalent of XXLARGE Billing warehouse time, shared with whatever else runs there per-second serverless compute at the serverless-task rate Privilege needed USAGE on the warehouse the account-level EXECUTE MANAGED TASK

Serverless suits short, frequent tasks, because it avoids a warehouse's 60-second minimum and idle tail. TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL (and SERVERLESS_TASK_MIN/MAX_STATEMENT_SIZE) let you tell Snowflake how fast it needs to finish. Warehouse tasks suit heavy jobs that already have a warehouse running, or that need predictable sizing.

docs.title: Task graphs
docs.text:
Tasks can depend on other tasks with AFTER, forming a graph (DAG) with one root task that has the schedule:

CREATE TASK learn_db.raw.load_root
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  SCHEDULE = 'USING CRON 0 * * * * UTC'
AS
  COPY INTO learn_db.raw.orders FROM @learn_db.raw.landing/orders/
  FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.csv_gz') ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';

CREATE TASK learn_db.raw.build_daily  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh AFTER learn_db.raw.load_root
AS
  INSERT OVERWRITE INTO learn_db.analytics.daily_revenue
  SELECT TO_DATE(ordered_at), channel, SUM(quantity * unit_price)
  FROM learn_db.raw.orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY ALL;

CREATE TASK learn_db.raw.build_customers WAREHOUSE = etl_wh AFTER learn_db.raw.load_root
AS
  INSERT OVERWRITE INTO learn_db.analytics.customer_totals
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*), SUM(quantity * unit_price)
  FROM learn_db.raw.orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY customer_id;

CREATE TASK learn_db.raw.notify_done WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  FINALIZE = learn_db.raw.load_root
AS
  CALL SYSTEM$SEND_EMAIL('my_email_int', 'data-team@example.com', 'Hourly load finished', 'See TASK_HISTORY for details.');

-- resume the root and all its dependents in one go
SELECT SYSTEM$TASK_DEPENDENTS_ENABLE('learn_db.raw.load_root');
  • build_daily and build_customers both run after the root, in parallel. A task can also list several predecessors (AFTER a, b), and then it waits for all of them.
  • A finalizer task (FINALIZE = <root>) runs once at the end of every graph run, whether or not the other tasks succeeded. Use it for notifications and cleanup.
  • Child tasks can't have their own schedule. Only the root is scheduled.
  • SYSTEM$SEND_EMAIL needs a notification integration (my_email_int here) that an administrator has created.

docs.title: Failures, retries, overlap
docs.text:
ALTER TASK learn_db.raw.load_root SET
  SUSPEND_TASK_AFTER_NUM_FAILURES = 3      -- stop retrying a broken graph forever
  TASK_AUTO_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 2             -- retry a failed graph run automatically
  USER_TASK_TIMEOUT_MS = 1800000           -- 30-minute cap per run
  OVERLAP_POLICY = NO_OVERLAP;             -- don't start a run while the previous one is still running

OVERLAP_POLICY (NO_OVERLAP, ALLOW_CHILD_OVERLAP, ALLOW_ALL_OVERLAP) replaces the deprecated ALLOW_OVERLAPPING_EXECUTION. NO_OVERLAP matters when a slow hourly run would otherwise race the next one. An ERROR_INTEGRATION sends failure notifications to a cloud messaging service.

Check what happened:

SELECT name, state, scheduled_time, completed_time, error_code, error_message, query_id
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TASK_HISTORY(
       SCHEDULED_TIME_RANGE_START => DATEADD('day', -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()),
       TASK_NAME => 'MERGE_ORDERS'))
ORDER BY scheduled_time DESC;

state values include SUCCEEDED, FAILED, SKIPPED (the WHEN condition was false, or a run was still going under NO_OVERLAP) and CANCELLED. A task graph that shows only SKIPPED for days may be correctly idle, or fed by a source that broke upstream. Alert on FAILED and on "no SUCCEEDED in N hours".

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
The task scheduler lives in cloud services. At each scheduled time (or, for triggered tasks, when change tracking reports new data in the stream), it evaluates the task's WHEN condition. SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA is answered from metadata, without a warehouse. If the condition holds, the scheduler starts a task run: it resumes the task's warehouse (or allocates serverless compute sized from the history of previous runs) and executes the body as the task's owner role (or as a specified user with EXECUTE AS USER). That's why privileges belong to the role that owns the task, not to whoever created or resumed it.

A graph run is identified by one root run. When the root succeeds, each child whose predecessors have all succeeded is queued. Children of a failed task don't run. The finalizer runs after everything else ends. Each run uses the task definitions as they were when the run started, so changing a task mid-run affects the next run. A stream consumed by a task's DML is advanced only if that run's transaction commits, so a failed run leaves the changes in the stream for the next attempt. This is what makes stream-plus-task pipelines safe to retry.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Never resuming the task (or resuming only the root without the children). Use SYSTEM$TASK_DEPENDENTS_ENABLE.
  • No WHEN condition on stream-driven tasks. The warehouse wakes to do nothing hundreds of times a day.
  • Cron schedules without a time zone, which shift by an hour at daylight-saving changes.
  • No failure alerting. A failed task just sits in TASK_HISTORY.
  • Overlapping runs of slow tasks. Set OVERLAP_POLICY = NO_OVERLAP.
  • Giving the task owner more privileges than the job needs. Tasks run with the owner's role.
  • Long-running heavy work as a serverless task without a size cap. Set SERVERLESS_TASK_MAX_STATEMENT_SIZE.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create the merge_orders task, resume it, insert some orders, and use TASK_HISTORY to find a SKIPPED run and a SUCCEEDED one.
  2. Rebuild it as a serverless triggered task with a 5-minute target completion interval. Compare the credits used per day (SERVERLESS_TASK_HISTORY in ACCOUNT_USAGE) with the warehouse version.
  3. Build the three-task graph plus a finalizer, then make build_daily fail (reference a table that doesn't exist). What runs, what doesn't, and what does the finalizer see?
  4. Write the alert query: every task with no successful run in the last 6 hours, but at least one run attempt.

docs.title: 08 · Dynamic Tables
docs.text: Streams and tasks (lessons 06–07) build incremental pipelines imperatively: you write the MERGE, schedule it, chain it, and handle failures. A dynamic table does it declaratively: you write the SELECT that defines the result, say how fresh it must be, and Snowflake works out the dependencies, schedules the refreshes, and (where it can) refreshes only what changed. For many transformation pipelines that removes most of the code. The trade-offs are in knowing when "only what changed" quietly turns into "everything, every time".

docs.title: A dynamic table
docs.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE learn_db.analytics.orders_enriched
  TARGET_LAG = '15 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = AUTO
  INITIALIZE = ON_CREATE
AS
SELECT o.order_id, o.ordered_at, TO_DATE(o.ordered_at) AS order_date, o.channel, o.sku,
       o.quantity, o.unit_price, o.quantity * o.unit_price AS amount, o.status,
       c.v:country::VARCHAR AS country
FROM learn_db.raw.orders o
JOIN learn_db.raw.customers_json c ON c.v:customer_id::NUMBER = o.customer_id;
  • TARGET_LAG is a freshness goal: the dynamic table's data should never be more than 15 minutes behind its sources. Snowflake schedules refreshes to meet it. The documented minimum is 60 seconds, and actual lag can exceed the target if refreshes take longer than the target allows.
  • WAREHOUSE runs the refreshes, so its credits are the cost.
  • REFRESH_MODE: AUTO (the default) picks incremental if the query supports it, otherwise full. INCREMENTAL and FULL force a mode. Newer modes, ADAPTIVE (incremental, reinitializing after large upstream changes) and CUSTOM_INCREMENTAL, are listed in the current reference.
  • INITIALIZE: ON_CREATE fills the table during CREATE, and ON_SCHEDULE defers it to the first scheduled refresh.

docs.title: Pipelines of dynamic tables
docs.text:
Dynamic tables can read other dynamic tables. Intermediate ones can use TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM, meaning "refresh only when something downstream needs fresh data":

CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE learn_db.analytics.orders_paid
  TARGET_LAG = DOWNSTREAM
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
AS
SELECT * FROM learn_db.analytics.orders_enriched WHERE status = 'paid';

CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE learn_db.analytics.daily_revenue_by_country
  TARGET_LAG = '1 hour'
  WAREHOUSE = etl_wh
AS
SELECT order_date, country, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM learn_db.analytics.orders_paid
GROUP BY order_date, country;

Snowflake builds the dependency graph from the queries themselves, with no AFTER clauses and no scheduling code. If the final table needs one-hour freshness, the upstream DOWNSTREAM tables refresh as needed to provide it, and all tables in one refresh read a consistent snapshot of the sources. Snowsight shows the graph and each table's lag.

docs.title: The silent fallback to full refresh
docs.text:
Incremental refresh processes only the rows that changed since the last refresh. Full refresh recomputes the entire result every time. With REFRESH_MODE = AUTO, if the query contains a construct that incremental refresh doesn't support, Snowflake's documentation says it "selects a full refresh instead, which reprocesses all data on every refresh". There's no error. The set of supported constructs keeps growing, and the current supported-queries page lists additions from 2025 and 2026 such as UNION, Cortex AI functions in SELECT, MIN_BY/MAX_BY, more outer-join patterns, and volatile scalar UDFs. So check the mode Snowflake actually chose for each table:

SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES IN SCHEMA learn_db.analytics;
-- columns refresh_mode (what it actually uses) and refresh_mode_reason (why it fell back)

For a small table the difference doesn't matter. For a large one it's the whole bill: a full refresh of a 1 TB result every 15 minutes is 96 full recomputations a day. Two protective habits:

  • On large tables, set REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL explicitly. Then an unsupported construct makes CREATE fail instead of silently choosing full refresh.
  • Keep the heavy, incremental-friendly logic (filters, joins, aggregations) in the large upstream dynamic tables, and put constructs that force full refresh into small downstream ones.

docs.title: Monitoring and control
docs.text:
SELECT name, state, refresh_action, refresh_trigger, data_timestamp,
       refresh_start_time, refresh_end_time,
       DATEDIFF('second', refresh_start_time, refresh_end_time) AS seconds,
       state_message
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.DYNAMIC_TABLE_REFRESH_HISTORY(NAME_PREFIX => 'LEARN_DB.ANALYTICS.'))
ORDER BY refresh_start_time DESC
LIMIT 50;

ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE learn_db.analytics.daily_revenue_by_country SUSPEND;
ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE learn_db.analytics.daily_revenue_by_country RESUME;
ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE learn_db.analytics.daily_revenue_by_country REFRESH;            -- refresh now
ALTER DYNAMIC TABLE learn_db.analytics.daily_revenue_by_country SET TARGET_LAG = '4 hours';

refresh_action shows whether each refresh was INCREMENTAL, FULL, NO_DATA (nothing changed, so little work), or a reinitialization. Refreshes that keep taking longer than the target lag are the main operational signal. Widen the lag, size up the warehouse, or simplify the query.

docs.title: Dynamic tables, streams and tasks, or a view?
docs.text:
Need Use A transformation result that should stay within N minutes of its sources dynamic table Complex procedural logic, side effects, calls to external systems, notifications streams + tasks (or procedures) Exact control over when and how each step runs streams + tasks Always-current results, cheap to compute at query time a view An expensive aggregate on one table, transparently used by queries (Enterprise) a materialized view

Snowflake's documentation includes a decision guide and a migration guide from streams and tasks to dynamic tables, which says something about the intended direction. For new transformation pipelines, start with dynamic tables and drop to streams and tasks where you need imperative control.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A dynamic table is a real table (micro-partitions, Time Travel, clustering) plus a stored query, a refresh mode and a target lag. Snowflake tracks the graph of dynamic tables and their base tables, and a scheduler picks refresh times for each table so that, given recent refresh durations, its data will be within the target lag. Refreshes of tables in the same graph are coordinated to read the same data timestamp, which is how downstream tables stay consistent with upstream ones.

Incremental refresh is built on the same change-tracking machinery as streams: Snowflake reads the changed rows of each source since the previous refresh's data timestamp and applies a differentiated version of the query to them. For a filter or projection, that's just running the query on the changed rows. For a join, it's changed-left with all-right plus all-left with changed-right. For an aggregation, it's recomputing only the groups whose inputs changed. When the query contains an operator Snowflake can't differentiate this way, the only correct option is to recompute everything, which is the full refresh. The cost of an incremental refresh scales with the changes (and with how scattered they are across micro-partitions), and the cost of a full refresh scales with the size of the inputs.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Assuming incremental. Check refresh_mode and refresh_mode_reason, and pin INCREMENTAL on big tables.
  • A target lag tighter than the refresh takes, which means constant refreshing and missed targets.
  • Very short lags everywhere. Each refresh costs warehouse time. Use DOWNSTREAM for intermediates and set the lag from real freshness needs.
  • Putting side effects in the pipeline. Dynamic tables are for deterministic transformations.
  • Using a shared interactive warehouse for refreshes. Give pipelines their own warehouse.
  • Forgetting dynamic tables have Time Travel and Fail-safe storage, which grows with full refreshes that rewrite everything (Level 1 · 08).

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build the three-table pipeline above on the course data, then check SHOW DYNAMIC TABLES for each table's actual refresh mode.
  2. Add a construct to orders_enriched that your account's documentation lists as unsupported for incremental refresh (check the current supported-queries page), and observe what AUTO chooses and what INCREMENTAL does.
  3. Insert 1,000 new orders and watch DYNAMIC_TABLE_REFRESH_HISTORY for the next refreshes of each table. Which ones refresh, and with which refresh_action?
  4. Rebuild the same result with a stream on raw.orders and a task graph. Compare lines of code, and credits used over a day.

docs.title: 09 · Unloading, External Tables & Iceberg
docs.text: So far, data has gone into Snowflake's own storage. Two other directions matter in real platforms: getting data out (to feed another system, a partner, or a data lake), and querying data that stays in your own cloud storage in open formats, either read-only through external tables or fully managed through Apache Iceberg tables, which other engines can read too.

docs.title: Unloading with COPY INTO a location
docs.text:
The same COPY command runs in reverse: from a table or query into a stage.

CREATE FILE FORMAT IF NOT EXISTS learn_db.raw.parquet_fmt TYPE = PARQUET;

COPY INTO @learn_db.raw.s3_landing/exports/paid_orders/
FROM (
    SELECT o.*, TO_CHAR(ordered_at, 'YYYY-MM') AS month
    FROM learn_db.raw.orders o
    WHERE status = 'paid'
)
PARTITION BY ('month=' || month || '/channel=' || channel)
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.parquet_fmt')
MAX_FILE_SIZE = 268435456          -- target 256 MB per file (default 16 MB, maximum 5 GB)
HEADER = TRUE                      -- keep column names in Parquet
INCLUDE_QUERY_ID = TRUE;           -- unique file names, so concurrent unloads can't overwrite each other

From the COPY INTO <location> reference:

  • Unloading runs in parallel, so it produces many files whose number and sizes depend on the data and the warehouse. MAX_FILE_SIZE is a target per thread (default 16 MB, maximum 5 GB).
  • SINGLE = TRUE writes one file, which uses one thread: slow for large data, and still subject to the size limit.
  • PARTITION BY takes an expression that evaluates to a string and uses it as a path prefix. That's the usual way to produce key=value/ directory layouts that other engines recognize as partitions.

Here's what such a layout looks like and how a reader benefits from it. DuckDB 1.5.6 locally (not Snowflake) wrote the course's paid orders partitioned by month and channel:

27 files; first three:
  export/month=2026-01/channel=app/data_0.parquet
  export/month=2026-01/channel=store/data_0.parquet
  export/month=2026-01/channel=web/data_0.parquet

-- DuckDB 1.5.6 (local), not Snowflake
SELECT COUNT(*) AS paid_web_june FROM read_parquet('export/**/*.parquet', hive_partitioning=true)
WHERE month = '2026-06' AND channel = 'web';

paid_web_june: 4408

A reader filtering on partition columns opens only the matching directory, one file out of 27 here. That's partition pruning at the directory level, the file-system version of lesson 01's min/max pruning. To download unloaded files from an internal stage, use GET (or snow stage copy @stage/path ./local/).

docs.title: External tables: query files where they are
docs.text:
An external table puts a table definition over files in an external stage. The data stays in your bucket and Snowflake reads it at query time:

CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE learn_db.raw.orders_lake (
    month      VARCHAR       AS (SPLIT_PART(SPLIT_PART(METADATA$FILENAME, 'month=', 2), '/', 1)),
    order_id   NUMBER        AS (VALUE:order_id::NUMBER),
    channel    VARCHAR       AS (VALUE:channel::VARCHAR),
    amount     NUMBER(12,2)  AS (VALUE:quantity::NUMBER * VALUE:unit_price::NUMBER(10,2))
)
PARTITION BY (month)
LOCATION = @learn_db.raw.s3_landing/exports/paid_orders/
FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'learn_db.raw.parquet_fmt')
AUTO_REFRESH = TRUE;

Every row is exposed as a VALUE variant, and columns are expressions over it. Partition columns derived from METADATA$FILENAME let Snowflake skip whole directories. AUTO_REFRESH keeps the file list current using cloud notifications, like Snowpipe. External tables are read-only and generally slower than native tables (no micro-partition statistics of Snowflake's own, and files read from your storage each time). They're good for exploring a lake, for rarely queried archives, and as a staging point. For data you query often, load it, or use Iceberg.

docs.title: Apache Iceberg tables
docs.text:
Iceberg is an open table format: Parquet data files plus metadata files that track snapshots, schemas and partitions, so many engines (Spark, Trino, DuckDB, Flink, Snowflake) can read and write the same table. Snowflake supports Iceberg tables in two forms, per its documentation:

Snowflake-managed (Snowflake is the catalog) Externally managed (another catalog) Writes from Snowflake yes, full DML limited / read-focused Table maintenance (e.g. compaction) Snowflake does it the external catalog/engine Data location your bucket (via an external volume) or Snowflake storage your bucket Other engines read it via the Snowflake Horizon Catalog's Iceberg REST API, or Open Catalog sync their own catalog Needs external volume (or SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED) external volume + catalog integration

A Snowflake-managed Iceberg table in your own S3 bucket:

CREATE EXTERNAL VOLUME lake_vol
  STORAGE_LOCATIONS = ((
    NAME = 'lake-eu'
    STORAGE_PROVIDER = 'S3'
    STORAGE_BASE_URL = 's3://my-company-lake/iceberg/'
    STORAGE_AWS_ROLE_ARN = 'arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/snowflake-lake'
  ));

CREATE ICEBERG TABLE learn_db.analytics.orders_iceberg (
    order_id NUMBER(38,0), ordered_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ, channel VARCHAR, amount NUMBER(12,2), status VARCHAR
)
  CATALOG = 'SNOWFLAKE'
  EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'lake_vol'
  BASE_LOCATION = 'orders_iceberg';

INSERT INTO learn_db.analytics.orders_iceberg
SELECT order_id, ordered_at, channel, quantity * unit_price, status FROM learn_db.raw.orders;

From then on it behaves much like a normal table in Snowflake (queries, DML, Time Travel within Iceberg's snapshot model), but its data and metadata are open files in your bucket that other engines can read. The cost model shifts too: you pay your cloud provider for that storage, rather than Snowflake.

Iceberg support is an area of fast change in Snowflake (catalog options, REST catalog access, supported types and operations). Snowflake's own documentation index advises preferring the current SQL reference over remembered syntax for Iceberg tables. Check it before relying on a specific capability.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
An unload is a parallel query whose final operator writes files instead of returning rows. Each warehouse thread writes its share, rolling to a new file when it reaches MAX_FILE_SIZE, which is why you get many files by default and one only with SINGLE. PARTITION BY routes each row to a file stream keyed by the expression's value.

An external table is metadata over a list of files. Snowflake keeps the file list (refreshed by notifications or ALTER EXTERNAL TABLE … REFRESH) and, at query time, applies partition-column filters to the file paths, then reads the surviving files from your storage. An Iceberg table keeps its own metadata tree (a metadata file pointing to manifest lists, manifests and data files, each manifest carrying column statistics), which is conceptually the same thing Snowflake does internally for micro-partitions, written in an open format. When Snowflake is the catalog, it writes and maintains that tree. When another catalog is, Snowflake reads the tree that catalog points to.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• SINGLE = TRUE for large unloads. One thread is slow, and the 5 GB file limit still applies.
  • Re-running an unload into the same path and mixing old and new files. Use a fresh prefix, or INCLUDE_QUERY_ID plus an OVERWRITE strategy.
  • Heavy, frequent queries on external tables. Load the data or use Iceberg.
  • No partition columns on external tables over large directory trees. Every query lists and reads everything.
  • Assuming every Snowflake feature works identically on Iceberg tables. Check the current reference.
  • Forgetting egress. Unloading across regions or clouds incurs data-transfer charges.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Unload the paid orders to an internal stage partitioned by month and channel, then use LIST and GET (or snow stage copy) to download them and read them with DuckDB or pandas.
  2. Create an external table over the unloaded files with a month partition column, and compare the partitions_scanned and elapsed time of a one-month query against the native table.
  3. Create a Snowflake-managed Iceberg table on a trial account's external volume (or with EXTERNAL_VOLUME = 'SNOWFLAKE_MANAGED'), insert the orders, and look at the files that appear in the storage location.
  4. Write down which of your organization's datasets should be native tables, external tables, or Iceberg tables, and why.

docs.title: 10 · Project — An Incremental ELT Pipeline
docs.text:
This project builds the pipeline shape that most Snowflake platforms run in some form:

files ──COPY/Snowpipe──▶ raw.orders ──append-only stream──▶ task: MERGE (dedup, ignore stale)
                                                                    │
                                                                    ▼
                                                     analytics.orders_clean ──dynamic table──▶ daily_revenue

Raw data is appended exactly as it arrives, including duplicates from at-least-once delivery and later updates to earlier orders (refunds). A task consumes only the new rows through a stream, deduplicates them, and upserts them into a current-state table, ignoring updates older than what's already there. A dynamic table keeps a daily aggregate incrementally up to date. Health and correctness checks are part of the deliverable.

What was tested, and how

The Snowflake script below was syntax-checked with sqlglot (10 statements parsed fully; CREATE STREAM, CREATE TASK and ALTER TASK were checked against the documentation). The heart of the pipeline, the MERGE statement, was tested for real. It was translated to DuckDB with sqlglot and run against seven batches of generated changes, with a batch table standing in for the stream, and after every batch the result was compared with a full rebuild from all raw rows. Streams, tasks and dynamic tables themselves weren't run.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
pipeline.sql:

-- Level 2 project: an incremental ELT pipeline (raw -> clean -> aggregates), fully inside Snowflake.

USE ROLE SYSADMIN;
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS pipeline_wh
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE
  STATEMENT_TIMEOUT_IN_SECONDS = 1800;

CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS shop;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS shop.raw;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS shop.analytics;

-- 1. Raw landing table: append-only, loaded by Snowpipe or a scheduled COPY (lesson 05)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS shop.raw.orders (
    order_id NUMBER(38,0), customer_id NUMBER(38,0), ordered_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ, channel VARCHAR, sku VARCHAR,
    quantity NUMBER(10,0), unit_price NUMBER(10,2), status VARCHAR, updated_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
    file_name VARCHAR, loaded_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()::TIMESTAMP_NTZ
) DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS = 1;

-- 2. An append-only stream: every row ever loaded, consumed once (lesson 06)
CREATE STREAM IF NOT EXISTS shop.raw.orders_changes ON TABLE shop.raw.orders APPEND_ONLY = TRUE;

-- 3. The clean, current-state table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS shop.analytics.orders_clean (
    order_id NUMBER(38,0), customer_id NUMBER(38,0), ordered_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ, channel VARCHAR, sku VARCHAR,
    quantity NUMBER(10,0), unit_price NUMBER(10,2), status VARCHAR, updated_at TIMESTAMP_NTZ
) CLUSTER BY (TO_DATE(ordered_at));

-- 4. The merge task: deduplicate the batch, ignore stale updates, upsert (lessons 06-07)
CREATE OR REPLACE TASK shop.raw.merge_orders
  WAREHOUSE = pipeline_wh
  SCHEDULE = '5 MINUTE'
  OVERLAP_POLICY = NO_OVERLAP
  SUSPEND_TASK_AFTER_NUM_FAILURES = 3
  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('shop.raw.orders_changes')
AS
MERGE INTO shop.analytics.orders_clean AS t
USING (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status, updated_at
    FROM shop.raw.orders_changes
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
) AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET
    customer_id = s.customer_id, ordered_at = s.ordered_at, channel = s.channel, sku = s.sku,
    quantity = s.quantity, unit_price = s.unit_price, status = s.status, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status, updated_at)
    VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.ordered_at, s.channel, s.sku, s.quantity, s.unit_price, s.status, s.updated_at);

ALTER TASK shop.raw.merge_orders RESUME;

-- 5. Aggregates as dynamic tables (lesson 08)
CREATE OR REPLACE DYNAMIC TABLE shop.analytics.daily_revenue
  TARGET_LAG = '30 minutes'
  WAREHOUSE = pipeline_wh
  REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL
AS
SELECT TO_DATE(ordered_at) AS order_date, channel,
       COUNT(*) AS orders,
       SUM(IFF(status = 'paid', quantity * unit_price, 0))     AS paid_revenue,
       SUM(IFF(status = 'refunded', quantity * unit_price, 0)) AS refunded_amount
FROM shop.analytics.orders_clean
GROUP BY TO_DATE(ordered_at), channel;

-- 6. Pipeline health: one query to run (or alert on) every hour
SELECT 'merge task' AS component, MAX(IFF(state = 'SUCCEEDED', completed_time, NULL)) AS last_success,
       COUNT_IF(state = 'FAILED') AS failures_24h
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TASK_HISTORY(
       SCHEDULED_TIME_RANGE_START => DATEADD('hour', -24, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()), TASK_NAME => 'MERGE_ORDERS'))
UNION ALL
SELECT 'daily_revenue refresh', MAX(IFF(state = 'SUCCEEDED', refresh_end_time, NULL)),
       COUNT_IF(state = 'FAILED')
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.DYNAMIC_TABLE_REFRESH_HISTORY(NAME => 'SHOP.ANALYTICS.DAILY_REVENUE'));

-- 7. Correctness check: the incremental table must equal a rebuild from raw
SELECT COUNT(*) AS mismatches FROM (
    SELECT order_id, status FROM shop.analytics.orders_clean
    EXCEPT
    SELECT order_id, status FROM shop.raw.orders
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
);

Choices worth noticing:

  • APPEND_ONLY = TRUE on the stream. The raw table is only ever appended to, so an append-only stream is the right (and cheaper) type (lesson 06).
  • QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() … = 1 in the USING subquery: one row per order_id per batch, the latest by updated_at.
  • WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at: a late-arriving, older update can never overwrite newer data.
  • WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA so the warehouse stays asleep when nothing arrived, plus OVERLAP_POLICY = NO_OVERLAP and SUSPEND_TASK_AFTER_NUM_FAILURES (lesson 07).
  • REFRESH_MODE = INCREMENTAL on the dynamic table, so if the query ever stops supporting incremental refresh, creation fails instead of silently switching to full refreshes (lesson 08).
  • Short retention on the raw table (it's reloadable from files), and a clustering key on the clean table, which receives scattered updates (lesson 02).

docs.title: Testing the MERGE logic
docs.text:
The MERGE, as it appears in the task (merge.sql):

MERGE INTO analytics.orders_clean AS t
USING (
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status, updated_at
    FROM raw.orders_changes
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
) AS s
ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s.updated_at > t.updated_at THEN UPDATE SET
    customer_id = s.customer_id, ordered_at = s.ordered_at, channel = s.channel, sku = s.sku,
    quantity = s.quantity, unit_price = s.unit_price, status = s.status, updated_at = s.updated_at
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (order_id, customer_id, ordered_at, channel, sku, quantity, unit_price, status, updated_at)
    VALUES (s.order_id, s.customer_id, s.ordered_at, s.channel, s.sku, s.quantity, s.unit_price, s.status, s.updated_at)

The test harness (test_pipeline.py) generates batches with new orders, status changes to earlier orders, and exact duplicates, applies them incrementally, and compares the result with a rebuild after every batch:

"""Test the pipeline's MERGE logic locally: DuckDB stands in for Snowflake, and a batch table stands in for the
append-only stream (rows loaded since the last successful merge). After every batch the incremental result must
equal a full rebuild from all raw rows."""
import random, duckdb, sqlglot
random.seed(7)
con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("CREATE SCHEMA raw; CREATE SCHEMA analytics;")
cols = "order_id BIGINT, customer_id BIGINT, ordered_at TIMESTAMP, channel VARCHAR, sku VARCHAR, quantity INT, unit_price DECIMAL(10,2), status VARCHAR, updated_at TIMESTAMP"
con.sql(f"CREATE TABLE raw.orders ({cols}, batch_id INT)")
con.sql(f"CREATE TABLE analytics.orders_clean ({cols})")
merge_sql = sqlglot.transpile(open("merge.sql").read(), read="snowflake", write="duckdb")[0]

def make_batch(batch_id, next_id, existing):
    rows, t = [], f"2026-10-{batch_id + 1:02d} 12:00:00"
    for _ in range(500):                                   # new orders
        rows.append((next_id, random.randint(1, 500), t, random.choice(["web", "app", "store"]),
                     f"SKU-{random.randint(1, 50):04d}", random.randint(1, 3), round(random.uniform(5, 99), 2), "paid", t))
        next_id += 1
    for oid in random.sample(existing, min(60, len(existing))):   # status changes to earlier orders
        rows.append((oid, 1, t, "web", "SKU-0001", 1, 10.00, "refunded", t))
    rows += random.sample(rows, 25)                        # exact duplicates, as at-least-once delivery produces
    random.shuffle(rows)
    return rows, next_id

def full_rebuild():
    return con.sql("""SELECT order_id, status FROM raw.orders
                      QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1
                      ORDER BY order_id""").fetchall()

next_id, existing = 1, []
for b in range(1, 6):
    rows, next_id = make_batch(b, next_id, existing)
    con.executemany("INSERT INTO raw.orders VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?, " + str(b) + ")", rows)
    # 'stream' = rows not yet consumed (this batch)
    con.sql(f"CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW raw.orders_changes AS SELECT * EXCLUDE (batch_id) FROM raw.orders WHERE batch_id = {b}")
    con.sql(merge_sql)
    existing = [r[0] for r in con.sql("SELECT order_id FROM analytics.orders_clean").fetchall()]
    inc = con.sql("SELECT order_id, status FROM analytics.orders_clean ORDER BY order_id").fetchall()
    full = full_rebuild()
    dupes = con.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) FROM analytics.orders_clean").fetchone()[0]
    refunded = sum(1 for _, s in inc if s == "refunded")
    print(f"batch {b}: raw rows {con.sql('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM raw.orders').fetchone()[0]:>5}  clean rows {len(inc):>5}  "
          f"refunded {refunded:>4}  duplicate ids {dupes}  incremental == full rebuild: {inc == full}")

# batch 6: a late, OUT-OF-ORDER update (older updated_at) for an order that was refunded in batch 2
victim = con.sql("SELECT order_id FROM analytics.orders_clean WHERE status = 'refunded' ORDER BY order_id LIMIT 1").fetchone()[0]
con.execute("INSERT INTO raw.orders VALUES (?, 1, '2026-10-01 12:00:00', 'web', 'SKU-0001', 1, 10.00, 'paid', '2026-10-01 13:00:00', 6)", [victim])
con.sql("CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW raw.orders_changes AS SELECT * EXCLUDE (batch_id) FROM raw.orders WHERE batch_id = 6")
con.sql(merge_sql)
print(f"batch 6: late stale update for order {victim}: status now "
      f"{con.sql(f'SELECT status FROM analytics.orders_clean WHERE order_id = {victim}').fetchone()[0]!r} (guard kept the newer value); "
      f"incremental == full rebuild: {con.sql('SELECT order_id, status FROM analytics.orders_clean ORDER BY order_id').fetchall() == full_rebuild()}")

# what happens without the QUALIFY dedup in the USING clause?
no_dedup = sqlglot.transpile(open("merge.sql").read().replace(
    "QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1", ""), read="snowflake", write="duckdb")[0]
con.sql("CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW raw.orders_changes AS SELECT * EXCLUDE (batch_id) FROM raw.orders WHERE batch_id = 5")
try:
    con.sql(no_dedup); print("merge without dedup: succeeded")
except Exception as e:
    print("merge without dedup:", type(e).__name__, str(e).splitlines()[0][:150])

# batch 7: a brand-new order delivered twice, merged WITHOUT the dedup
con.execute("INSERT INTO raw.orders VALUES (999999, 1, '2026-10-09 12:00:00', 'web', 'SKU-0001', 1, 10.00, 'paid', '2026-10-09 12:00:00', 7)")
con.execute("INSERT INTO raw.orders VALUES (999999, 1, '2026-10-09 12:00:00', 'web', 'SKU-0001', 1, 10.00, 'paid', '2026-10-09 12:00:00', 7)")
con.sql("CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW raw.orders_changes AS SELECT * EXCLUDE (batch_id) FROM raw.orders WHERE batch_id = 7")
con.sql(no_dedup)
print("batch 7 without dedup: rows for order 999999 in orders_clean =",
      con.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM analytics.orders_clean WHERE order_id = 999999").fetchone()[0])

batch 1: raw rows   525  clean rows   500  refunded    0  duplicate ids 0  incremental == full rebuild: True
batch 2: raw rows  1110  clean rows  1000  refunded   60  duplicate ids 0  incremental == full rebuild: True
batch 3: raw rows  1695  clean rows  1500  refunded  114  duplicate ids 0  incremental == full rebuild: True
batch 4: raw rows  2280  clean rows  2000  refunded  172  duplicate ids 0  incremental == full rebuild: True
batch 5: raw rows  2865  clean rows  2500  refunded  229  duplicate ids 0  incremental == full rebuild: True
batch 6: late stale update for order 1: status now 'refunded' (guard kept the newer value); incremental == full rebuild: True
merge without dedup: succeeded
batch 7 without dedup: rows for order 999999 in orders_clean = 2

What the run shows:

  • Batches 1–5: after each batch, the incremental table equals a full rebuild (True), with no duplicate order IDs, even though every batch contained 25 duplicated rows and, from batch 2, 60 refunds of earlier orders.
  • Batch 6: a stale update (older updated_at) for an already-refunded order arrived late. The guard kept 'refunded', and the table still equals the rebuild.
  • Without the QUALIFY dedup: re-merging batch 5 didn't fail in DuckDB, and in batch 7 a new order delivered twice was inserted twice. Snowflake's protection against ambiguous merges (ERROR_ON_NONDETERMINISTIC_MERGE, on by default) is documented for updating or deleting a target row that matches several source rows, so it wouldn't catch these duplicate inserts either. Deduplicating the source is what prevents them, in any engine.

docs.title: Running it in Snowflake
docs.text:
1. Run pipeline.sql (snow sql -c trial -f pipeline.sql).
  2. Load the Level 1 order files into shop.raw.orders with an updated_at column (for a first load, updated_at = ordered_at). Within five minutes the task merges them, and within the target lag the dynamic table shows daily revenue.
  3. Simulate refunds by appending rows for existing order IDs with status = 'refunded' and a later updated_at, plus some exact duplicates. Check that orders_clean reflects the refunds without duplicates.
  4. Run the health query and the correctness check (mismatches must be 0).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each part does one job with clear guarantees. The append-only stream records rows added to raw.orders since the task's last committed MERGE. If the task run fails, its transaction doesn't commit, the offset doesn't move, and the next run sees the same rows plus newer ones. Because the MERGE is idempotent for a given set of rows (dedup plus "only if newer"), replaying rows after a failure, or receiving the same row twice, can't change the result. That's what makes the pipeline safe under the at-least-once behaviour of loaders, streams and retries. The dynamic table reads orders_clean through change tracking and recomputes only the affected days and channels. The health query and the correctness check turn the silent failure modes (a suspended task, a failing refresh, a logic error) into numbers someone can alert on.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No dedup in the MERGE source. Duplicate inserts, as batch 7 showed.
  • No "only if newer" guard. Late events overwrite current state.
  • A standard stream on an append-only table, which costs more for no benefit.
  • Forgetting to resume the task.
  • No correctness check. Incremental pipelines drift silently. Compare against a rebuild regularly.
  • A dynamic table on AUTO that quietly falls back to full refresh on a large table.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the pipeline in a trial account with the Level 1 data, then append 1,000 refunds and 100 duplicates and confirm mismatches = 0.
  2. Break the pipeline on purpose: change the task to reference a missing column. What does the health query show, what happens to the stream, and does the data catch up after you fix it?
  3. Extend test_pipeline.py with deletions (an is_deleted flag) and add a WHEN MATCHED AND s.is_deleted THEN DELETE branch. Keep the full-rebuild comparison passing.
  4. Replace the task and MERGE with a dynamic table that computes orders_clean directly from raw.orders using QUALIFY. Check which refresh mode Snowflake chooses, and compare the cost with the task-based version.

docs.title: Level 3 · Security, Governance & Sharing
docs.text:
Level 3 is about who may see and do what, and how you prove it. Snowflake gives you a deep toolbox (roles, policies, tags, secure views, shares, audit views), and most real-world failures come from how the pieces combine rather than from any one of them. Along the way you'll see administrators inherit raw PII through an innocent-looking role grant, a network policy change modelled before it can lock anyone out, a key-pair sign-in token built and verified by hand, a view whose safety depends on the optimizer's plan, and a grant script whose tests found three design faults.

What was run

Nothing here was run on Snowflake. Effective access through role hierarchies was computed with a small RBAC model and tested with pytest. Network policy evaluation was modelled in Python, a key-pair JWT was built and verified locally with PyJWT, and the view-leak and audit queries ran in DuckDB 1.5.6 on synthetic data, always labelled as such. All Snowflake SQL was syntax-checked and verified against the October 2026 documentation, including areas that changed in 2025–2026 (the end of single-factor passwords, programmatic access tokens, network rules).

Prerequisites: Levels 1 and 2.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Access Control: Roles, Privileges & Hierarchies — system roles, access and functional roles, future grants, managed-access schemas, and effective access computed from a grant script.
  2. Authentication: MFA, Key Pairs, OAuth & SSO — the end of single-factor passwords, user types, key-pair JWTs, PATs, SSO and authentication policies.
  3. Network Policies & Private Connectivity — network rules and policies, precedence modelled offline, private connectivity and egress.
  4. Masking & Row Access Policies — writing policies, CURRENT_ROLE vs IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION, mapping tables and testing.
  5. Object Tagging & Data Classification — allowed values, inheritance and propagation, tag-based masking and sensitive data classification.
  6. Secure Views & Secure Functions — how a normal view can leak, what SECURE changes and costs.
  7. Secure Data Sharing & the Marketplace — shares, database roles, per-consumer rows, reader accounts and listings.
  8. Encryption, Key Management & Compliance — the key hierarchy, rotation vs rekeying, Tri-Secret Secure and shared responsibility.
  9. Auditing with ACCOUNT_USAGE & Access History — login, query and access history, latency, and answering "who read this column?".
  10. Project — A Governed Multi-Team Platform — tested role design, tag-based masking, region row access, network rules and a PII-holder alert.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: You can secure and govern a shared platform. Level 4 is about building on Snowflake and running it well: UDFs, stored procedures and Snowpark, Cortex AI functions, cost management, warehouse scaling, replication and failover, CI/CD with dbt and Snowflake CLI, and migrating from another warehouse, ending with a cost-aware platform capstone.

docs.title: 01 · Access Control: Roles, Privileges & Hierarchies
docs.text: In Snowflake, privileges are granted to roles, and roles are granted to users (and to other roles). Nothing is accessible unless a grant allows it. That model is simple, and in a real account it grows into hundreds of roles and thousands of grants that nobody can hold in their head. This lesson covers the built-in roles, the design pattern that keeps custom roles manageable, the features that keep grants from rotting, and a small offline tool for answering "who can read this table?" from a grant script.

docs.title: The system roles
docs.text:
From Snowflake's documentation:

Role Purpose ACCOUNTADMIN Top-level role. Encapsulates SYSADMIN and SECURITYADMIN; account parameters, billing. Grant to very few users. SECURITYADMIN Manages any grant globally (MANAGE GRANTS); creates and manages users and roles. Inherits USERADMIN. USERADMIN Creates users and roles (CREATE USER, CREATE ROLE). SYSADMIN Creates warehouses, databases and the objects in them. Custom roles should roll up to it. PUBLIC Granted automatically to every user and role. Anything it owns is available to everyone. ORGADMIN / GLOBALORGADMIN Organization-level tasks (accounts, org-wide usage). GLOBALORGADMIN exists only in the organization account.

Snowflake's own recommendations for ACCOUNTADMIN: require MFA for its users, assign it to at least two users (resetting a lone administrator's lost credentials goes through support procedures that can take up to two business days), and don't use it to create objects. Day-to-day work happens in custom roles under SYSADMIN.

docs.title: Designing roles: access roles and functional roles
docs.text:
The pattern that scales is two layers:

  • Access roles hold privileges on objects, one per (container, level): sales_mart_read, sales_mart_write, sales_raw_read. They are never granted to users directly.
  • Functional roles describe what people do (analyst, data_engineer, finance_viewer) and are composed from access roles. Users get functional roles.
USE ROLE USERADMIN;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_mart_read;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_mart_write;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_raw_read;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS analyst;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS data_engineer;

USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sales TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_write;
GRANT INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_write;
GRANT ROLE sales_mart_read TO ROLE sales_mart_write;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sales TO ROLE sales_raw_read;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sales.raw TO ROLE sales_raw_read;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.raw TO ROLE sales_raw_read;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.raw TO ROLE sales_raw_read;

GRANT ROLE sales_mart_read TO ROLE analyst;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE bi_wh TO ROLE analyst;
GRANT ROLE analyst TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT ROLE sales_mart_write TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT ROLE sales_raw_read TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE etl_wh TO ROLE data_engineer;

-- every functional role rolls up to SYSADMIN, so administrators can manage what these roles own
GRANT ROLE analyst TO ROLE SYSADMIN;
GRANT ROLE data_engineer TO ROLE SYSADMIN;

GRANT ROLE analyst TO USER ana;
GRANT ROLE data_engineer TO USER ben;

Three details make the difference between grants that work and grants that rot:

  • Reading a table needs USAGE on its database and schema as well as SELECT on the table. Missing USAGE is the most common "it says the table doesn't exist" problem.
  • ON FUTURE TABLES grants privileges on tables created later. ON ALL TABLES covers only those that exist now. You almost always want both.
  • A role inherits everything granted to roles granted to it. data_engineer gets everything analyst can do.

docs.title: Inspecting grants
docs.text:
SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE analyst;              -- what this role has been granted
SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE analyst;              -- who (users, roles) has this role
SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE sales.mart.daily_revenue;
SHOW FUTURE GRANTS IN SCHEMA sales.mart;
SHOW GRANTS TO USER ana;

These show direct grants. Effective access through the hierarchy has to be computed, and that's the job of the next section's tool (or of the GRANTS_TO_ROLES and GRANTS_TO_USERS views in ACCOUNT_USAGE, Level 3 · 09).

docs.title: Who can read this table? An offline analyser
docs.text:
Grant scripts belong in version control, and reviewing them is much easier with a tool that computes effective access. Here is a deliberately small model of Snowflake's RBAC in Python. It ignores ownership, secondary roles and database roles, and covers the grant forms above:

"""A small model of Snowflake role-based access control, for reasoning about grant scripts offline.
Understands:  GRANT ROLE r TO ROLE p | GRANT ROLE r TO USER u |
              GRANT <privs> ON <TYPE> <name> TO ROLE r   (privs comma-separated; TYPE = WAREHOUSE, DATABASE, SCHEMA, TABLE, VIEW)
              GRANT <privs> ON ALL|FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA <schema> TO ROLE r
It computes effective privileges through the role hierarchy (a role has the privileges of every role granted to it).
It is a teaching model: it ignores ownership, secondary roles, database roles and managed-access rules."""
import re
from collections import defaultdict

class Account:
    def __init__(self):
        self.parents = defaultdict(set)      # role -> roles it is granted to (its "parents")
        self.children = defaultdict(set)     # role -> roles granted to it (it inherits these)
        self.user_roles = defaultdict(set)
        self.privs = defaultdict(set)        # role -> {(PRIV, TYPE, NAME)}
        self.roles = {"ACCOUNTADMIN", "SECURITYADMIN", "USERADMIN", "SYSADMIN", "PUBLIC"}
        for child, parent in [("SYSADMIN", "ACCOUNTADMIN"), ("SECURITYADMIN", "ACCOUNTADMIN"), ("USERADMIN", "SECURITYADMIN")]:
            self._role_to_role(child, parent)

    def _role_to_role(self, child, parent):
        self.children[parent].add(child); self.parents[child].add(parent); self.roles |= {child, parent}

    def run(self, script):
        script = re.sub(r"--[^\n]*", "", script)            # drop comments first, then split statements
        for stmt in [s.strip() for s in script.split(";") if s.strip()]:
            s = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", stmt).upper()
            if s.startswith("USE ROLE "):
                continue                                  # session context only
            if m := re.fullmatch(r"CREATE ROLE (IF NOT EXISTS )?(\S+)", s):
                self.roles.add(m[2])
            elif m := re.fullmatch(r"GRANT ROLE (\S+) TO ROLE (\S+)", s):
                self._role_to_role(m[1], m[2])
            elif m := re.fullmatch(r"GRANT ROLE (\S+) TO USER (\S+)", s):
                self.user_roles[m[2]].add(m[1])
            elif m := re.fullmatch(r"GRANT (.+?) ON (ALL|FUTURE) TABLES IN SCHEMA (\S+) TO ROLE (\S+)", s):
                for p in m[1].split(","):
                    self.privs[m[4]].add((p.strip(), "TABLE", m[3] + ".*"))
            elif m := re.fullmatch(r"GRANT (.+?) ON (WAREHOUSE|DATABASE|SCHEMA|TABLE|VIEW) (\S+) TO ROLE (\S+)", s):
                for p in m[1].split(","):
                    self.privs[m[4]].add((p.strip(), m[2], m[3]))
            else:
                raise ValueError(f"not understood: {stmt}")

    def inherited(self, role):
        seen, stack = set(), [role]
        while stack:
            r = stack.pop()
            if r not in seen:
                seen.add(r); stack.extend(self.children[r])
        return seen

    def effective(self, role):
        return {p for r in self.inherited(role) for p in self.privs[r]}

    def can(self, role, priv, typ, name):
        for p, t, n in self.effective(role):
            if p in (priv, "ALL") and t == typ and (n == name or (n.endswith(".*") and name.startswith(n[:-1]))):
                return True
        return False

    def who_can(self, priv, typ, name):
        return sorted(u for u, rs in self.user_roles.items() if any(self.can(r, priv, typ, name) for r in rs))

    def orphans(self):
        """custom roles that SYSADMIN does not inherit: objects they own escape SYSADMIN's oversight"""
        return sorted(r for r in self.roles if r not in self.inherited("SYSADMIN") and r not in
                      {"ACCOUNTADMIN", "SECURITYADMIN", "USERADMIN", "PUBLIC"} and r not in self.inherited("SECURITYADMIN"))

Run against the grant script above, plus an intern role that someone granted directly on a PII table and forgot to attach to the hierarchy:

acct = Account()
acct.run(open("grants.sql").read())          # the script above, plus the intern's three statements
for q in [("SELECT", "TABLE", "SALES.MART.DAILY_REVENUE"), ("SELECT", "TABLE", "SALES.RAW.CUSTOMERS_PII"),
          ("UPDATE", "TABLE", "SALES.MART.DAILY_REVENUE")]:
    print(f"{q[0]:6} on {q[2]:26} -> users: {acct.who_can(*q)}")
print("data_engineer inherits:", sorted(acct.inherited("DATA_ENGINEER")))
print("roles SYSADMIN cannot see into:", acct.orphans())

SELECT on SALES.MART.DAILY_REVENUE   -> users: ['ANA', 'BEN']
SELECT on SALES.RAW.CUSTOMERS_PII    -> users: ['BEN', 'CY']
UPDATE on SALES.MART.DAILY_REVENUE   -> users: ['BEN']
data_engineer inherits: ['ANALYST', 'DATA_ENGINEER', 'SALES_MART_READ', 'SALES_MART_WRITE', 'SALES_RAW_READ']
roles SYSADMIN cannot see into: ['INTERN']

The report surfaces two things a reviewer wants to know: the intern can read the PII table, through a direct grant nobody would find by looking at the access roles, and INTERN is an orphan outside the SYSADMIN hierarchy, so objects it creates would be invisible to the administrators who are supposed to manage them.

The first version of this tool had its own bug, and it's instructive. It dropped any statement that started with a comment line, so the -- users heading silently swallowed GRANT ROLE analyst TO USER ana, and the report said Ana couldn't read the mart. A security tool that silently misreads its input is worse than none. Test it on cases where you know the answer.

docs.title: Keeping grants manageable
docs.text:
Managed access schemas. In a normal schema, each object's owner can grant access to it. In a schema created WITH MANAGED ACCESS, only the schema owner (or a role with MANAGE GRANTS) can grant privileges on objects inside, which centralizes control:

CREATE SCHEMA sales.mart WITH MANAGED ACCESS;
ALTER SCHEMA sales.raw ENABLE MANAGED ACCESS;

Database roles are roles that live inside a database. They're the unit for granting access to shared databases (Level 3 · 07), and they travel with a database when it's cloned or replicated:

CREATE DATABASE ROLE sales.reader;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sales.mart TO DATABASE ROLE sales.reader;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO DATABASE ROLE sales.reader;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE sales.reader TO ROLE analyst;

Secondary roles. A session has one primary role, which determines what owns newly created objects, and can also activate secondary roles whose privileges are combined for reads:

USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL;      -- every role granted to the user contributes privileges
USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE;     -- only the primary role

Per Snowflake's docs, privileges granted directly to users (rather than to roles) are only considered when secondary roles are set to ALL. Prefer roles anyway.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Every securable object has exactly one owner role, which has full control, including granting privileges on it (unless the object is in a managed access schema). When a statement runs, Snowflake checks the privileges of the session's primary role and its inherited roles (and secondary roles, if active) for each object involved. The role hierarchy is a directed graph. Granting role A to role B makes B a parent of A, and B inherits A's privileges, transitively. The system roles are already wired into it (USERADMIN → SECURITYADMIN → ACCOUNTADMIN, SYSADMIN → ACCOUNTADMIN), which is why custom roles should be granted to SYSADMIN: otherwise objects they own fall outside the hierarchy that administrators control.

Future grants are stored on the container (schema or database) and applied automatically when a matching object is created there. Schema-level future grants take precedence over database-level ones for the same object type.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Granting privileges to users directly, or functional roles that hold object privileges directly. Use access roles.
  • Forgetting USAGE on the database and schema.
  • Only ON ALL TABLES, so tomorrow's table is inaccessible. Add ON FUTURE TABLES.
  • Custom roles not rolled up to SYSADMIN. Orphaned ownership.
  • Using ACCOUNTADMIN for daily work, or having only one ACCOUNTADMIN user.
  • Objects owned by PUBLIC. Everyone can access them.
  • Reviewing grant scripts by eye. Compute effective access, and test the tool that computes it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Build the access-role and functional-role structure for two domains (sales, hr) with read and write levels, in a trial account. Then answer with SHOW GRANTS and your own reasoning: can an analyst read hr.mart.salaries?
  2. Extend rbac.py to understand GRANT DATABASE ROLE … TO ROLE … and GRANT OWNERSHIP ON TABLE …, and add a report of every user who can write to any table in sales.mart.
  3. Create a managed access schema and show that a table owner who isn't the schema owner can't grant SELECT on their own table.
  4. Find every custom role in your account that isn't granted (directly or indirectly) to SYSADMIN, using SHOW ROLES and SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE with RESULT_SCAN.

docs.title: 02 · Authentication: MFA, Key Pairs, OAuth & SSO
docs.text: Authentication answers who is this? before access control (the previous lesson) answers what may they do?. In Snowflake this area has changed more in 2025–2026 than in the previous decade, because Snowflake has been retiring single-factor password sign-ins account by account. This lesson covers the rules as they stand, the methods to use for people and for programs, and what a key-pair sign-in actually sends, built and verified locally.

docs.title: The end of single-factor passwords
docs.text:
Snowflake's documentation ("Planning for the deprecation of single-factor password sign-ins") lays out a phased timeline. Its estimated dates, as published in October 2026:

Estimated date Affected users Phase Sep 2025 – Jan 2026 human users mandatory MFA for all Snowsight users May 2026 – Jul 2026 human users, legacy service users strong authentication for new users Aug 2026 – Oct 2026 human users, legacy service users strong authentication for all users

When the final phase is enforced, all human users must use a second factor with a password, and non-human users are blocked from password authentication altogether. Snowflake notifies each account of its enforcement date, and the documentation notes that some account types (reader accounts, trial accounts and Snowflake Postgres) are excluded. Because the final phase falls in exactly the months this course was written, check your account's notification and the current page rather than relying on these dates.

The distinction that drives everything is the user's TYPE:

TYPE Who Allowed to authenticate with PERSON (or unset) humans SSO, or password plus MFA, or key pair / PAT for programmatic tools SERVICE applications, pipelines key pair, OAuth, programmatic access tokens, workload identity federation; no password LEGACY_SERVICE transitional password temporarily; being phased out 
CREATE USER etl_service TYPE = SERVICE DEFAULT_ROLE = data_engineer DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = etl_wh;
ALTER USER old_bi_tool SET TYPE = LEGACY_SERVICE;     -- buys time; plan the migration
SHOW USERS;                                           -- check the type column across the account

docs.title: MFA for people
docs.text: Snowflake supports three second factors: passkeys (which Snowflake's documentation recommends for security and usability), authenticator apps generating time-based one-time codes (TOTP), and Duo. Users enroll in Snowsight. For SSO users, MFA is normally enforced by the identity provider, and an authentication policy decides whether Snowflake additionally requires its own.

docs.title: Key pairs for programs, and what they actually send
docs.text:
Lesson 02 of Level 1 set up key-pair authentication for Snowflake CLI. Here is what a driver does with the key, built locally from Snowflake's documented claim format and verified the way the server verifies it. Nothing is sent anywhere:

import base64, hashlib, time, json
import jwt                                            # PyJWT
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import serialization

private_key = serialization.load_pem_private_key(open("rsa_key.p8", "rb").read(), password=None)
public_der = private_key.public_key().public_bytes(serialization.Encoding.DER,
                                                   serialization.PublicFormat.SubjectPublicKeyInfo)
fingerprint = "SHA256:" + base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha256(public_der).digest()).decode()

account, user = "MYORG-MYACCOUNT", "ANA"              # upper case, '.' in the account replaced by '-'
now = int(time.time())
claims = {"iss": f"{account}.{user}.{fingerprint}", "sub": f"{account}.{user}", "iat": now, "exp": now + 3600}
token = jwt.encode(claims, private_key, algorithm="RS256")
print("fingerprint:", fingerprint)
print("JWT header :", json.dumps(jwt.get_unverified_header(token)))
print("JWT claims :", json.dumps({k: claims[k] for k in ("iss", "sub")}))
print("token length:", len(token), "characters")
decoded = jwt.decode(token, private_key.public_key(), algorithms=["RS256"])   # what the server does
print("verified with public key:", decoded["sub"])

fingerprint: SHA256:xWy4qmg9a9Y2zY8a0g/qRNp2QGRbDv7emETjmB0BSSU=
JWT header : {"alg": "RS256", "typ": "JWT"}
JWT claims : {"iss": "MYORG-MYACCOUNT.ANA.SHA256:xWy4qmg9a9Y2zY8a0g/qRNp2QGRbDv7emETjmB0BSSU=", "sub": "MYORG-MYACCOUNT.ANA"}
token length: 571 characters
verified with public key: MYORG-MYACCOUNT.ANA
token from another key: InvalidSignatureError

The fingerprint is the same one computed in Level 1 · 02, because it's the same throwaway key. The token names the user and the fingerprint of the key that signed it, so Snowflake knows which registered public key to check the signature against. A token signed by any other key fails verification (the last line, from a second test in the same script). Snowflake's documentation adds two rules seen in the code: the account and user must be upper case, and the token is valid for at most one hour whatever exp says. Drivers create and refresh these tokens for you. Building one by hand is only needed for raw HTTP clients such as the SQL API.

docs.title: Rotating keys without downtime
docs.text:
A user can have two registered public keys at once, which makes rotation a three-step change with no outage:

ALTER USER etl_service SET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2 = 'MIIBIjANBgkqh...new key...';   -- 1. add the new key
-- 2. deploy the new private key to the application and confirm it signs in (DESC USER shows both fingerprints)
ALTER USER etl_service UNSET RSA_PUBLIC_KEY;                                  -- 3. remove the old key

docs.title: Programmatic access tokens
docs.text:
A programmatic access token (PAT) is a secret string a program can use in place of a password: for drivers, the SQL API and tools that only accept a "password" field.

ALTER USER etl_service ADD PROGRAMMATIC ACCESS TOKEN etl_pipeline
  ROLE_RESTRICTION = 'DATA_ENGINEER'
  DAYS_TO_EXPIRY = 30
  COMMENT = 'nightly ELT job';

From the documentation: tokens expire after 15 days by default, can be given up to 365 days (both adjustable with an authentication policy), and by default a user must be subject to a network policy to generate or use one. For service users that's mandatory, which ties the token to known network locations. ROLE_RESTRICTION limits what the token can do to one role. The token value is shown once, at creation, so store it in a secret manager immediately.

docs.title: OAuth, SSO and workload identity
docs.text:
• SSO for people. SAML 2.0 (or OIDC) through your identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID and others), configured as a security integration. Users sign in through the identity provider, which also enforces its own MFA. Combined with SCIM provisioning, users and role memberships are managed in the identity provider rather than in Snowflake.
