  • OAuth for applications acting for a user. Snowflake OAuth (Snowflake issues the tokens, for partner tools like BI products) or External OAuth (your identity provider issues them).
  • Workload identity federation lets workloads running in AWS, Azure or GCP authenticate with their cloud identity instead of a stored secret. It wasn't exercised here, so see Snowflake's documentation for the current providers.

docs.title: Authentication policies
docs.text:
An authentication policy restricts how users may sign in: which clients, which methods, and MFA requirements. Set it on the account and override it for specific users:

CREATE AUTHENTICATION POLICY humans_sso_or_mfa
  CLIENT_TYPES = ('SNOWFLAKE_UI', 'DRIVERS', 'SNOWFLAKE_CLI')
  AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = ('SAML', 'PASSWORD')
  MFA_ENROLLMENT = 'REQUIRED';

CREATE AUTHENTICATION POLICY services_keypair_only
  AUTHENTICATION_METHODS = ('KEYPAIR', 'PROGRAMMATIC_ACCESS_TOKEN');

ALTER ACCOUNT SET AUTHENTICATION POLICY humans_sso_or_mfa;
ALTER USER etl_service SET AUTHENTICATION POLICY services_keypair_only;

Snowflake's guidance includes keeping a separate, less restrictive policy for a break-glass administrator, so that a misconfigured account-level policy can't lock everyone out.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every sign-in goes to the cloud services layer, which applies, in order: network policy (is this IP or private endpoint allowed? next lesson), authentication policy (is this client and method allowed for this user?), the method itself (verify a password plus second factor, a JWT signature against the registered public keys, an OAuth or SAML assertion against the integration's trusted issuer, a PAT against its stored hash), and the user's type restrictions. Success creates a session token tied to the user, and from then on access control works on the session's roles. Key pairs and workload identity are the strongest options for programs because no reusable secret is ever sent: each sign-in carries a fresh, short-lived signed token.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Service accounts using passwords, often with TYPE unset (treated as a human). Make them TYPE = SERVICE with key pairs, and plan ahead for the enforcement date.
  • Shared human logins for tools. Each tool gets its own service user, with its own policy and role.
  • PATs without expiry discipline, or stored in code. Use short expiry, a role restriction and a secret manager.
  • Rotating keys by replacing the only key. Use RSA_PUBLIC_KEY_2 and overlap.
  • An account-wide authentication policy with no break-glass exception.
  • Assuming last year's rules. This area changed through 2025–2026. Re-read the current pages.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. List every user in a trial account with its TYPE, has_password, has_rsa_public_key and has_mfa columns from SHOW USERS (via RESULT_SCAN). Which users would be blocked under the final enforcement phase?
  2. Create a SERVICE user with a key pair, then rotate it to a second key with zero failed sign-ins. Prove it with your pipeline's logs and DESC USER.
  3. Extend make_jwt.py to read the account and user from your Snowflake CLI connection, then call the Snowflake SQL API with the token and X-Snowflake-Authorization-Token-Type: KEYPAIR_JWT to run SELECT CURRENT_USER().
  4. Write the authentication policies for your organization: humans via SSO, services via key pair or PAT, and one break-glass administrator. Explain the precedence.

docs.title: 03 · Network Policies & Private Connectivity
docs.text: Authentication proves who someone is. A network policy decides where they may connect from. A stolen key used from an attacker's laptop is still a valid key, but if the account only accepts connections from your VPN and your pipeline's NAT gateway, it doesn't get in. Network policies are one of the cheapest, highest-value controls in Snowflake, and since 2025–2026 they're also a prerequisite for features such as programmatic access tokens for service users (Level 3 · 02).

docs.title: Network rules and network policies
docs.text:
Snowflake separates what an address is from what you do with it:

  • A network rule is a schema-level object that names a set of network identifiers: IPv4/IPv6 ranges, AWS VPC endpoint IDs, Azure private-link IDs, GCP Private Service Connect IDs (for inbound), or host:port pairs (for outbound).
  • A network policy combines rules into an allowed list and a blocked list, and is attached to the account, a user, or a security integration.
USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS security_db;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS security_db.network;

CREATE NETWORK RULE security_db.network.corp_vpn      TYPE = IPV4 MODE = INGRESS VALUE_LIST = ('203.0.113.0/24');
CREATE NETWORK RULE security_db.network.office_lisbon TYPE = IPV4 MODE = INGRESS VALUE_LIST = ('198.51.100.16/28');
CREATE NETWORK RULE security_db.network.etl_nat       TYPE = IPV4 MODE = INGRESS VALUE_LIST = ('192.0.2.10/32');
CREATE NETWORK RULE security_db.network.known_bad     TYPE = IPV4 MODE = INGRESS VALUE_LIST = ('203.0.113.66/32');

CREATE NETWORK POLICY account_default
  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULE_LIST = ('security_db.network.corp_vpn', 'security_db.network.office_lisbon')
  BLOCKED_NETWORK_RULE_LIST = ('security_db.network.known_bad');

CREATE NETWORK POLICY etl_only
  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULE_LIST = ('security_db.network.etl_nat');

ALTER ACCOUNT SET NETWORK_POLICY = account_default;
ALTER USER etl_service SET NETWORK_POLICY = etl_only;

(The older ALLOWED_IP_LIST and BLOCKED_IP_LIST properties still work, but Snowflake's documentation says new policies should use network rules, and advises against mixing both in one policy.)

docs.title: How a request is judged
docs.text:
From Snowflake's documentation:

  1. The blocked list is applied first. An address that matches a blocked rule is refused, even if it's also in the allowed list.
  2. Otherwise the address must match the allowed list.
  3. When policies exist at several levels, the most specific one wins: a user's policy overrides the account's (security-integration policies have their own precedence rules).
  4. For requests arriving over private connectivity, if the allowed list contains private-endpoint rules (AWSVPCEID, AZURELINKID), IPv4/IPv6 rules are ignored for those requests.

These rules can be modelled exactly, which lets you test a policy change before applying it to an account where a mistake locks everyone out. A small evaluator (Python, ipaddress module, run locally), configured with the rules and policies above:

"""Evaluate Snowflake-style network policies offline (a model of the documented rules):
- a policy has allowed and blocked network rules (IPv4 CIDR lists here);
- the blocked list is applied first; then the request must match the allowed list;
- the most specific policy wins: user > account (security-integration policies are not modelled)."""
import ipaddress

RULES = {   # network rule name -> CIDR list (as in CREATE NETWORK RULE ... VALUE_LIST)
    "corp_vpn":       ["203.0.113.0/24"],
    "office_lisbon":  ["198.51.100.16/28"],
    "etl_nat":        ["192.0.2.10/32"],
    "known_bad":      ["203.0.113.66/32"],
}
POLICIES = {
    "account_default": {"allowed": ["corp_vpn", "office_lisbon"], "blocked": ["known_bad"]},
    "etl_only":        {"allowed": ["etl_nat"],                   "blocked": []},
}
ACCOUNT_POLICY = "account_default"
USER_POLICY = {"ETL_SERVICE": "etl_only"}          # ALTER USER etl_service SET NETWORK_POLICY = etl_only

def in_rules(ip, rule_names):
    return any(ipaddress.ip_address(ip) in ipaddress.ip_network(c) for r in rule_names for c in RULES[r])

def decide(user, ip):
    name = USER_POLICY.get(user, ACCOUNT_POLICY)
    p = POLICIES[name]
    if in_rules(ip, p["blocked"]):
        return name, "DENY (blocked list)"
    return name, "ALLOW" if in_rules(ip, p["allowed"]) else "DENY (not in allowed list)"

for user, ip, note in [("ANA", "203.0.113.25", "on the VPN"),
                       ("ANA", "203.0.113.66", "VPN address on the blocked list"),
                       ("ANA", "198.51.100.20", "Lisbon office"),
                       ("ANA", "198.51.100.40", "outside the office /28"),
                       ("ETL_SERVICE", "192.0.2.10", "pipeline's NAT gateway"),
                       ("ETL_SERVICE", "203.0.113.25", "stolen key used from the VPN")]:
    policy, verdict = decide(user, ip)
    print(f"{user:12} {ip:15} {note:34} policy={policy:16} {verdict}")

ANA          203.0.113.25    on the VPN                         policy=account_default  ALLOW
ANA          203.0.113.66    VPN address on the blocked list    policy=account_default  DENY (blocked list)
ANA          198.51.100.20   Lisbon office                      policy=account_default  ALLOW
ANA          198.51.100.40   outside the office /28             policy=account_default  DENY (not in allowed list)
ETL_SERVICE  192.0.2.10      pipeline's NAT gateway             policy=etl_only         ALLOW
ETL_SERVICE  203.0.113.25    stolen key used from the VPN       policy=etl_only         DENY (not in allowed list)

Two lines are worth a second look. 203.0.113.66 is inside the VPN range and on the blocked list, and blocked wins. And ETL_SERVICE is denied from the VPN, an address the account policy allows, because its own user-level policy is the most specific one and allows only the NAT gateway. That's exactly the protection you want for a service user's key: it's useless outside the pipeline's network.

docs.title: Don't lock yourself out
docs.text:
A network policy on the account applies to every user, administrators included. Before ALTER ACCOUNT SET NETWORK_POLICY:

  • confirm your own current address is allowed (SELECT CURRENT_IP_ADDRESS(););
  • set it first on a test user (ALTER USER test_user SET NETWORK_POLICY = …) and sign in as that user;
  • keep a break-glass administrator with a user-level policy that allows a known, controlled location;
  • remember that BI tools, ETL services and Snowflake Native Apps connecting from vendor IP ranges need rules too.

docs.title: Private connectivity
docs.text:
Business Critical Edition (and above) supports private connectivity, such as AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link and Google Cloud Private Service Connect, so traffic from your cloud network reaches Snowflake without crossing the public internet. Combined with network rules of type AWSVPCEID/AZURELINKID/GCPPSCID and a policy that allows only those, the account becomes unreachable from the internet entirely. Setting it up involves your cloud account's networking and DNS, and Snowflake's system functions for authorizing endpoints, which weren't exercised for this course. Follow the provider-specific guides.

Internal stages can be restricted to private endpoints as well (network rules in INTERNAL_STAGE mode, with an account parameter enabled), which matters because PUT/GET traffic goes to the stage's cloud storage, not to Snowflake's service endpoint.

docs.title: Egress: controlling what Snowflake can reach
docs.text:
Rules with MODE = EGRESS and TYPE = HOST_PORT describe outbound destinations. They're used with external access integrations, which let Python UDFs and procedures call external APIs, so code in Snowflake can only reach hosts you've explicitly listed:

CREATE NETWORK RULE security_db.network.fx_api_egress
  MODE = EGRESS TYPE = HOST_PORT VALUE_LIST = ('api.exchangerate.example:443');

CREATE EXTERNAL ACCESS INTEGRATION fx_api_access
  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULES = (security_db.network.fx_api_egress)
  ENABLED = TRUE;

Level 4 · 03 uses this from a Python function.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Network policy checks happen in the cloud services layer at authentication time, before credentials are even evaluated (Level 3 · 02). The service determines the request's source (the client's public IP, or the private endpoint ID it arrived through), finds the most specific policy for the user or integration involved, evaluates blocked rules, then allowed rules, and refuses the connection if they don't permit it. (How a policy change affects sessions that are already open isn't covered here. Test it in your own account before relying on it in an incident.) Egress rules are enforced differently: the sandbox that runs UDFs and procedures can only open network connections to destinations listed in an external access integration the function was created with.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Applying an untested account policy and locking out administrators and every integration.
  • 0.0.0.0/0 in an allowed list, "temporarily".
  • No user-level policies for service users, which leaves stolen keys usable from anywhere the account allows.
  • Mixing old IP lists and network rules in one policy.
  • Forgetting vendor IPs for SaaS tools that connect to Snowflake.
  • Securing the service endpoint but not internal stages in a private-connectivity design.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Extend netpolicy.py to support IPv6 rules and a security-integration level, and add a test where a user policy is less restrictive than the account policy. Which one applies?
  2. In a trial account, create a network rule for your current IP (from CURRENT_IP_ADDRESS()), a policy, and apply it to a test user. Sign in as that user from another network (a phone hotspot) and observe the refusal.
  3. Write a query over SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY that lists failed sign-ins in the last 7 days by client_ip and error_message. Which ones look like network-policy blocks?
  4. Design the network policies for an account used by an office, a VPN, two SaaS BI tools and one ETL service, including a break-glass path.

docs.title: 04 · Masking & Row Access Policies
docs.text: Role-based access control (lesson 01) works at the level of whole objects: a role can read a table or it can't. Real requirements are finer. Support staff may see customers' emails but analysts see them masked; the EU team sees EU customers and nobody else's; a fraud investigator needs full card numbers that everyone else sees as ****1234. Snowflake implements these with policies that are attached to tables and evaluated on every query: masking policies for columns and row access policies for rows. Both require Enterprise Edition or higher.

docs.title: A masking policy
docs.text:
A masking policy is a function from the column value (and, optionally, other columns) to what the current session may see:

USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS security_db.policies;

CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.mask_email
  AS (val VARCHAR) RETURNS VARCHAR ->
  CASE
    WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val
    WHEN val IS NULL THEN NULL
    ELSE '***@' || SPLIT_PART(val, '@', 2)
  END;

ALTER TABLE sales.mart.customers MODIFY COLUMN email SET MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.mask_email;
  • The policy's input and output types must match the column's type.
  • A column has at most one masking policy, but one policy can protect any number of columns.
  • The policy applies wherever the column is read: in SELECTs, through views, in joins, in CREATE TABLE AS. A user without PII_READER who copies the table copies masked values.
  • Keep policies in a dedicated schema owned by a security role, so table owners can't drop or change them.

docs.title: CURRENT_ROLE() or IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION()?
docs.text:
The condition in the policy decides who sees what, and the obvious way to write it is subtly wrong. CURRENT_ROLE() = 'PII_READER' is true only when that exact role is the session's primary role. IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') is true when the role is the primary role, inherited through the hierarchy, or active as a secondary role. Here's the difference for a typical hierarchy, computed with the RBAC model from lesson 01 (Python, locally; the model ignores secondary roles):

"""Which masking-policy condition shows PII to whom? Compares CURRENT_ROLE() = 'PII_READER'
with IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') (role hierarchy aware), using the RBAC model from lesson 01."""
from rbac import Account
acct = Account()
acct.run("""
CREATE ROLE pii_reader; CREATE ROLE analyst; CREATE ROLE data_engineer; CREATE ROLE support;
GRANT ROLE pii_reader TO ROLE support;
GRANT ROLE analyst TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT ROLE pii_reader TO ROLE data_engineer;
GRANT ROLE analyst TO ROLE sysadmin; GRANT ROLE data_engineer TO ROLE sysadmin; GRANT ROLE support TO ROLE sysadmin;
""")
def mask(email): return "***@" + email.split("@")[1]
email = "ana.lima@example.com"
print(f"{'session primary role':22} {'CURRENT_ROLE() check':24} {'IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION check':24}")
for role in ["PII_READER", "SUPPORT", "DATA_ENGINEER", "ANALYST", "SYSADMIN", "ACCOUNTADMIN"]:
    current = email if role == "PII_READER" else mask(email)
    in_session = email if "PII_READER" in acct.inherited(role) else mask(email)
    print(f"{role:22} {current:24} {in_session:24}")

session primary role   CURRENT_ROLE() check     IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION check
PII_READER             ana.lima@example.com     ana.lima@example.com    
SUPPORT                ***@example.com          ana.lima@example.com    
DATA_ENGINEER          ***@example.com          ana.lima@example.com    
ANALYST                ***@example.com          ***@example.com         
SYSADMIN               ***@example.com          ana.lima@example.com    
ACCOUNTADMIN           ***@example.com          ana.lima@example.com
  • With CURRENT_ROLE(), only a session using PII_READER as its primary role sees emails. SUPPORT, which was granted PII_READER precisely so support staff could see them, gets masked values. That's the most common masking-policy bug report.
  • With IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION(), inheritance works as intended for SUPPORT and DATA_ENGINEER, and ANALYST stays masked. But SYSADMIN and ACCOUNTADMIN see the raw data too, because every custom role rolls up to them (lesson 01's recommended hierarchy).

The second point is a design decision, not a bug. If administrators must not see PII, express that explicitly, for example by granting PII roles outside the SYSADMIN branch and managing them from a dedicated security role. Whatever you choose, write it down and test it.

docs.title: Conditional masking: using another column
docs.text:
Policies can take extra arguments from other columns in the same row:

CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.mask_email_unless_consented
  AS (val VARCHAR, marketing_consent BOOLEAN) RETURNS VARCHAR ->
  CASE
    WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val
    WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('MARKETING') AND marketing_consent THEN val
    ELSE '***@' || SPLIT_PART(val, '@', 2)
  END;

ALTER TABLE sales.mart.customers MODIFY COLUMN email
  SET MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.mask_email_unless_consented USING (email, marketing_consent);

docs.title: Row access policies
docs.text:
A row access policy returns TRUE for rows the session may see. Scaling it beyond a couple of roles needs a mapping table that says which roles see which regions:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS security_db.policies.region_access (role_name VARCHAR, region VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO security_db.policies.region_access VALUES
  ('SALES_EU', 'EU'), ('SALES_US', 'US'), ('SALES_GLOBAL', 'EU'), ('SALES_GLOBAL', 'US'), ('SALES_GLOBAL', 'APAC');

CREATE OR REPLACE ROW ACCESS POLICY security_db.policies.region_rows
  AS (row_region VARCHAR) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
  IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('DATA_ENGINEER')
  OR EXISTS (
       SELECT 1 FROM security_db.policies.region_access m
       WHERE IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION(m.role_name) AND m.region = row_region
     );

ALTER TABLE sales.mart.orders ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY security_db.policies.region_rows ON (region);
  • Granting a new team access is an INSERT into the mapping table, with no policy change.
  • A table can have one row access policy, but the policy can take several columns.
  • Snowflake's documentation recommends keeping the mapping table in the same database as the protected table, and for performance, considering a memoizable function in place of the mapping table lookup, and testing with realistic workloads. The policy runs as part of every query.
  • Rows a session can't see behave as if they don't exist: COUNT(*), SUM and joins all see the filtered table. Two analysts with different roles get different, consistent answers to the same query.

docs.title: Testing policies without switching users
docs.text:
EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT runs a query as if the session had a given role or set of roles, so you can check policies from one administrative session:

EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(CURRENT_ROLE => 'ANALYST')
  AS SELECT email FROM sales.mart.customers LIMIT 5;

EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(SNOWFLAKE$SESSION_ACTIVATED_ROLES => ('SUPPORT', 'PII_READER', 'PUBLIC'))
  AS SELECT email FROM sales.mart.customers LIMIT 5;

Make this part of deployment: for each policy, a small set of POLICY_CONTEXT queries with the expected visible or masked result per role. It's the SQL counterpart of the Python model above.

docs.title: Where policies are attached
docs.text:
SELECT * FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.POLICY_REFERENCES(POLICY_NAME => 'security_db.policies.mask_email'));
SELECT * FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.POLICY_REFERENCES(REF_ENTITY_NAME => 'sales.mart.customers', REF_ENTITY_DOMAIN => 'table'));

Attaching policies column by column doesn't scale to hundreds of tables. The next lesson attaches them to tags, so every column tagged pii=email is masked automatically.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Policies are schema-level objects evaluated by the query compiler. When a query references a protected column, the compiler rewrites the query so that the column's every occurrence is wrapped in the policy expression, with the session's context (current role, activated roles, user) available to functions like IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION. A row access policy becomes an extra predicate applied to the table before anything else touches it. Because the rewrite happens below views and joins, there's no way to read around a policy by querying through a view or copying the data. The masked values are what the warehouse ever computes with.

This also explains the performance advice. The policy body runs for every row (or is joined into the plan). A mapping table lookup per row is a join, so policies that call subqueries can slow large scans, and memoizable functions let Snowflake cache the lookup result per query.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• CURRENT_ROLE() = 'X' when inherited or secondary roles should count. Use IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION.
  • Forgetting that administrators inherit everything under the SYSADMIN hierarchy.
  • Policy owned by the same role that owns the table. The table owner could detach it. Separate duties.
  • Policy type mismatches (a VARCHAR policy on a VARIANT column).
  • Mapping tables nobody owns. They become the real access-control list, so treat them that way.
  • Never testing with POLICY_CONTEXT.
  • Assuming masked data is safe to copy into an unprotected table. It is, because it's masked, but now the team can never get the real values from that copy.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Implement mask_email with CURRENT_ROLE() first, then with IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION(), and run the same POLICY_CONTEXT queries for SUPPORT and DATA_ENGINEER. Reproduce the model's table in your account.
  2. Write a masking policy for a card-number column that shows the last four digits to SUPPORT and the full number only to FRAUD_INVESTIGATOR.
  3. Add the region row access policy to the course's orders table (add a region column derived from country), and prove with POLICY_CONTEXT that SALES_EU sees only EU rows and SALES_GLOBAL sees all.
  4. Decide whether SYSADMIN should see PII in your organization. Then change the role design so the model's output matches that decision.

docs.title: 05 · Object Tagging & Data Classification
docs.text: Attaching a masking policy to each column (lesson 04) works for ten columns. It doesn't work for ten thousand across hundreds of tables that teams create every week. Tags let you describe data once (pii = 'email', cost_center = 'marketing') and drive governance from those descriptions: masking that follows the tag, cost reports by tag, audits of where sensitive data lives. Sensitive data classification goes a step further and proposes the tags for you. This lesson covers both, including why proposed tags still need a human.

docs.title: Creating and setting tags
docs.text:
USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS security_db.tags;

CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS security_db.tags.pii
  ALLOWED_VALUES 'email', 'phone', 'name', 'address', 'national_id'
  COMMENT = 'Kind of personal data in a column';

CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS security_db.tags.cost_center
  COMMENT = 'Who pays for this object';

ALTER TABLE sales.mart.customers MODIFY COLUMN email SET TAG security_db.tags.pii = 'email';
ALTER TABLE sales.mart.customers MODIFY COLUMN phone SET TAG security_db.tags.pii = 'phone';
ALTER WAREHOUSE bi_wh SET TAG security_db.tags.cost_center = 'analytics';
ALTER DATABASE sales SET TAG security_db.tags.cost_center = 'sales';

From Snowflake's documentation:

  • ALLOWED_VALUES restricts a tag to a fixed vocabulary, so nobody can set pii = 'emial'.
  • Tags are inherited down the object hierarchy. A tag set on a database applies to its schemas, tables and columns, unless a lower level sets its own value. cost_center = 'sales' on the database tags every table in it.
  • Tags can be configured to propagate automatically from source objects to targets (for example, from a table to tables created from it).
  • Quotas: at most 50 tags per object, and at most 50 different tags across the columns of one table.

Finding tags:

SELECT * FROM TABLE(sales.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TAG_REFERENCES('sales.mart.customers', 'TABLE'));
SELECT * FROM TABLE(sales.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TAG_REFERENCES_ALL_COLUMNS('sales.mart.customers', 'TABLE'));

SELECT object_database, object_schema, object_name, column_name, tag_value
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.TAG_REFERENCES
WHERE tag_name = 'PII'
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3, 4;

The apply_method column in these results shows whether a tag was set manually, inherited or propagated.

docs.title: Tag-based masking: protect every tagged column
docs.text:
Set masking policies on the tag, and every column carrying that tag is masked by the policy matching the column's data type, with no per-column ALTER:

CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.pii_string
  AS (val VARCHAR) RETURNS VARCHAR ->
  CASE
    WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val
    WHEN SYSTEM$GET_TAG_ON_CURRENT_COLUMN('security_db.tags.pii') = 'email' THEN '***@' || SPLIT_PART(val, '@', 2)
    ELSE '*** masked ***'
  END;

CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.pii_number
  AS (val NUMBER) RETURNS NUMBER ->
  CASE WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val ELSE NULL END;

ALTER TAG security_db.tags.pii SET MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.pii_string,
                                   MASKING POLICY security_db.policies.pii_number;
  • A tag can carry one masking policy per data type. A VARCHAR column tagged pii uses pii_string, and a NUMBER column uses pii_number.
  • SYSTEM$GET_TAG_ON_CURRENT_COLUMN lets one policy behave differently per tag value: partial masking for emails, full masking for everything else.
  • A masking policy assigned directly to a column takes precedence over a tag-based one, which is how you make exceptions.
  • Because tags can be set at the table, schema or database level, tagging a whole schema pii masks every string column in it. That's powerful, and too broad for most schemas. Tag columns.

The effect is a governance workflow where new tables are protected as soon as their columns are tagged correctly, which moves the problem to getting the tags right.

docs.title: Sensitive data classification
docs.text:
Sensitive data classification (Enterprise Edition) samples column values, assigns each sensitive column a semantic category (such as EMAIL, NAME, PHONE_NUMBER) and a privacy category (identifier, quasi-identifier, sensitive), and records them as system tags (SNOWFLAKE.CORE.SEMANTIC_CATEGORY, SNOWFLAKE.CORE.PRIVACY_CATEGORY). A classification profile associated with a database classifies its tables and views automatically, and can map those system tags onto your own tags, so a column classified as EMAIL gets security_db.tags.pii = 'email' and therefore the masking policy:

CREATE OR REPLACE SNOWFLAKE.DATA_PRIVACY.CLASSIFICATION_PROFILE security_db.tags.default_profile({
    'minimum_object_age_for_classification_days': 0,
    'auto_tag': true
  });

ALTER DATABASE sales SET CLASSIFICATION_PROFILE = 'security_db.tags.default_profile';

The current documentation also describes custom categories (your own detectors) and an optional AI mode. Check it for the profile options available in your account. This feature wasn't run for this course.

docs.title: Why classification still needs review
docs.text:
Classification is sample-based and probabilistic. To see why that matters, here is a toy classifier (written for this lesson, not Snowflake's) that samples 1,000 customers from the course data and tests each column against simple detectors:

"""A toy column classifier (NOT Snowflake's): sample values, test each column against simple detectors,
and report the share of non-null sampled values that match. Illustrates why classification is
sample-based and probabilistic."""
import json, random, re
random.seed(1)
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("customers.json")]
flat = [{"customer_id": r["customer_id"], "name": r["name"], "country": r["country"], "signup": r["signup"],
         "email": r["contact"]["email"], "phone": r["contact"]["phone"]} for r in rows]
DETECTORS = {
    "EMAIL": re.compile(r"^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}$"),
    "PHONE_NUMBER": re.compile(r"^\+?[0-9][0-9\- ]{6,}$"),
    "COUNTRY": re.compile(r"^(PT|ES|FR|DE|IN|US|BR|GB)$"),
    "DATE": re.compile(r"^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$"),
}
sample = random.sample(flat, 1000)
for col in flat[0]:
    values = [str(r[col]) for r in sample if r[col] is not None]
    best = max(DETECTORS, key=lambda d: sum(bool(DETECTORS[d].match(v)) for v in values))
    share = sum(bool(DETECTORS[best].match(v)) for v in values) / len(values)
    nulls = sum(r[col] is None for r in sample)
    label = best if share >= 0.8 else "-"
    print(f"{col:12} nulls {nulls:>3}/1000  best match {best:13} {share:6.1%}  -> {label}")

customer_id  nulls   0/1000  best match EMAIL           0.0%  -> -
name         nulls   0/1000  best match EMAIL           0.0%  -> -
country      nulls   0/1000  best match COUNTRY       100.0%  -> COUNTRY
signup       nulls   0/1000  best match PHONE_NUMBER  100.0%  -> PHONE_NUMBER
email        nulls   0/1000  best match EMAIL         100.0%  -> EMAIL
phone        nulls 120/1000  best match PHONE_NUMBER  100.0%  -> PHONE_NUMBER

It found the email and country columns correctly, and found phone numbers despite 120 null values in the sample. It also labelled signup dates as phone numbers: a value like 2024-11-23 matches a loose phone pattern just as well as a date pattern, and the tie went to the detector listed first. Snowflake's classifier is far more sophisticated than three regular expressions, but the general lesson carries over. Automated classification produces proposals with false positives and false negatives (a free-text "notes" column full of phone numbers that only sometimes matches, an ID that looks like a national identifier). Review the proposed categories, especially before they drive masking automatically, and audit the results periodically.

docs.title: Tags for cost allocation
docs.text:
Tags aren't only for security. Tagging warehouses, databases and users with cost_center lets you attribute credits:

SELECT t.tag_value AS cost_center, SUM(m.credits_used) AS credits_30d
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY m
JOIN SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.TAG_REFERENCES t
  ON t.domain = 'WAREHOUSE' AND t.object_name = m.warehouse_name AND t.tag_name = 'COST_CENTER'
WHERE m.start_time > DATEADD('day', -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 DESC;

Level 4 · 05 builds on this for chargeback.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A tag is a schema-level object, and a tag assignment is metadata linking (tag, value) to an object or column. When a query touches a column, the compiler resolves its effective tags: the column's own assignments, plus those inherited from its table, schema and database, with the most specific level winning. If any effective tag has a masking policy for the column's data type (and no masking policy is set directly on the column), the compiler applies that policy exactly as in lesson 04, with SYSTEM$GET_TAG_ON_CURRENT_COLUMN returning the resolved tag value. Classification runs as a background service that reads samples of column values, evaluates them with its detectors, and writes system tag assignments, which from then on behave like any other tags.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Free-form tag values. Use ALLOWED_VALUES.
  • Tagging at the schema level for masking. Every column of that type gets masked. Tag the columns.
  • One masking policy per tag "for strings" and nothing for numbers or dates, leaving those columns unprotected.
  • Trusting automatic classification without review. It proposes, and someone accountable approves.
  • Tags that nobody queries. Build the audit and cost reports that make them worth maintaining.
  • Forgetting direct policies override tag policies. An old per-column policy silently wins.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create the pii tag with allowed values and tag-based masking policies for VARCHAR and NUMBER, then tag the course's customer columns and verify masking with POLICY_CONTEXT for a role without PII_READER.
  2. Tag the sales database with cost_center = 'sales' and one table with cost_center = 'marketing'. Query TAG_REFERENCES and confirm which value each table resolves to.
  3. Fix the toy classifier so dates aren't classified as phone numbers (a stricter phone pattern? a priority order?). Then construct an input that fools your fixed version.
  4. In a trial account, associate a classification profile with a database containing the course's customers, and compare Snowflake's semantic categories with the toy's.

docs.title: 06 · Secure Views & Secure Functions
docs.text: A view is the classic way to expose part of a table: some columns, some rows. It looks like an access-control boundary, but by default a view in Snowflake is not a security boundary. The optimizer is free to rearrange a query through a view, and the view's SQL text is visible to people who can see the view. Secure views (and secure functions) close both gaps, at a price in performance. They're also the default for sharing data with other accounts (next lesson).

docs.title: How a normal view can leak
docs.text:
A view that exposes only the sales team's salaries:

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW hr.mart.sales_salaries AS
SELECT employee, salary FROM hr.raw.salaries WHERE team = 'sales';

A user who may query only this view wants to know whether anyone in the company earns over 400,000. They can't see those rows, but they can try to make the database evaluate their own expression on them:

SELECT employee
FROM hr.mart.sales_salaries
WHERE 1 / IFF(salary > 400000, 0, 1) = 1;      -- divides by zero only for salaries above 400,000

If the optimizer evaluates the user's predicate before the view's team = 'sales' filter (pushing predicates down and reordering them is a normal optimization), a hidden row with a salary over 400,000 triggers a division-by-zero error. The error itself answers the question. Snowflake's documentation describes exactly this risk with a "widgets" example: for a non-secure view, internal optimizations that need access to the base table's data "might allow data that is hidden from users of the view to be exposed through user code, such as user-defined functions, or other programmatic methods."

Whether the leak happens depends on the plan the optimizer happens to choose. DuckDB 1.5.6 run locally (not Snowflake), with the same table, view and a probe using error():

-- DuckDB 1.5.6 (local), not Snowflake
SELECT employee FROM sales_salaries
WHERE CASE WHEN salary > 400000 THEN error('someone earns over 400k') ELSE TRUE END;

[('ana',), ('ben',)]

SEQ_SCAN … Filters: team='sales'   →   FILTER: CASE WHEN ((salary > 400000)) THEN … error(…) …

Here the plan applied the view's filter inside the scan, before the probe, so nothing leaked. That's the point: with a normal view, safety is an accident of the plan, and a different engine, version or data distribution can produce a different order. A secure view makes the ordering a guarantee instead of an accident.

docs.title: Secure views
docs.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE SECURE VIEW hr.mart.sales_salaries AS
SELECT employee, salary FROM hr.raw.salaries WHERE team = 'sales';

ALTER VIEW hr.mart.some_old_view SET SECURE;

SECURE changes two things, per the documentation:

  1. No leaking optimizations. Snowflake doesn't use the internal optimizations that could expose base-table data through user code. The view's own logic is applied before user predicates can see the rows.
  2. The definition is hidden from users who aren't the owner, in SHOW VIEWS, GET_DDL, the information schema, and even the Query Profile. The internals of a secure view aren't shown there even to its owner, because non-owners might have access to the owner's Query Profile.

The cost: secure views "can execute more slowly than non-secure views", because the optimizer has fewer options. So use SECURE where a view is an access boundary or exposes data to another account, and plain views where it's just a convenience for people who could read the base tables anyway.

SELECT table_catalog, table_schema, table_name, is_secure
FROM hr.INFORMATION_SCHEMA.VIEWS
WHERE table_schema = 'MART';

docs.title: Filtering by who's asking
docs.text:
Secure views can use context functions to show each user or role only their rows. That's row-level security without a row access policy, and common before policies existed:

CREATE OR REPLACE SECURE VIEW sales.mart.my_region_orders AS
SELECT o.*
FROM sales.mart.orders o
JOIN security_db.policies.region_access m
  ON m.region = o.region
 AND IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION(m.role_name);

For new designs, prefer a row access policy (lesson 04): it's attached to the table itself, so every access path is filtered, not just this view. Secure views remain the tool for shaping data (joins, aggregates, renamed columns) for a particular audience, especially another account.

docs.title: Secure functions
docs.text:
UDFs have the same two issues. A normal UDF's body is visible to anyone who can describe it, and the optimizer may evaluate it in ways that expose inputs. SECURE fixes both:

CREATE OR REPLACE SECURE FUNCTION finance.mart.discount_for(customer_tier VARCHAR, order_total NUMBER(12,2))
RETURNS NUMBER(12,2)
AS
$$
  CASE customer_tier
    WHEN 'gold'     THEN order_total * 0.12          -- pricing logic you don't want to publish
    WHEN 'platinum' THEN order_total * 0.18
    ELSE 0
  END
$$;

Use it when the function's logic is confidential (pricing, scoring), or when it's shared with other accounts.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A view is stored as a query that the compiler inlines into every query that uses it. Once inlined, a normal view is just part of one big query, and the optimizer may push the user's filters down, reorder predicates, evaluate expressions early, or use the view's base-table statistics. All of these are good for speed, and some can evaluate user-supplied expressions on rows the view would have removed. For a secure view, the compiler keeps the view as an opaque boundary. The view's filters and projections are applied first, and only their output reaches operators that evaluate user expressions. That rules out the reordering and the optimizations that depend on it, which is the performance cost. Hiding the definition is a separate, simpler rule: metadata commands and the Query Profile redact the view text and internals for anyone but the owner (and not even the owner in the profile).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a normal view as an access boundary. Its safety depends on the plan. Use SECURE (or a policy on the table).
  • Making every view secure. You pay in performance where no boundary exists.
  • Secure views that use CURRENT_ROLE() where role inheritance should count. Use IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION, as in lesson 04.
  • Expecting to debug a secure view in the Query Profile. Its internals are hidden there. Test the defining query separately.
  • Sharing non-secure views without thinking. Shares accept only secure views unless created with SECURE_OBJECTS_ONLY = FALSE. That option exists for performance, and it hands the protections above to the consumer.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create the salaries table and the non-secure view in a trial account, run the division-by-zero probe, and check the Query Profile for where the filters were applied. Repeat with a SECURE view.
  2. As a role that doesn't own the view, run SHOW VIEWS and SELECT GET_DDL('VIEW', …) for both versions. What can you see?
  3. Measure a heavier query (an aggregation over SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF1.ORDERS) through a normal and a secure view with the result cache off. Is there a difference for your query?
  4. Rewrite my_region_orders as a row access policy on the base table, and list the access paths the policy covers that the view didn't.

docs.title: 07 · Secure Data Sharing & the Marketplace
docs.text: Sending data to another company usually means exports, files, pipelines and stale copies. In Snowflake, a provider can share live tables and views with another Snowflake account, and the consumer queries them directly. Per Snowflake's documentation, no data is copied or transferred: sharing works through the services layer and metadata store, shared data takes no storage in the consumer's account, and the consumer pays only for the compute it uses to query. This lesson covers shares from both sides, sharing different rows with different consumers, reader accounts, and listings.

docs.title: The provider side
docs.text:
A share is an object that bundles privileges on database objects and the list of consumer accounts:

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;                 -- or a role granted CREATE SHARE

CREATE SHARE sales_partner_share COMMENT = 'Daily sales for partner retailers';

-- option 1 (recommended): grant through a database role, which the share then receives
CREATE DATABASE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales.partner_reader;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sales.shared TO DATABASE ROLE sales.partner_reader;
GRANT SELECT ON VIEW sales.shared.partner_daily_sales TO DATABASE ROLE sales.partner_reader;

GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sales TO SHARE sales_partner_share;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE sales.partner_reader TO SHARE sales_partner_share;

-- add consumers (organization-based account identifiers)
ALTER SHARE sales_partner_share ADD ACCOUNTS = partnerorg.retail_eu, partnerorg.retail_us;

SHOW SHARES;
DESC SHARE sales_partner_share;

The documentation also allows granting privileges directly to the share (GRANT SELECT ON VIEW … TO SHARE …). Database roles are the better unit. A provider can define several (say partner_reader and partner_finance), and the consumer can map each to different roles on their side.

Rules worth knowing:

  • Shared objects are read-only for consumers: they can't insert, update or delete.
  • A share accepts secure views (and other secure objects) by default. Shares created with SECURE_OBJECTS_ONLY = FALSE can include ordinary views, for performance. In that case the optimizer protections from lesson 06 no longer apply, so only do it when the consumer is allowed to see everything the view reads.
  • A direct share works only between accounts in the same region. Across regions or clouds, use a listing with cross-cloud auto-fulfillment, or replicate the data to an account in the consumer's region and share from there.
  • Revoking a grant or removing an account from the share takes effect immediately.

docs.title: The consumer side
docs.text:
The consumer sees the share as available and creates a read-only database from it:

SHOW SHARES;                                     -- inbound shares appear with kind = INBOUND

CREATE DATABASE partner_sales FROM SHARE providerorg.provider_account.sales_partner_share;

GRANT DATABASE ROLE partner_sales.partner_reader TO ROLE analyst;    -- map provider database roles to local roles

SELECT * FROM partner_sales.shared.partner_daily_sales WHERE sale_date >= CURRENT_DATE - 7;

(Shares built without database roles are granted locally with GRANT IMPORTED PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE partner_sales TO ROLE analyst.) The consumer runs the queries on its own warehouses and pays for that compute. The provider pays for storage, just as before sharing.

docs.title: Different rows for different consumers
docs.text:
A single share to many consumers usually needs each consumer to see only their own rows. Inside a shared secure view, CURRENT_ACCOUNT() returns the consumer's account (its account locator), which turns into an entitlement filter. Snowflake's own sharing example uses exactly this pattern:

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sales.shared.partner_entitlements (consumer_account VARCHAR, partner_id NUMBER);
INSERT INTO sales.shared.partner_entitlements VALUES ('XY11111', 101), ('XY22222', 202);   -- consumer account locators

CREATE OR REPLACE SECURE VIEW sales.shared.partner_daily_sales AS
SELECT s.sale_date, s.partner_id, s.sku, s.units, s.revenue
FROM sales.mart.partner_daily_sales s
JOIN sales.shared.partner_entitlements e
  ON e.partner_id = s.partner_id
 AND e.consumer_account = CURRENT_ACCOUNT();

The view must be SECURE, or the entitlement logic could be bypassed (lesson 06), and the entitlement table stays in the provider account, out of the share. Onboarding a partner becomes two steps: add their account to the share, and insert their entitlement row. Test it as a consumer. Snowflake offers a simulation for exactly this, which per the documentation only works when the current role owns the view:

ALTER SESSION SET SIMULATED_DATA_SHARING_CONSUMER = 'XY11111';
SELECT DISTINCT partner_id FROM sales.shared.partner_daily_sales;       -- expect only 101
ALTER SESSION UNSET SIMULATED_DATA_SHARING_CONSUMER;

Whatever identifier you store in the entitlement table, it must be the one the context function returns in the consumer's account. Verify with the simulation before onboarding a real partner.

docs.title: Reader accounts: sharing with someone who has no Snowflake account
docs.text:
A reader account is a Snowflake account the provider creates and manages for a consumer without one:

CREATE MANAGED ACCOUNT partner_acme_reader
  ADMIN_NAME = acme_admin, ADMIN_PASSWORD = '<a strong generated password>',
  TYPE = READER;

Snowflake's documentation is direct about the cost: the provider pays for all credits consumed by warehouses in the reader account, and they "can consume an unlimited number of credits", so set up a resource monitor on every reader-account warehouse (Level 4 · 05). A reader account is primarily for querying the provider's shared data. It's not a general-purpose account.

docs.title: Listings and the Marketplace
docs.text:
A listing wraps a share with product metadata (description, sample queries, refresh schedule, terms) and offers it privately to named accounts or publicly on the Snowflake Marketplace. Listings are also how data reaches consumers in other regions and clouds, through cross-cloud auto-fulfillment, which replicates the data where it's needed. Paid listings, usage metrics and consumer analytics are part of the provider experience. Listings are managed mainly in Snowsight's provider studio (with SQL and API equivalents). They weren't exercised for this course.

As a consumer, the Marketplace is a source of third-party data (weather, financial, demographic) that appears as a database in your account, without a pipeline.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A share is metadata: a list of objects, the privileges granted on them, and the consumer accounts. When a consumer creates a database from a share, Snowflake creates a catalogue entry in the consumer's account that points at the provider's micro-partitions. Queries from the consumer are compiled and pruned by the services layer exactly like local queries, but the micro-partition files they read belong to the provider's tables, and they're executed on the consumer's warehouse. That's why there's nothing to copy, why the data is always current (a provider commit creates a new table version that consumers see immediately), and why revoking access is instant (the pointer is removed). Because both accounts must reach the same storage, direct shares are limited to one region. Cross-region sharing needs the micro-partitions replicated to the consumer's region first, which is what listing auto-fulfillment and database replication do (Level 4 · 07).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Sharing raw tables when a secure view with an entitlement filter is what the contract allows.
  • Non-secure views in a share without understanding what SECURE_OBJECTS_ONLY = FALSE gives up.
  • Entitlement filters with no test for each consumer. Use the simulation parameter.
  • Reader accounts without resource monitors. The provider pays for unlimited compute.
  • Expecting a direct share to reach another region. Use a listing or replication.
  • Breaking consumers with schema changes. Shared views are an API. Version them (partner_daily_sales_v2) and announce changes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. With two trial accounts in the same region (or one account using SIMULATED_DATA_SHARING_CONSUMER), share the course's daily revenue through a secure view and a database role, and query it from the consumer.
  2. Implement the entitlement view for three partners and prove with the simulation that each sees only its own rows.
  3. Create a reader account, put a 10-credit monthly resource monitor on its warehouse, and explain who receives the alerts.
  4. Draft a listing description for the shared dataset: contents, refresh schedule, sample queries and change policy.

docs.title: 08 · Encryption, Key Management & Compliance
docs.text: Security reviews of a Snowflake deployment almost always ask the same questions. Is the data encrypted? With whose keys? How are keys rotated? Can we revoke Snowflake's access? Which compliance programmes does it support? Most of the answers are "Snowflake does it by default", and a few depend on your edition and on choices you make. This lesson collects what Snowflake's documentation says, so you can answer accurately rather than from memory.

docs.title: Encrypted by default, end to end
docs.text:
From Snowflake's documentation on end-to-end encryption:

  • All customer data at rest is encrypted, and data is encrypted in transit (TLS) to and from the Snowflake service. There's nothing to turn on.
  • Data loaded into tables is stored in Snowflake's file format, encrypted. When it's processed, it's decrypted for the operation and re-encrypted afterwards.
  • Files in internal stages are encrypted by Snowflake automatically, on upload by the client.
  • Files in external stages (your own bucket) are your storage, encrypted as your bucket is configured. Snowflake recommends client-side encryption for them, and supports it for loading and unloading with a stage-level MASTER_KEY (a 128- or 256-bit AES key, Base64-encoded), or with the cloud provider's server-side encryption options:
CREATE STAGE learn_db.raw.s3_encrypted
  URL = 's3://my-company-landing/encrypted/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_landing_int
  ENCRYPTION = (TYPE = 'AWS_SSE_KMS' KMS_KEY_ID = 'arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:123456789012:key/1a2b3c4d-0000-0000-0000-000000000000');
  • Results unloaded to a stage are encrypted per the stage's settings.

docs.title: The key hierarchy
docs.text:
Snowflake's documentation describes a hierarchical key model with four levels, each encrypting ("wrapping") the keys below it:

root key            (in a cloud-provider hardware security module, HSM)
 └─ account master key    (one hierarchy per customer account)
     └─ table master key  (per table)
         └─ file keys     (per micro-partition file)

Two consequences matter. Every account has its own hierarchy, so one customer's keys never protect another's data. And each key protects only a small amount of data, which limits the impact of any single key and makes rotation practical.

docs.title: Rotation vs rekeying
docs.text:
These are different operations, and security questionnaires often confuse them:

Key rotation Periodic rekeying What happens keys older than 30 days are retired, and new keys are created for new data data protected by a retired key older than one year is re-encrypted with a new key Old key kept, used only to decrypt existing data, destroyed when no longer needed destroyed once its data has been re-encrypted Edition all Enterprise and higher, enabled by ACCOUNTADMIN Cost to you none Snowflake documents a possible additional storage charge during the transition 
ALTER ACCOUNT SET PERIODIC_DATA_REKEYING = TRUE;     -- Enterprise+, ACCOUNTADMIN

Rotation is cheap because creating a new key affects only data written afterwards. Rekeying is a real rewrite of stored data, which is why it runs on a yearly cycle, and why a policy that demands "all data re-encrypted under a fresh key regularly" is a rekeying requirement, not a rotation one.

docs.title: Tri-Secret Secure: your key in the chain
docs.text: On Business Critical Edition and above, Tri-Secret Secure combines a Snowflake-maintained key with a customer-managed key held in your cloud provider's key management service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault or Google Cloud KMS) into a composite master key that protects your data. The practical effect: if you revoke Snowflake's access to your key, Snowflake can no longer decrypt your data. That's a strong control for regulated data, and also an availability risk. A mistaken key-policy change or a deleted key makes your data unreadable, by you as well. Enabling it is a coordinated process involving Snowflake Support and your key-management team. It wasn't run for this course, so follow the current documentation step by step.

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text:
Snowflake publishes its certifications and attestations (such as SOC reports, ISO certifications and PCI DSS) and supports regulated workloads (such as HIPAA) on qualifying editions and regions. The current list and its conditions live on Snowflake's Trust Center and compliance pages, and they change, so this course doesn't reproduce it. What matters for practitioners is the shared responsibility split:

Snowflake is responsible for You are responsible for encryption at rest and in transit, key hierarchy, rotation choosing the edition and region your obligations require physical and infrastructure security, service availability users, roles, MFA and authentication policies (lessons 01–02) providing audit data (access history, login history) network policies and private connectivity (lesson 03) classifying and masking sensitive data (lessons 04–05) reviewing and retaining audit logs (next lesson) external stage buckets and their encryption

An auditor asking "is personal data protected?" will want evidence from your side of that table: who can read the customers table, who did read it last month, and how you know.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each micro-partition file is encrypted with its own file key. The file key is stored only in encrypted form, wrapped by the table's master key, which is wrapped by the account master key, which is wrapped by the root key in the HSM. To read a file, the service unwraps the chain from the top, which requires the HSM. That's why keys never leave hardware protection in plain form at the root. Rotating a key means new data gets wrapped under a new key, while old wrapped keys remain readable by their retired parent until they're no longer needed. Rekeying re-encrypts the affected data files themselves under fresh keys, so it's proportional to data volume.

With Tri-Secret Secure, the account-level key material depends on both Snowflake's key and the key in your KMS. Snowflake must call your KMS to obtain it, so revoking that permission breaks the chain at the account level, and every file below becomes undecryptable.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unencrypted external stage buckets because "Snowflake encrypts everything". Your bucket is your responsibility.
  • Confusing rotation with rekeying in policy documents and questionnaires.
  • Promising customer-managed keys on Standard or Enterprise. Tri-Secret Secure requires Business Critical or higher.
  • Tri-Secret Secure without key-lifecycle discipline. A deleted or mis-scoped key is a self-inflicted outage.
  • Copying a compliance list from a blog post. Check Snowflake's current Trust Center pages for your edition and region.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write the one-page answer to a customer's security questionnaire section on encryption for your account: at rest, in transit, key ownership, rotation, rekeying, and external stages. Cite the documentation pages you used.
  2. Check whether periodic rekeying is enabled in your account (SHOW PARAMETERS LIKE 'PERIODIC_DATA_REKEYING' IN ACCOUNT), and decide whether it should be.
  3. Configure an external stage on a bucket with server-side KMS encryption, load the course's order files through it, and confirm that loading still works when the bucket requires encryption.
  4. List the controls from lessons 01–07 that an auditor would ask you to evidence for a table containing personal data, and the query or screen you would show for each.

docs.title: 09 · Auditing with ACCOUNT_USAGE & Access History
docs.text: Every control in this level, whether roles, authentication, network policies or masking, needs evidence that it works and is used. Snowflake records the evidence in the SNOWFLAKE database, mainly in the ACCOUNT_USAGE schema: who logged in from where, every query, every grant, and, with Access History, which columns each query actually read. This lesson covers how to use those views, and the one detail that makes or breaks a data-access audit.

docs.title: ACCOUNT_USAGE vs INFORMATION_SCHEMA
docs.text:
From Snowflake's documentation:

SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE each database's INFORMATION_SCHEMA Scope the whole account one database (plus account-level table functions) Includes dropped objects yes (with a DELETED timestamp) no Latency 45 minutes to 3 hours, varies by view none Retention of history 1 year 7 days to 6 months, varies

Use INFORMATION_SCHEMA for "what's happening right now" and ACCOUNT_USAGE for audits, trends and anything older than a few days. For data you must keep longer than a year, copy the views into your own tables on a schedule (a task, Level 2 · 07).

docs.title: Who can read the audit views
docs.text:
Grant the SNOWFLAKE database's built-in database roles, rather than ACCOUNTADMIN, to auditors and platform teams:

Database role Gives visibility into SNOWFLAKE.OBJECT_VIEWER object metadata SNOWFLAKE.USAGE_VIEWER historical usage (queries, metering) SNOWFLAKE.GOVERNANCE_VIEWER governance data (policies, tags, access history) SNOWFLAKE.SECURITY_VIEWER security data (logins, users, grants) 
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS auditor;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.GOVERNANCE_VIEWER TO ROLE auditor;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.SECURITY_VIEWER TO ROLE auditor;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE bi_wh TO ROLE auditor;

docs.title: Sign-ins
docs.text:
SELECT event_timestamp, user_name, client_ip, reported_client_type,
       first_authentication_factor, second_authentication_factor, is_success, error_message
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY
WHERE event_timestamp > DATEADD('day', -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
  AND is_success = 'NO'
ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC;

Useful audits from this view: failed sign-ins per user and IP (password spraying), successful password sign-ins without a second factor (lesson 02's enforcement), and sign-ins from IPs outside your network rules (which shouldn't succeed if network policies are in place).

docs.title: Grants and role changes
docs.text:
-- who holds ACCOUNTADMIN, directly
SELECT grantee_name AS user_name, created_on
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.GRANTS_TO_USERS
WHERE role = 'ACCOUNTADMIN' AND deleted_on IS NULL;

-- privileges granted in the last 7 days, by whom
SELECT created_on, privilege, granted_on, name, grantee_name, granted_by
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.GRANTS_TO_ROLES
WHERE created_on > DATEADD('day', -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY created_on DESC;

These are the inputs for an effective-access calculation like the rbac.py model in lesson 01: load them into its Account instead of a hand-written script, and you get "who can read this table?" from the live account.

docs.title: Access History: who read which columns
docs.text:
Access History (Enterprise Edition) records, for each query, which objects and columns it read and wrote. The ACCESS_HISTORY view has, among others, these columns per query: query_id, query_start_time, user_name, direct_objects_accessed, base_objects_accessed, objects_modified, policies_referenced, and parent/root query IDs for queries run from procedures.

The two "accessed" columns are the important distinction. From the documentation's view example:

  • direct_objects_accessed lists the objects named in the query. For a query on a view, that's the view and its projected columns.
  • base_objects_accessed lists the underlying tables and columns the data actually came from, including columns used only to filter.

An audit of "who read customers' emails?" that looks only at direct objects misses everyone who read them through a view. To show the difference, here are four invented access-history records in the documented JSON shape, with the same audit query run in DuckDB 1.5.6 locally. This is synthetic data, not Snowflake output:

"""Synthetic ACCESS_HISTORY rows in the documented JSON shape (objectName / objectDomain / columns[columnName]),
and the 'who read customers.email?' audit, run in DuckDB. The rows are invented test data, not Snowflake output."""
import json, duckdb
def obj(name, cols, domain="Table"):
    return {"objectName": name, "objectDomain": domain, "columns": [{"columnName": c} for c in cols]}
rows = [
  ("q1", "2026-10-01 09:00", "ANA", [obj("SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS", ["CUSTOMER_ID", "COUNTRY"])],
                                    [obj("SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS", ["CUSTOMER_ID", "COUNTRY"])]),
  ("q2", "2026-10-02 10:30", "BEN", [obj("SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS", ["EMAIL"])],
                                    [obj("SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS", ["EMAIL"])]),
  # CY reads a VIEW that exposes email: the view is the direct object, the table column is the base object
  ("q3", "2026-10-03 14:00", "CY",  [obj("SALES.MART.CUSTOMER_CONTACTS", ["CONTACT_EMAIL"], "View")],
                                    [obj("SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS", ["EMAIL", "CUSTOMER_ID"])]),
  ("q4", "2026-10-04 08:15", "DEE", [obj("SALES.MART.ORDERS", ["ORDER_ID", "AMOUNT"])],
                                    [obj("SALES.MART.ORDERS", ["ORDER_ID", "AMOUNT"])]),
]
con = duckdb.connect()
con.sql("CREATE TABLE access_history (query_id VARCHAR, query_start_time TIMESTAMP, user_name VARCHAR, direct_objects_accessed JSON, base_objects_accessed JSON)")
con.executemany("INSERT INTO access_history VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)", [(q, t, u, json.dumps(d), json.dumps(b)) for q, t, u, d, b in rows])
for label, col in (("direct_objects_accessed", "direct_objects_accessed"), ("base_objects_accessed", "base_objects_accessed")):
    print(f"who read SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS.EMAIL, judged by {label}:")
    print(con.sql(f"""
      SELECT DISTINCT user_name, query_id
      FROM access_history,
           UNNEST(CAST(json_extract({col}, '$[*]') AS JSON[])) AS o(obj),
           UNNEST(CAST(json_extract(obj, '$.columns[*]') AS JSON[])) AS c(cj)
      WHERE (obj->>'objectName') = 'SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS' AND (cj->>'columnName') = 'EMAIL'
      ORDER BY query_id""").fetchall())

who read SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS.EMAIL, judged by direct_objects_accessed:
[('BEN', 'q2')]
who read SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS.EMAIL, judged by base_objects_accessed:
[('BEN', 'q2'), ('CY', 'q3')]

Judged by direct_objects_accessed, only Ben read the email column. Judged by base_objects_accessed, Cy did too, by querying CUSTOMER_CONTACTS, a view whose CONTACT_EMAIL column comes from CUSTOMERS.EMAIL. The Snowflake version of the correct audit:

SELECT DISTINCT ah.user_name, ah.query_id, ah.query_start_time
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.ACCESS_HISTORY ah,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => ah.base_objects_accessed) obj,
     LATERAL FLATTEN(input => obj.value:"columns") col
WHERE obj.value:"objectName"::VARCHAR = 'SALES.MART.CUSTOMERS'
  AND col.value:"columnName"::VARCHAR = 'EMAIL'
  AND ah.query_start_time > DATEADD('day', -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY ah.query_start_time DESC;

Note the double FLATTEN (objects, then columns) from Level 1 · 07. policies_referenced shows whether a masking or row access policy was applied. Combine it with the query above to separate users who saw masked emails from those who saw raw ones, which is usually the real question.

Access History also powers lineage: objects_modified records which columns a statement wrote and from which source columns, so you can trace, say, where data derived from EMAIL ended up.

docs.title: Turning audits into alerts
docs.text:
Snowflake alerts run a condition on a schedule and act when it returns rows:

CREATE OR REPLACE ALERT security_db.network.too_many_failed_logins
  WAREHOUSE = bi_wh
  SCHEDULE = '60 MINUTE'
  IF (EXISTS (
    SELECT user_name FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY
    WHERE is_success = 'NO' AND event_timestamp > DATEADD('hour', -2, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
    GROUP BY user_name HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10))
  THEN
    CALL SYSTEM$SEND_EMAIL('my_email_int', 'security@example.com',
                           'Snowflake: repeated failed sign-ins', 'Check LOGIN_HISTORY for the last 2 hours.');

ALTER ALERT security_db.network.too_many_failed_logins RESUME;

Because ACCOUNT_USAGE can lag by up to a few hours, set the alert's look-back window wider than its schedule (here 2 hours checked hourly), and accept that it's a detective control, not a real-time one.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: ACCOUNT_USAGE views are shared to every account from Snowflake through the SNOWFLAKE database, which is itself a share (lesson 07). The data is produced by Snowflake's services as they run your account: the authentication service writes login events, the query service writes query and access records, the metadata store emits grant and object changes. These records are processed into the views asynchronously, which is the source of the latency. Access History's column-level detail comes from the compiler: when it resolves a query, including expanding views and applying policies, it knows exactly which base columns contribute to each output and filter, and it records that resolution alongside the query.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Auditing reads with direct_objects_accessed only. It misses access through views.
  • Granting ACCOUNTADMIN to auditors. Use the SNOWFLAKE database roles.
  • Real-time expectations from ACCOUNT_USAGE. Latency is up to hours.
  • Relying on one year of retention for multi-year obligations. Archive the views yourself.
  • Alerts whose look-back equals their schedule. Late-arriving records are missed. Overlap the windows.
  • Not distinguishing masked from unmasked reads. Use policies_referenced.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create the auditor role with the two database roles and confirm it can query LOGIN_HISTORY and ACCESS_HISTORY but not your business tables.
  2. Create a view over customers that exposes email under another name, query it as an analyst, wait for the latency, and find that read with the base_objects_accessed query.
  3. Extend the audit to report, per user, whether the email values they saw were masked (policies_referenced).
  4. Build a daily task that copies the previous day's LOGIN_HISTORY and ACCESS_HISTORY rows into an archive table, so you can keep them beyond one year.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Governed Multi-Team Platform
docs.text:
This project puts Level 3 together. Two teams (sales and HR), a support desk and an auditor share one account. The requirements are the kind a security review writes down:

  1. Analysts read curated marts only. Engineers also read raw data and write marts. Nobody crosses teams.
  2. Customer emails and phones are masked for everyone except support agents. Salaries are visible only to HR analysts.
  3. Administrators don't see raw PII or salaries just because they're administrators.
  4. Each role sees order rows only for the regions it's entitled to.
  5. Service users connect only from known networks.
  6. An auditor can review access history and grants without being able to read business data.
  7. If someone later grants a PII role to the wrong person, the security team hears about it the next morning.

What makes this a project rather than a pile of SQL is the last step: the access design is tested. Requirements 1–3 are checked by 20 automated tests against the grant script, and those tests found three real mistakes in the design while it was being written for this lesson.

What was run

The grants were executed by the course's RBAC model (rbac.py, from lesson 01), which computes effective access through the role hierarchy, and checked with pytest. All runs shown are real output. The policy, network and alert SQL was syntax-checked and verified against Snowflake's documentation, but not executed on Snowflake. policy_tests.sql states what each query must return, for you to run in a trial account.

docs.title: The design
docs.text:
ACCOUNTADMIN
                     /          \
              SECURITYADMIN    SYSADMIN                         PII_STEWARD   (priya; outside the admin tree)
                    |          /      \                          /        \
                 AUDITOR  SALES_ENG   HR_ENG               SUPPORT_AGENT   SALARY_READER
                   (otto)   (ben)    |                        (sam)           (hana, as a secondary role)
                            |      HR_ANALYST (hana)            |
                     SALES_ANALYST (ana)                     PII_READER

Functional roles (who you are) receive access roles (what you can touch: sales_mart_read, sales_mart_write, hr_mart_read, and so on), as in lesson 01. Everything that can see raw PII hangs under PII_STEWARD, a role owned by a named data-protection owner and deliberately not granted to SYSADMIN. That is the whole trick behind requirement 3: in Snowflake every privilege flows upward through role grants, so the only way to keep a role's power away from administrators is to keep the role out of their hierarchy.

docs.title: Step 1 — Roles and grants
docs.text:
grants.sql:

-- 1. access roles: (domain, layer, level)
USE ROLE USERADMIN;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_raw_read;   CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_mart_read;  CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_mart_write;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS hr_mart_read;     CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS hr_mart_write;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS pii_reader;       CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS salary_reader;
-- 2. functional roles
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_analyst;    CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS sales_engineer;   CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS hr_engineer;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS hr_analyst;       CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS support_agent;  CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS auditor;
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS pii_steward;      -- owns and manages every role that can see raw PII

USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sales TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_read;
GRANT INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.mart TO ROLE sales_mart_write;
GRANT ROLE sales_mart_read TO ROLE sales_mart_write;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE sales TO ROLE sales_raw_read;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA sales.raw TO ROLE sales_raw_read;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA sales.raw TO ROLE sales_raw_read;
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE hr TO ROLE hr_mart_read;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA hr.mart TO ROLE hr_mart_read;
GRANT SELECT ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA hr.mart TO ROLE hr_mart_read;
GRANT INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON FUTURE TABLES IN SCHEMA hr.mart TO ROLE hr_mart_write;
GRANT ROLE hr_mart_read TO ROLE hr_mart_write;

GRANT ROLE sales_mart_read TO ROLE sales_analyst;   GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE sales_bi_wh TO ROLE sales_analyst;
GRANT ROLE sales_analyst TO ROLE sales_engineer;
GRANT ROLE sales_mart_write TO ROLE sales_engineer; GRANT ROLE sales_raw_read TO ROLE sales_engineer;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE sales_etl_wh TO ROLE sales_engineer;
GRANT ROLE hr_mart_read TO ROLE hr_analyst;         GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE hr_bi_wh TO ROLE hr_analyst;
GRANT ROLE hr_analyst TO ROLE hr_engineer;          GRANT ROLE hr_mart_write TO ROLE hr_engineer;
GRANT ROLE sales_mart_read TO ROLE support_agent;   GRANT ROLE pii_reader TO ROLE support_agent;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE support_wh TO ROLE support_agent;

-- 3. hierarchy: functional roles under SYSADMIN, EXCEPT roles that can see raw PII: those sit under pii_steward,
--    which is deliberately outside the admin hierarchy so administrators don't inherit PII access (lesson 04)
GRANT ROLE sales_engineer TO ROLE SYSADMIN;  GRANT ROLE hr_engineer TO ROLE SYSADMIN;
GRANT ROLE support_agent TO ROLE pii_steward;  GRANT ROLE salary_reader TO ROLE pii_steward;
GRANT ROLE auditor TO ROLE SECURITYADMIN;

-- 4. people
GRANT ROLE sales_analyst TO USER ana;   GRANT ROLE sales_engineer TO USER ben;
GRANT ROLE hr_analyst TO USER hana;     GRANT ROLE salary_reader TO USER hana;   -- used as a secondary role
GRANT ROLE support_agent TO USER sam;   GRANT ROLE auditor TO USER otto;
GRANT ROLE pii_steward TO USER priya;   -- a named data-protection owner, not an administrator

docs.title: Step 2 — The access matrix as tests
docs.text:
The requirements become a table of (user, privilege, table, allowed?) cases plus three structural rules. test_access.py:

"""The access matrix the platform promises, checked against grants.sql with the RBAC model.
Run with: pytest -q test_access.py"""
import pytest
from rbac import Account

acct = Account(); acct.run(open("grants.sql").read())
SALES_MART, SALES_RAW, HR_MART = "SALES.MART.ORDERS", "SALES.RAW.ORDERS", "HR.MART.SALARIES"

EXPECTED = [  # (user, privilege, table, allowed?)
    ("ANA",  "SELECT", SALES_MART, True),  ("ANA",  "SELECT", SALES_RAW, False), ("ANA",  "SELECT", HR_MART, False),
    ("ANA",  "UPDATE", SALES_MART, False),
    ("BEN",  "SELECT", SALES_MART, True),  ("BEN",  "SELECT", SALES_RAW, True),  ("BEN",  "UPDATE", SALES_MART, True),
    ("BEN",  "SELECT", HR_MART, False),
    ("HANA", "SELECT", HR_MART, True),     ("HANA", "SELECT", SALES_MART, False),("HANA", "UPDATE", HR_MART, False),
    ("SAM",  "SELECT", SALES_MART, True),  ("SAM",  "UPDATE", SALES_MART, False),("SAM",  "SELECT", HR_MART, False),
    ("OTTO", "SELECT", SALES_MART, False), ("OTTO", "SELECT", HR_MART, False),
]

@pytest.mark.parametrize("user,priv,table,allowed", EXPECTED)
def test_access_matrix(user, priv, table, allowed):
    assert (user in acct.who_can(priv, "TABLE", table)) == allowed

def test_only_the_pii_branch_is_outside_the_admin_hierarchy():
    assert acct.orphans() == ["PII_READER", "PII_STEWARD", "SALARY_READER", "SUPPORT_AGENT"]

def test_only_support_inherits_pii_reader():
    holders = sorted(r for r in acct.roles if "PII_READER" in acct.inherited(r) and r != "PII_READER")
    assert holders == ["PII_STEWARD", "SUPPORT_AGENT"]

def test_admins_do_not_inherit_pii_reader():
    for admin in ("SYSADMIN", "ACCOUNTADMIN", "SECURITYADMIN"):
        assert "PII_READER" not in acct.inherited(admin)

def test_admins_do_not_inherit_salary_access():
    # the salary masking policy unmasks for SALARY_READER, so no administrator may inherit it
    assert "SALARY_READER" in acct.roles
    for admin in ("SYSADMIN", "ACCOUNTADMIN", "SECURITYADMIN"):
        assert "SALARY_READER" not in acct.inherited(admin)

docs.title: What the tests caught
docs.text:
The first version of the grant script granted support_agent and pii_steward to SYSADMIN like every other functional role, and hr_mart_write was created but never granted to anyone. The first run:

FAILED test_access.py::test_no_orphan_roles_except_pii_reader - AssertionErro...
FAILED test_access.py::test_only_support_inherits_pii_reader - AssertionError...
FAILED test_access.py::test_admins_do_not_inherit_pii_reader - AssertionError...
3 failed, 16 passed in 0.02s

(The orphan test was renamed after the fix to say what it now checks.) Two design faults, both easy to miss by reading the script: every administrator inherited raw PII (through SYSADMIN → SUPPORT_AGENT → PII_READER), and an access role was orphaned, so HR engineers couldn't write their own mart. Moving the PII branch under PII_STEWARD and granting hr_mart_write to hr_engineer fixed both.

The third fault appeared while writing the salary masking policy. The obvious rule, "unmask for HR_ANALYST", fails requirement 3, because HR_ANALYST sits under HR_ENGINEER, which sits under SYSADMIN. Asking the model confirmed it ('HR_ANALYST' in acct.inherited('SYSADMIN') returned True). So the test came first, and failed:

test_access.py:36: AssertionError
=========================== short test summary info ============================
FAILED test_access.py::test_admins_do_not_inherit_salary_access - AssertionEr...
1 failed, 19 passed in 0.02s

The fix: a dedicated SALARY_READER role under PII_STEWARD, granted to hana directly as a user (she activates it as a secondary role), and a masking policy keyed on that role. The final run:

============================== 20 passed in 0.03s ==============================

The lesson generalises: any policy that checks IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('X') grants its exception to every role above X. Check the hierarchy above every role you name in a policy.

docs.title: Step 3 — Policies, network and audit
docs.text:
policies.sql. The policies use the patterns from lessons 03–05 and 09: one tag with two masking policies attached (one per data type), a mapping-table row access policy, network rules, the SNOWFLAKE database roles for the auditor, and a daily alert that enforces the same holder rule as the tests, but against the live account:

-- Governance objects for the platform. Run as SECURITYADMIN (policies, tags, network) and ACCOUNTADMIN where noted.
USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS governance;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS governance.policies WITH MANAGED ACCESS;

-- 1. classification vocabulary
CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS governance.policies.pii
  ALLOWED_VALUES 'email', 'phone', 'name', 'salary', 'national_id';

-- 2. tag-based masking: one policy per data type
CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY governance.policies.pii_string AS (val VARCHAR) RETURNS VARCHAR ->
  CASE
    WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') THEN val
    WHEN SYSTEM$GET_TAG_ON_CURRENT_COLUMN('governance.policies.pii') = 'email' THEN '***@' || SPLIT_PART(val, '@', 2)
    ELSE '*** masked ***'
  END;
