CREATE OR REPLACE MASKING POLICY governance.policies.pii_number AS (val NUMBER) RETURNS NUMBER ->
  CASE WHEN IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('PII_READER') OR IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION('SALARY_READER') THEN val ELSE NULL END;
ALTER TAG governance.policies.pii SET MASKING POLICY governance.policies.pii_string,
                                     MASKING POLICY governance.policies.pii_number;

ALTER TABLE sales.mart.customers MODIFY COLUMN email SET TAG governance.policies.pii = 'email';
ALTER TABLE sales.mart.customers MODIFY COLUMN phone SET TAG governance.policies.pii = 'phone';
ALTER TABLE hr.mart.salaries MODIFY COLUMN salary SET TAG governance.policies.pii = 'salary';

-- 3. row access by region, driven by a mapping table
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS governance.policies.region_access (role_name VARCHAR, region VARCHAR);
INSERT INTO governance.policies.region_access VALUES
  ('SALES_ANALYST', 'EU'), ('SALES_ENGINEER', 'EU'), ('SALES_ENGINEER', 'US'), ('SUPPORT_AGENT', 'EU');
CREATE OR REPLACE ROW ACCESS POLICY governance.policies.region_rows AS (row_region VARCHAR) RETURNS BOOLEAN ->
  EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM governance.policies.region_access m
          WHERE IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION(m.role_name) AND m.region = row_region);
ALTER TABLE sales.mart.orders ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY governance.policies.region_rows ON (region);

-- 4. network: everyone from the VPN; the ETL service only from its NAT gateway
CREATE NETWORK RULE governance.policies.corp_vpn TYPE = IPV4 MODE = INGRESS VALUE_LIST = ('203.0.113.0/24');
CREATE NETWORK RULE governance.policies.etl_nat  TYPE = IPV4 MODE = INGRESS VALUE_LIST = ('192.0.2.10/32');
CREATE NETWORK POLICY corp_only ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULE_LIST = ('governance.policies.corp_vpn');
CREATE NETWORK POLICY etl_only  ALLOWED_NETWORK_RULE_LIST = ('governance.policies.etl_nat');
ALTER USER etl_service SET NETWORK_POLICY = etl_only;
-- apply to the account only after testing on a user (lesson 03):
-- ALTER ACCOUNT SET NETWORK_POLICY = corp_only;

-- 5. auditing (ACCOUNTADMIN)
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.GOVERNANCE_VIEWER TO ROLE auditor;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.SECURITY_VIEWER TO ROLE auditor;

-- 6. daily alert: the PII and salary roles must stay with their approved holders (the same rule test_access.py checks)
USE ROLE SECURITYADMIN;
CREATE OR REPLACE ALERT governance.policies.pii_holders_check
  WAREHOUSE = admin_wh
  SCHEDULE = 'USING CRON 0 7 * * * UTC'
  IF (EXISTS (
    SELECT name, grantee_name FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.GRANTS_TO_ROLES
    WHERE deleted_on IS NULL AND granted_on = 'ROLE'
      AND name IN ('PII_READER', 'SALARY_READER', 'SUPPORT_AGENT')
      AND grantee_name NOT IN ('SUPPORT_AGENT', 'PII_STEWARD')
    UNION ALL
    SELECT role, grantee_name FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.GRANTS_TO_USERS
    WHERE deleted_on IS NULL
      AND role IN ('PII_READER', 'SALARY_READER', 'SUPPORT_AGENT', 'PII_STEWARD')
      AND grantee_name NOT IN ('SAM', 'HANA', 'PRIYA')
  ))
  THEN
    CALL SYSTEM$SEND_EMAIL('security_email_int', 'security-team@example.com',
      'PII role granted outside the approved set',
      'A PII or salary role has a holder outside the approved list. Check GRANTS_TO_ROLES and GRANTS_TO_USERS.');
ALTER ALERT governance.policies.pii_holders_check RESUME;

Points worth noticing:

  • Tag-based masking. Classifying a new column (SET TAG … = 'email') protects it immediately, with no policy change. A tag can carry one masking policy per data type, which is why there are two. Inside the string policy, SYSTEM$GET_TAG_ON_CURRENT_COLUMN lets one policy mask emails and other strings differently.
  • The managed-access schema keeps policies and the mapping table under the schema owner's control. Object owners can't grant on them.
  • The row access policy reads a mapping table. Onboarding a role to a region is an INSERT, not a policy change. Protect that table as carefully as the policy itself.
  • The network policy is applied to the service user first. The account-level policy stays commented out until it has been tested, because a wrong account-level policy locks everyone out (lesson 03).
  • The alert checks state, not events. ACCOUNT_USAGE views lag by up to a few hours. A rule like "nobody outside this list holds the role" works whatever the lag. "Alert on grants in the last hour" would miss some.

docs.title: Step 4 — Verify the policies
docs.text:
Snowflake can simulate a query as another role with EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT. Per the documentation, the role running it must own the tables and hold the APPLY privilege for the policies, and the result reflects the role hierarchy and grants. policy_tests.sql (expected result in each comment):

-- Expected results per role, run after policies.sql. POLICY_CONTEXT must be run by a role that OWNS the tables
-- and has APPLY on the policies (in this design, the schema owner with the APPLY privileges granted).
-- 1. analyst: emails masked, EU rows only
EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(CURRENT_ROLE => 'SALES_ANALYST')
  AS SELECT COUNT_IF(email LIKE '***@%') = COUNT(*) AS all_masked FROM sales.mart.customers;            -- TRUE
EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(CURRENT_ROLE => 'SALES_ANALYST')
  AS SELECT ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT region) AS regions FROM sales.mart.orders;                                -- ["EU"]
-- 2. support agent: raw emails (inherits PII_READER), EU rows only
EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(CURRENT_ROLE => 'SUPPORT_AGENT')
  AS SELECT COUNT_IF(email LIKE '***@%') AS masked_rows FROM sales.mart.customers;                      -- 0
-- 3. sales engineer: masked emails, EU and US rows
EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(CURRENT_ROLE => 'SALES_ENGINEER')
  AS SELECT ARRAY_AGG(DISTINCT region) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY region) AS regions FROM sales.mart.orders;  -- ["EU","US"]
-- 4. SYSADMIN: masked emails and no salaries (PII_READER and SALARY_READER are outside its hierarchy)
EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(CURRENT_ROLE => 'SYSADMIN')
  AS SELECT COUNT_IF(email LIKE '***@%') = COUNT(*) AS all_masked FROM sales.mart.customers;            -- TRUE
EXECUTE USING POLICY_CONTEXT(CURRENT_ROLE => 'SYSADMIN')
  AS SELECT COUNT(salary) AS visible_salaries FROM hr.mart.salaries;                                     -- 0
-- 5. signed in as hana, with the secondary role active: every salary visible
USE ROLE hr_analyst;
USE SECONDARY ROLES ALL;
SELECT COUNT(salary) = COUNT(*) AS all_visible FROM hr.mart.salaries;                                    -- TRUE

The last check signs in as hana, because it depends on a secondary role that only her user holds.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a query runs, Snowflake first checks privileges: the session's primary and secondary roles, expanded through the role hierarchy, must hold SELECT on the table and USAGE on its schema and database. That's what the RBAC model computes, and it's what the 16-row access matrix tests. Then, during compilation, the services layer rewrites the query: the row access policy becomes a filter on the table, and each tagged column is wrapped in its masking policy expression. Both are evaluated against the session's context (IS_ROLE_IN_SESSION, CURRENT_USER), so they inherit exactly the same role hierarchy as privileges do. That's why the structural tests matter as much as the matrix. A masking rule is only as narrow as the set of roles that inherit the role it names. Network policies sit in front of all of this, at sign-in. The alert is just a scheduled query on the audit views, so it closes the loop: the tests check the design before deployment, and the alert checks that the deployed account still matches it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Granting every functional role to SYSADMIN, including the PII ones. Administrators then inherit raw PII. That's the bug this project's first test run found.
  • Masking policies that name a role low in the hierarchy. Every role above it is also unmasked.
  • Orphaned access roles. A role with grants but no holders is dead weight, or a sign that someone can't do their job.
  • Testing access by hand once. Grant scripts change. Keep the matrix as code and run it on every change.
  • An account-level network policy applied before testing on one user.
  • Alerts on recent events from ACCOUNT_USAGE. Their latency makes "last hour" checks unreliable. Check state.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run grants.sql, policies.sql and policy_tests.sql in a trial account (create the sales, hr, warehouses and users first, replacing the example IP ranges and email address). Does every query in policy_tests.sql return the expected value? Note any differences and explain them.
  2. Add a finance team with its own raw and mart schemas. Extend the expected matrix first, watch the new tests fail, then change the grants until they pass.
  3. Add a region restriction for support agents in the US. Which file changes: the policy, the mapping table or the grants?
  4. Grant pii_reader to sales_analyst in a test copy of grants.sql. Which tests fail? Then do the same in the trial account and confirm that the alert would fire on its next run (run its condition query by hand).
  5. Write a sixth structural test: no user holds both SALES_ENGINEER and HR_ENGINEER, directly or through a role.

docs.title: Level 4 · Building, Scaling & Operating
docs.text:
Level 4 is about building on Snowflake and running it well: code that runs next to the data, AI functions in SQL, and the operational disciplines (cost, scaling, continuity, deployment, migration) that decide whether a platform stays healthy as it grows. Along the way you'll see a "vectorized" handler run more than twice as slowly as the plain one, label descriptions multiply an AI function's input tokens about six times, 86% of a warehouse bill attributed to nobody, four small clusters beat a larger warehouse when queries don't scale with size, a dbt incremental model pass every test while serving stale revenue, and translated SQL that compiles but returns different answers.

What was run

Nothing here was run on Snowflake. Snowpark code ran in Snowpark's own local testing mode (Snowpark 1.53.0), a dbt project ran with dbt-core 1.12.5 on DuckDB 1.5.6, UDF handlers and a UDTF ran as plain Python, and the capstone's chargeback query ran in DuckDB with pytest and a mutation check. Costs, scaling and data loss come from small models with their assumptions stated. All Snowflake SQL was syntax-checked and verified against the October 2026 documentation, including features that are new in 2025–2026: Cortex AI functions and model access control, Adaptive Warehouses, Gen2 as the default, Optimized Refresh and RPO Assurance, and dbt Projects on Snowflake.

Prerequisites: Levels 1–3, and Python for lessons 02, 03 and 10.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. UDFs & Stored Procedures — SQL UDFs and table functions, Snowflake Scripting with transactions, and owner's vs caller's rights.
  2. Snowpark for Python — lazy DataFrames pushed down as SQL, the to_pandas trap, pandas on Snowflake, and unit tests in local testing mode.
  3. Python UDFs, Vectorized UDFs & UDTFs — runtimes and packages, external access, when batching helps (measured), and a sessionizing table function.
  4. Cortex AI Functions — classify, filter, sentiment and structured extraction in SQL, access control, data residency and token costs.
  5. Cost Management: Monitors, Budgets & Attribution — where credits go, the idle gap in per-query attribution, tags, resource monitors and budgets.
  6. Warehouse Scaling: Up, Out & Adaptive — scale-up vs scale-out modelled, multi-cluster policies, query acceleration, Gen2 and Adaptive Warehouses.
  7. Replication, Failover & Business Continuity — replication and failover groups, refresh modes, data loss modelled, Client Redirect and a runbook.
  8. dbt & CI/CD for Snowflake — a tested dbt project, an incremental bug only a rebuild comparison caught, clones per pull request, and dbt Projects on Snowflake.
  9. Migrating to Snowflake — translation and its semantic traps, moving data, and reconciliation that catches export bugs.
  10. Capstone — A Cost-Aware Data Platform — owned warehouses, monitors and budgets, and a tested monthly chargeback that assigns every credit.

docs.title: After Level 4
docs.text: You've covered Snowflake from architecture to operations. Good next steps: run the capstone in a trial account with your own workloads, take the dbt and data engineering path further, or pair this course with the PySpark Mastery Path to compare the two platforms on the same pipeline.

docs.title: 01 · UDFs & Stored Procedures
docs.text: Sooner or later, the same expression appears in twenty queries, or a job needs several statements to run as one unit. Snowflake has two tools for that, and choosing between them is the first decision. A user-defined function (UDF) computes a value (or a table) inside a SQL statement. A stored procedure runs statements: it's invoked with CALL, and can create, insert, delete and control flow. This lesson covers both in SQL, and the security question every procedure raises: whose privileges does it run with?

docs.title: Function or procedure?
docs.text:
UDF Stored procedure Called inside a statement: SELECT net_amount(amount, 10) … on its own: CALL archive_old_orders(90) Returns one value per row (scalar) or a set of rows (table function) one value (or a table), once May run DML/DDL no yes Typical use reusable calculations, parsing, business rules admin jobs, multi-step loads, anything with control flow

Both can be written in SQL, Python, Java, Scala or JavaScript, per Snowflake's documentation (lesson 03 covers Python).

docs.title: SQL UDFs
docs.text:
A scalar SQL UDF is an expression with a name:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sales.mart.net_amount(amount NUMBER(12,2), discount_pct NUMBER(5,2))
RETURNS NUMBER(12,2)
COMMENT = 'Order amount after a percentage discount'
AS
$$
  amount * (1 - discount_pct / 100)
$$;

SELECT order_id, amount, sales.mart.net_amount(amount, 10) AS net FROM sales.mart.orders LIMIT 5;

A table function (UDTF) returns rows, and is used in FROM with TABLE(…):

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sales.mart.orders_for(cust NUMBER)
RETURNS TABLE (order_id NUMBER, order_date DATE, amount NUMBER(12,2))
AS
$$
  SELECT order_id, order_date, amount FROM sales.mart.orders WHERE customer_id = cust
$$;

SELECT * FROM TABLE(sales.mart.orders_for(101)) ORDER BY order_date;

-- and per row of another table, as a lateral join
SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM sales.mart.customers c, TABLE(sales.mart.orders_for(c.customer_id)) o;

Functions are overloaded by argument types: net_amount(NUMBER, NUMBER) and net_amount(NUMBER) are two different functions, and DROP FUNCTION and GRANT … ON FUNCTION need the signature (net_amount(NUMBER, NUMBER)). To call a function, a role needs USAGE on it (and on its database and schema).

docs.title: Stored procedures in Snowflake Scripting
docs.text:
Snowflake Scripting is Snowflake's procedural SQL: variables, IF, loops, cursors and exception handlers. A procedure that moves orders older than a cutoff into an archive table must do two statements, and they must succeed or fail together:

CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE ops.archive_old_orders(keep_days NUMBER)
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE SQL
EXECUTE AS OWNER
AS
$$
DECLARE
  cutoff DATE DEFAULT DATEADD(day, -keep_days, CURRENT_DATE());
  n_archived NUMBER;
  n_deleted NUMBER;
BEGIN
  BEGIN TRANSACTION;
  INSERT INTO sales.mart.orders_archive SELECT * FROM sales.mart.orders WHERE order_date < :cutoff;
  n_archived := SQLROWCOUNT;
  DELETE FROM sales.mart.orders WHERE order_date < :cutoff;
  n_deleted := SQLROWCOUNT;
  COMMIT;
  RETURN 'archived ' || n_archived || ', deleted ' || n_deleted;
EXCEPTION
  WHEN OTHER THEN
    ROLLBACK;
    RAISE;
END;
$$;

CALL ops.archive_old_orders(90);

Three details make it correct:

  • One cutoff, computed once. Both statements use the same variable, so a row can't be copied by one and missed by the other because the date changed between them. (Inside SQL statements, variables are referenced with a colon: :cutoff.)
  • An explicit transaction. Without it, a failure after the INSERT would leave rows in both tables. The handler rolls back and re-raises, so the caller (a task, an orchestrator) sees the failure instead of a cheerful return value.
  • It's safe to run twice. The second call finds nothing older than the cutoff.

The same logic, written as a Python procedure and run with Snowpark's local testing mode (an in-memory emulation that ships with the Snowpark library, no account involved), on ten orders that are 20, 40, … 200 days old:

# Snowpark local testing (in-memory, no Snowflake account): the archive procedure's logic, called twice.
import datetime as dt
from snowflake.snowpark import Session
from snowflake.snowpark.functions import col, lit, sproc, current_date, dateadd
from snowflake.snowpark.types import IntegerType, StringType

session = Session.builder.config("local_testing", True).create()
today = dt.date(2026, 10, 14)
rows = [(i, today - dt.timedelta(days=i * 20), 10.0 * i) for i in range(1, 11)]   # 20, 40, ... 200 days old
session.create_dataframe(rows, schema=["order_id", "order_date", "amount"]).write.save_as_table("orders")
session.create_dataframe([], schema=session.table("orders").schema).write.save_as_table("orders_archive")

@sproc(name="archive_old_orders", input_types=[IntegerType()], return_type=StringType(), session=session, replace=True)
def archive_old_orders(session, keep_days):
    cutoff = today - dt.timedelta(days=keep_days)
    orders = session.table("orders")
    old = orders.filter(col("order_date") < lit(cutoff))
    n = old.count()
    old.write.save_as_table("orders_archive", mode="append")        # 1. copy
    deleted = orders.delete(orders["order_date"] < lit(cutoff))     # 2. delete the same predicate
    return f"archived {n}, deleted {deleted.rows_deleted}"

print("1st call:", session.call("archive_old_orders", 90))
print("2nd call:", session.call("archive_old_orders", 90))
print("orders left:", session.table("orders").count(), "| archived:", session.table("orders_archive").count())

1st call: archived 6, deleted 6
2nd call: archived 0, deleted 0
orders left: 4 | archived: 6

Six orders are older than 90 days. The second call archives nothing, which is the idempotence you want from anything a scheduler might retry. Local testing has documented limits: it doesn't run raw SQL strings, and it ignores registration options such as execute_as, so it can test your logic, but not rights or transactions. Those need a real account.

docs.title: Owner's rights vs caller's rights
docs.text:
This is the part of procedures that matters most for security. From Snowflake's documentation:

Owner's rights (EXECUTE AS OWNER, the default) Caller's rights (EXECUTE AS CALLER) Privileges used the procedure owner's the caller's Database and schema the ones the procedure was created in the caller's current ones Caller's session variables can't read or set them can read and set them Caller's session parameters only a documented subset can be used; can't set them can read and set them Warehouse the caller's current warehouse the caller's current warehouse

Owner's rights are how you delegate a narrow power safely. The archive_old_orders procedure above can be owned by a role that may delete from orders, while support engineers get only USAGE on the procedure. They can archive, with the exact logic in the procedure, but they can't run an arbitrary DELETE. That only stays safe if the procedure can't be steered into doing something else. An owner's rights procedure that builds SQL from its arguments (EXECUTE IMMEDIATE 'DELETE FROM ' || table_arg) hands the owner's privileges to anyone who can call it. Bind values (:cutoff) instead of concatenating them, and never take object names from callers without validating them against a fixed list.

Caller's rights suit utility procedures that should do only what the caller could do anyway: a helper that runs a sequence of statements in the caller's schema, or one that needs the caller's session variables. Snowflake also offers restricted caller's rights, where an administrator limits which of the caller's privileges a caller's rights procedure may use.

GRANT USAGE ON PROCEDURE ops.archive_old_orders(NUMBER) TO ROLE support_engineer;   -- note the signature
ALTER PROCEDURE ops.archive_old_orders(NUMBER) EXECUTE AS CALLER;                   -- switching modes later is possible

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
A SQL UDF is stored as an expression (or a query, for a table function), and it's evaluated as part of the query that calls it, row by row or as a row source. That's why a UDF can't change data or control a transaction: it's an expression, not a program. A secure function (Level 3 · 06) additionally hides its body and limits the optimizations applied around it.

A stored procedure is a program. CALL starts it in the cloud services layer, which runs its statements one by one, each as a normal query on the caller's current warehouse. Variables and control flow live in the procedure's execution context. Each statement it issues is compiled with the privileges of the owner or the caller, depending on the mode, and appears as a separate query in query history, next to the CALL itself. Transactions inside a procedure follow the usual rules: without BEGIN TRANSACTION, each DML statement commits on its own (autocommit).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Procedures where a UDF would do (and vice versa). If it computes a value inside a query, it's a function.
  • Multi-statement changes without a transaction, leaving half-finished work after a failure.
  • Swallowing exceptions. A handler that returns 'error' makes a failed job look successful to the scheduler. Re-raise.
  • Building SQL by concatenating arguments in owner's rights procedures. That's SQL injection with the owner's privileges.
  • Forgetting the signature in GRANT, DROP and ALTER on overloaded functions and procedures.
  • Assuming the caller's context in an owner's rights procedure: its database, schema and session variables aren't the caller's.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create net_amount and orders_for in a trial account, then find them in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.FUNCTIONS. Use orders_for in a lateral join for five customers.
  2. Create archive_old_orders and make it fail halfway (for example, drop the archive table's grant). Confirm that orders is unchanged afterwards and that the CALL reports an error.
  3. Grant USAGE on the procedure to a role that can't delete from orders, and call it as that role. Then switch the procedure to caller's rights and call it again. Explain both results.
  4. Extend archive_local.py into a pytest file with three tests: the cutoff boundary (an order exactly 90 days old), an empty table, and two consecutive calls.

docs.title: 02 · Snowpark for Python
docs.text: SQL is excellent at set logic and awkward at everything around it: reuse, parameters, branching, tests. Snowpark is Snowflake's library for writing data transformations in Python (and Java and Scala) without moving the data out of Snowflake. You build a query with a DataFrame API. Snowpark turns it into SQL, and the warehouse runs it. This lesson covers how that works, the one habit that defeats it, and how to unit-test transformations with no account at all, which was how every result below was produced.

docs.title: A session
docs.text:
A Snowpark session is a connection. It can reuse the same connections.toml profile Snowflake CLI uses (Level 1 · 02):

from snowflake.snowpark import Session

session = Session.builder.config("connection_name", "learn").create()
print(session.get_current_role(), session.get_current_warehouse())

docs.title: DataFrames are lazy plans
docs.text:
A Snowpark DataFrame is not data. It's a description of a query. Each method returns a new, bigger description, and nothing runs until you call an action (collect(), show(), count(), to_pandas(), write.save_as_table()). At that point, Snowpark generates SQL for the whole chain, and Snowflake executes it on the session's warehouse:

from snowflake.snowpark.functions import col, sum as sum_

orders = session.table("sales.mart.orders")
eu_daily = (orders.filter(col("region") == "EU")
                  .group_by("order_date")
                  .agg(sum_("amount").alias("revenue")))      # still nothing has run
eu_daily.explain()                                            # prints the generated SQL and the plan
eu_daily.write.save_as_table("sales.mart.eu_daily_revenue", mode="overwrite")   # runs one INSERT … SELECT in Snowflake

The aggregation runs where the data is, with pruning, the caches and the warehouse's full parallelism (Level 2). Python only sends SQL and receives a status.

docs.title: The habit that defeats it
docs.text:
pdf = session.table("sales.mart.orders").to_pandas()          # pulls the whole table into your laptop's memory
eu = pdf[pdf["REGION"] == "EU"].groupby("ORDER_DATE")["AMOUNT"].sum()

This works on a sample and fails in production. Every row crosses the network, and the work runs on one Python process instead of a warehouse. Rule of thumb: filter and aggregate in Snowpark, and call to_pandas() only on results small enough to read. If your team thinks in pandas, Snowflake's pandas on Snowflake (the Modin-based snowflake.snowpark.modin API, installed with snowflake-snowpark-python[modin]) offers pandas syntax that is executed in Snowflake instead of locally. Per its documentation, converting back with to_pandas() still materialises everything locally.

docs.title: Transformations as functions
docs.text:
Snowpark's real advantage over SQL files is structure. Write each transformation as a function from DataFrames to a DataFrame, with no session and no SQL strings inside, and it becomes reusable and testable. transforms.py, a daily report over a raw feed that re-sends orders when they change:

"""Transformations for the daily customer report. Pure functions of DataFrames: no session, no SQL strings."""
from snowflake.snowpark import DataFrame
from snowflake.snowpark.functions import col, sum as sum_, count, count_distinct, row_number
from snowflake.snowpark.window import Window

def latest_version(orders: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
    """Keep the most recent version of each order (the raw feed re-sends updated orders)."""
    w = Window.partition_by("order_id").order_by(col("updated_at").desc())
    return orders.with_column("rn", row_number().over(w)).filter(col("rn") == 1).drop("rn")

def region_summary(orders: DataFrame) -> DataFrame:
    return (latest_version(orders)
            .filter(col("status") != "cancelled")
            .group_by("region")
            .agg(count("order_id").alias("orders"),
                 count_distinct("customer_id").alias("customers"),
                 sum_("amount").alias("revenue")))

docs.title: Testing without an account
docs.text:
The Snowpark library includes a local testing mode: Session.builder.config("local_testing", True) creates an in-memory session that executes DataFrame operations in Python. It's designed for exactly this kind of unit test. test_transforms.py (each case states one rule the report must follow):

import datetime as dt
import pytest
from snowflake.snowpark import Session
from transforms import region_summary

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def session():
    return Session.builder.config("local_testing", True).create()

def t(h): return dt.datetime(2026, 10, 14, h)

@pytest.fixture
def orders(session):
    return session.create_dataframe([
        # order_id, customer_id, region, amount, status, updated_at
        (1, 101, "EU", 100.0, "placed",    t(9)),
        (1, 101, "EU", 120.0, "placed",    t(11)),   # order 1 updated: only this version counts
        (2, 101, "EU",  30.0, "placed",    t(10)),   # same customer, second order
        (3, 102, "EU",  50.0, "placed",    t(9)),
        (3, 102, "EU",  50.0, "cancelled", t(12)),   # order 3 later cancelled
        (4, 201, "US",  80.0, "placed",    t(9)),
    ], schema=["order_id", "customer_id", "region", "amount", "status", "updated_at"])

def by_region(df):
    return {r["REGION"]: (r["ORDERS"], r["CUSTOMERS"], r["REVENUE"]) for r in df.collect()}

def test_updated_orders_count_once(orders):
    assert by_region(region_summary(orders))["EU"][0] == 2

def test_revenue_uses_latest_amount_and_skips_cancelled(orders):
    assert by_region(region_summary(orders))["EU"][2] == 150.0

def test_customers_are_distinct(orders):
    assert by_region(region_summary(orders))["EU"][1] == 1

def test_regions_are_independent(orders):
    assert by_region(region_summary(orders))["US"] == (1, 1, 80.0)

The first run, with count("customer_id") as originally written:

E       assert np.int64(2) == 1
FAILED test_transforms.py::test_customers_are_distinct - assert np.int64(2) == 1
1 failed, 3 passed in 0.87s

Customer 101 placed two EU orders, so count counted them twice. It counts non-null values, not distinct ones. count_distinct fixed it:

test_transforms.py::test_updated_orders_count_once PASSED
test_transforms.py::test_revenue_uses_latest_amount_and_skips_cancelled PASSED
test_transforms.py::test_customers_are_distinct PASSED
test_transforms.py::test_regions_are_independent PASSED
============================== 4 passed in 0.69s ===============================

And the result itself (still the local session, Snowpark 1.53.0):

-------------------------------------------------
|"REGION"  |"ORDERS"  |"CUSTOMERS"  |"REVENUE"  |
-------------------------------------------------
|EU        |2         |1            |150.0      |
|US        |1         |1            |80.0       |
-------------------------------------------------

Order 1 counts once at its updated amount (120), order 3 is dropped as cancelled, and EU revenue is 120 + 30 = 150.

docs.title: What local testing can't tell you
docs.text: Per Snowflake's documentation, the local mode doesn't parse SQL strings (session.sql(…), string filters), implements only a subset of Snowflake's functions, ignores query tags and query history, and doesn't validate packages. It also doesn't generate real SQL: in this run, df.queries returned a placeholder (SELECT MOCK_TEST_FAKE_QUERY()). So use it for logic, which is where most bugs are, and run a smaller set of integration tests against a real development database for SQL generation, performance and permissions. The documented way to keep one test suite for both is a fixture that creates either a local or a real session from a command-line flag, and pytest.mark.skipif for cases the local mode can't support.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
Each DataFrame holds a logical plan: a tree of operations (scan, filter, project, aggregate, join, window). Methods add nodes. An action asks Snowpark's plan compiler to turn the tree into SQL text, which the client sends to Snowflake like any other query. That's why Snowpark code shows up in QUERY_HISTORY as ordinary SQL, why it gets the same optimizer, pruning and caches, and why it uses the session's role and warehouse. Python itself does very little until data comes back.

In local testing mode the same plan tree is walked by an in-memory executor written in Python (using pandas). It implements each node's semantics (grouping, windows, nulls) as Snowflake documents them, for the operations it supports. That gives fast, deterministic unit tests, at the cost of fidelity at the edges, so a test passing locally means the logic is right, not that the generated SQL is.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• to_pandas() on large tables, then doing the work in pandas. Push the work down and bring back results.
  • Loops of small actions. Calling .collect() per customer is a query per customer. Express it as one DataFrame operation (a join or a window) instead.
  • SQL strings inside transformations (filter("amount > 20"), session.sql(…)). They're untestable locally and lose the API's checks. Use column expressions.
  • No tests, or only end-to-end tests against a shared database. Unit-test the logic locally, integration-test the rest.
  • Treating a passing local test as proof the warehouse will behave the same. Check unsupported functions and run integration tests.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Install snowflake-snowpark-python (with pandas), copy transforms.py and test_transforms.py, and run the tests. Then break latest_version (order by updated_at ascending) and confirm which tests fail.
  2. Add a fifth test: an order whose only version is cancelled must not create a region row with zero orders. Does the current code pass it?
  3. With a trial account, run region_summary on sales.mart.orders, call .explain(), and compare the generated SQL with what you would have written.
  4. Rewrite the report with pandas on Snowflake and compare the query count in QUERY_HISTORY for both versions.

docs.title: 03 · Python UDFs, Vectorized UDFs & UDTFs
docs.text: Some logic is easier in Python than in SQL: parsing a messy string, scoring with a trained model, calling a library. Snowflake runs Python inside the warehouse, next to the data, as user-defined functions. This lesson covers the three shapes (scalar, vectorized and table functions), how packages get there, and a measurement that complicates the usual advice that vectorized UDFs are always faster.

docs.title: A scalar Python UDF
docs.text:
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION sales.mart.email_domain(email VARCHAR)
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE PYTHON
RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.12'
HANDLER = 'domain'
AS
$$
def domain(email):
    if email is None or "@" not in email:
        return None
    return email.split("@", 1)[1].lower()
$$;

SELECT sales.mart.email_domain(email) AS domain, COUNT(*) FROM sales.mart.customers GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;

RUNTIME_VERSION pins the Python version. Per the documentation (October 2026) the supported versions are 3.10 to 3.14. HANDLER names the function to call. SQL NULL arrives as Python None, so handle it explicitly, as above.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Third-party libraries come from three places:

  • The Snowflake Anaconda channel, listed with PACKAGES = ('pandas', 'numpy'). Available versions are listed in INFORMATION_SCHEMA.PACKAGES.
  • PyPI, through Snowflake's Artifact Repository: set ARTIFACT_REPOSITORY = snowflake.snowpark.pypi_shared_repository and list the packages. Per the documentation, the database role SNOWFLAKE.PYPI_REPOSITORY_USER is required and is granted to PUBLIC by default. A default repository can also be set for an account, database or schema with DEFAULT_PYTHON_ARTIFACT_REPOSITORY.
  • Your own code, uploaded to a stage and listed with IMPORTS = ('@stage/mylib.zip').
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ml.scoring.parse_phone(raw VARCHAR)
RETURNS VARCHAR
LANGUAGE PYTHON
RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.12'
ARTIFACT_REPOSITORY = snowflake.snowpark.pypi_shared_repository
PACKAGES = ('phonenumbers')
HANDLER = 'parse'
AS
$$
import phonenumbers

def parse(raw):
    if raw is None:
        return None
    try:
        return phonenumbers.format_number(phonenumbers.parse(raw, "GB"), phonenumbers.PhoneNumberFormat.E164)
    except phonenumbers.NumberParseException:
        return None
$$;

Handler code can't reach the internet by default. Calling an external API needs an external access integration: network rules (MODE = EGRESS) for the allowed hosts, optional secrets for credentials, and EXTERNAL_ACCESS_INTEGRATIONS = (…) on the function. Treat it as a security review item, like the network policies in Level 3 · 03.

docs.title: Vectorized UDFs
docs.text:
A scalar handler is called once per row. A vectorized handler is called once per batch of rows, which arrive as a pandas DataFrame with columns in argument order (df[0], df[1], …), and it returns a pandas Series or array:

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION ml.scoring.churn_score(amount FLOAT, tenure_months FLOAT)
RETURNS FLOAT
LANGUAGE PYTHON
RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.12'
PACKAGES = ('pandas', 'numpy')
HANDLER = 'score'
AS
$$
import numpy as np
import pandas
from _snowflake import vectorized

@vectorized(input=pandas.DataFrame)
def score(df):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(0.004 * df[0] - 0.03 * df[1] + 0.5)))
$$;

The usual advice is "vectorize for speed". Here's what that actually depends on. The same two handlers (email parsing and a numeric score), each written both ways and timed on one million rows, locally:

# Local timing of UDF HANDLERS only (plain Python 3.14 + pandas 2.3 on this machine, not Snowflake):
# the same logic called once per row (scalar UDF) vs once per batch of 8,192 rows (vectorized UDF).
import math, time, numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
N, BATCH = 1_000_000, 8192
emails = pd.Series([f"user{i}@{d}" for i, d in enumerate(rng.choice(["example.com", "Mail.Example.org"], N))])
amount, tenure = pd.Series(rng.uniform(1, 500, N)), pd.Series(rng.integers(0, 120, N).astype(float))

def run(name, scalar, vectorized, cols):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); a = [scalar(*row) for row in zip(*cols)]; t1 = time.perf_counter()
    b = pd.concat([vectorized(pd.DataFrame({i: c[s:s + BATCH] for i, c in enumerate(cols)}))
                   for s in range(0, N, BATCH)])
    t2 = time.perf_counter()
    same = np.allclose(a, b) if isinstance(a[0], float) else list(b) == a
    print(f"{name:<14} scalar {t1 - t0:5.2f} s   vectorized {t2 - t1:5.2f} s   identical results: {same}")

# 1. string parsing
run("email domain",
    lambda e: e.split("@", 1)[1].lower(),
    lambda df: df[0].str.split("@", n=1).str[1].str.lower(),
    [emails])
# 2. numeric scoring
run("churn score",
    lambda a, t: 1 / (1 + math.exp(-(0.004 * a - 0.03 * t + 0.5))),
    lambda df: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(0.004 * df[0] - 0.03 * df[1] + 0.5))),
    [amount, tenure])
print(f"rows: {N:,}  batch: {BATCH:,}")

email domain   scalar  0.18 s   vectorized  0.44 s   identical results: True
churn score    scalar  0.22 s   vectorized  0.04 s   identical results: True
rows: 1,000,000  batch: 8,192

Batching made the numeric score about five times faster in this run, because np.exp on a whole column runs in compiled code. It made the string parsing more than twice as slow: pandas' .str methods still process one string at a time in Python, plus the overhead of building Series. Two caveats keep this honest. These are handler timings on one machine, and they leave out the cost of moving rows between Snowflake's query engine and the Python process, which this run can't measure. Snowflake's documentation is careful here too: it promises vectorized UDFs "the potential for better performance if your Python code operates efficiently on batches of rows". So measure your own function on a warehouse before deciding. The rule this run supports is narrower than "vectorize everything": vectorize when the handler's work is array math. For string-heavy logic, first check whether built-in SQL (SPLIT_PART(email, '@', 2)) can do it with no Python at all.

max_batch_size in the decorator only limits batch size, for handlers that can't take large batches. The documentation says not to use it to request bigger batches.

docs.title: Table functions (UDTFs)
docs.text:
A Python UDTF is a class. Snowflake partitions the input with OVER (PARTITION BY …), calls __init__ once per partition, process once per row (in ORDER BY order if you give one), and end_partition once at the end. Both process and end_partition can yield output rows. Sessionizing clickstream events, a classic job that's awkward in SQL:

import datetime as dt

class Sessionize:
    """UDTF handler: one instance per partition (customer), rows arrive in ORDER BY event_ts order."""
    GAP = dt.timedelta(minutes=30)

    def __init__(self):
        self.session_no, self.last_ts, self.events = 0, None, 0

    def process(self, event_ts, page):
        if self.last_ts is None or event_ts - self.last_ts > self.GAP:
            self.session_no += 1
        self.last_ts = event_ts
        self.events += 1
        yield (self.session_no, event_ts, page)           # one output row per input row

    def end_partition(self):
        yield (None, None, f"summary: {self.events} events in {self.session_no} sessions")

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION web.mart.sessionize(event_ts TIMESTAMP_NTZ, page VARCHAR)
RETURNS TABLE (session_no NUMBER, event_ts TIMESTAMP_NTZ, page VARCHAR)
LANGUAGE PYTHON
RUNTIME_VERSION = '3.12'
HANDLER = 'Sessionize'
AS
$$
# (the class above)
$$;

SELECT e.customer_id, s.session_no, s.event_ts, s.page
FROM web.raw.events e,
     TABLE(web.mart.sessionize(e.event_ts, e.page) OVER (PARTITION BY e.customer_id ORDER BY e.event_ts)) s;

The handler's contract can be checked locally without Snowflake. A small driver calls it the way the documentation describes, with a new instance per partition and rows in order:

101 1 09:00 home
101 1 09:10 product
101 1 09:35 cart
101 2 11:00 home
101 2 11:05 checkout
101 summary: 5 events in 2 sessions
102 1 10:00 home
102 summary: 1 events in 1 sessions

Customer 101's 85-minute gap between 09:35 and 11:00 starts session 2. The end_partition summary row shows where per-partition totals belong. (In this layout, summary rows have NULL session and timestamp. A real function would usually emit one or the other, not both.)

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a query calls a Python UDF, each warehouse node starts Python worker processes in a secure sandbox, with the requested runtime and packages installed. The query engine sends rows to the workers, and the workers send results back. For a scalar UDF the handler runs once per row. For a vectorized UDF, rows are grouped into batches and converted to pandas DataFrames. For a UDTF, rows are routed so that each partition is processed by one handler instance, in the requested order. Workers run in parallel across nodes and cores, so a Python UDF scales with the warehouse, but it's still Python. A built-in SQL function runs inside the engine with no data movement or interpreter at all. That's why the best Python UDF is often the one you didn't need. When you do need one, memory-heavy work (large models, big libraries) may need a Snowpark-optimized warehouse, which has more memory per node.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Python for what SQL already does. SPLIT_PART, REGEXP_SUBSTR and TRY_TO_NUMBER beat any handler.
  • Not handling None. A NULL input will crash email.split.
  • Vectorizing string logic and expecting speed. Measure. Vectorization pays off for array math.
  • Unpinned packages in production functions. Pin versions ('numpy==2.2.6') once a function is in use, so a rebuild doesn't silently change results.
  • Loading a model on every call. Load it at module level or in __init__ (once per process or partition), not inside the handler.
  • UDTFs without ORDER BY when the logic depends on order, such as sessionization.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create email_domain in a trial account and compare its run time on SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF10.CUSTOMER (use C_NAME || '@example.com') with SPLIT_PART, using the Query Profile.
  2. Run handler_bench.py on your machine. Then add a third case (for example, a regex) and predict which version wins before running it.
  3. Create the vectorized churn_score and a scalar version of it, run both on 10 million generated rows, and compare.
  4. Extend Sessionize to emit, from end_partition only, one row per session with its start, end and number of pages. Test it with the local driver first.

docs.title: 04 · Cortex AI Functions
docs.text:
Support tickets, reviews, call notes, contracts: most companies have more text than anyone reads. Cortex AI functions run large language models from SQL, inside Snowflake's service perimeter, so classifying a million tickets is a SELECT rather than a pipeline to an external API. This lesson covers the functions, who may call them, where the data goes, and the part that surprises teams on their first bill: how tokens add up.

Not run for this course

Cortex functions need a Snowflake account in a supported region, so none were called here and no model outputs are shown. Syntax, privileges, billing rules and limits come from Snowflake's documentation as of October 2026. This area changes monthly: functions move from preview to GA, and models are added and retired. Check the function reference and the regional availability page before relying on any detail.

docs.title: The functions
docs.text:
Per the documentation, the task-specific functions include:

Function Does Returns AI_CLASSIFY assigns text (or an image or document) to one or more of your categories object with a labels array AI_FILTER evaluates a natural-language condition BOOLEAN, usable in WHERE and JOIN … ON AI_SENTIMENT overall sentiment, optionally per aspect (up to 10) object with categories: positive, negative, neutral, mixed or unknown AI_EXTRACT pulls named fields out of text or documents object AI_SUMMARIZE_AGG, AI_AGG summarise or answer a prompt across many rows string AI_TRANSLATE, AI_REDACT translate, remove PII string AI_EMBED, AI_SIMILARITY vectors and similarity for search and clustering vector, number AI_COMPLETE general prompt to a chosen model, optionally with a response schema string or object

Some are preview features. The documentation marks each one, and only GA functions are meant for production.

docs.title: Examples on support tickets
docs.text:
-- route tickets: one label each, with descriptions to sharpen the boundaries
SELECT ticket_id,
       AI_CLASSIFY(body,
         [ {'label': 'billing', 'description': 'charges, refunds, invoices, payment failures'},
           {'label': 'bug',     'description': 'a feature that worked before or should work does not work'},
           {'label': 'how-to',  'description': 'questions about how to use an existing feature'},
           {'label': 'account', 'description': 'users, admins, access, sign-in and workspace settings'} ],
         {'task_description': 'Route customer support tickets for a SaaS product'}
       ):labels[0]::VARCHAR AS queue
FROM support.raw.tickets;

-- a semantic WHERE clause
SELECT ticket_id, body
FROM support.raw.tickets
WHERE created_at >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
  AND AI_FILTER(PROMPT('The customer says they are considering cancelling: {0}', body));

-- aspect-based sentiment
SELECT ticket_id, AI_SENTIMENT(body, ['pricing', 'support', 'reliability']) AS sentiment
FROM support.raw.tickets;

-- structured extraction with a typed response format
SELECT ticket_id,
       AI_COMPLETE(
         model => 'llama3.3-70b',
         prompt => 'Extract the order number and the product mentioned in this ticket: ' || body,
         response_format => TYPE OBJECT(order_number STRING, product STRING),
         model_parameters => {'temperature': 0}
       ) AS extracted
FROM support.raw.tickets;

-- one answer across many rows (not limited by a single context window, per the documentation)
SELECT AI_AGG(body, 'List the three most common reasons for refund requests, with one example each')
FROM support.raw.tickets
WHERE created_at >= DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP());

Two behaviours to plan for. Errors return NULL by default, row by row, and the query still succeeds. Pass return_error_details => TRUE (the last argument) to get an object with the value or the error, and count the failures. And outputs are probabilistic. temperature defaults to 0 for AI_COMPLETE, but a model or function version change can still change results, so store the outputs you depend on rather than recomputing them.

docs.title: Who may call them
docs.text:
From the documentation on privileges:

  • A role needs both the account privilege USE AI FUNCTIONS and one of the database roles SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER or SNOWFLAKE.AI_FUNCTIONS_USER.
  • By default, USE AI FUNCTIONS and CORTEX_USER are granted to PUBLIC, so every user can call them. AI_FUNCTIONS_USER isn't.
  • Which models a role can use is controlled by model RBAC: application roles such as SNOWFLAKE."CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-LLAMA3.3-70B". The older account parameter CORTEX_MODELS_ALLOWLIST is being deprecated (since August 2026 it can only be set to 'None').
  • ACCOUNTADMIN always has access to all models, including as a secondary role. Test restrictions with another role and USE SECONDARY ROLES NONE.
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
REVOKE USE AI FUNCTIONS ON ACCOUNT FROM ROLE PUBLIC;
REVOKE DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER FROM ROLE PUBLIC;

CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS ai_user;
GRANT USE AI FUNCTIONS ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE ai_user;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER TO ROLE ai_user;
GRANT APPLICATION ROLE SNOWFLAKE."CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-LLAMA3.3-70B" TO ROLE ai_user;
GRANT ROLE ai_user TO ROLE support_analytics;

SHOW APPLICATION ROLES LIKE 'CORTEX-MODEL%' IN APPLICATION SNOWFLAKE;

Whether to lock it down is a governance decision, not a technical one. Leaving it open means anyone who can read a table can send it to a model, and spend credits doing so. Masking and row access policies (Level 3) still apply to what a role can read, and so to what it can send.

docs.title: Where the data goes
docs.text:
The models run inside Snowflake's service perimeter, but not necessarily in your region. If a model isn't available locally, cross-region inference (account parameter CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION) can route the request elsewhere. Per the documentation, data at rest stays in your account's region. The prompt and response travel encrypted to the processing region and aren't persisted there, and billing happens in your region. The default depends on the account: new organizations created after March 9, 2026 default to ANY_REGION. If your obligations require in-region processing, check the parameter and set it explicitly:

SHOW PARAMETERS LIKE 'CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION' IN ACCOUNT;
ALTER ACCOUNT SET CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION = 'DISABLED';      -- or a list of allowed regions

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Cortex AI functions are billed per token (credits per million tokens, by function and model, in Snowflake's Service Consumption Table), plus the warehouse that runs the query. The documented rules that matter most:

  • For generating functions (AI_COMPLETE, AI_CLASSIFY, AI_FILTER, AI_AGG, AI_SUMMARIZE, AI_TRANSLATE), input and output tokens are both billed. For embeddings and similarity, input only.
  • Task-specific functions add their own prompt to your text, so billed tokens exceed your text.
  • For AI_CLASSIFY, the labels, descriptions and examples are billed as input for every row, not once per query.
  • Snowflake recommends a warehouse no larger than MEDIUM. A larger one doesn't make these functions faster.

The third rule is easy to overlook, because the labels look like a constant in the query. A lower-bound model of input tokens for the routing query above over one million tickets, using the documented four-characters-per-token convention:

# Lower-bound input-token model for AI_CLASSIFY over 1,000,000 tickets, using the documented ~4 characters per token
# convention and the documented rule that labels, descriptions and examples are billed as input FOR EVERY ROW.
# The function's own hidden prompt (also billed, per the docs) is unknown and left out, so real numbers are higher.
import json
tok = lambda s: len(s) / 4
tickets = ["My invoice for September shows a double charge for the Pro plan, please refund one of them.",
           "The export to CSV button does nothing since yesterday's update.",
           "How do I add a second admin to our workspace?",
           "Card declined again although the bank says everything is fine. Order 88231."]
avg_ticket = sum(map(tok, tickets)) / len(tickets)

labels = ["billing", "bug", "how-to", "account"]
described = [{"label": "billing", "description": "charges, refunds, invoices, payment failures"},
             {"label": "bug", "description": "a feature that worked before or should work does not work"},
             {"label": "how-to", "description": "questions about how to use an existing feature"},
             {"label": "account", "description": "users, admins, access, sign-in and workspace settings"}]
examples = [{"input": t, "labels": [l], "explanation": "matches the category description"}
            for t, l in zip(tickets[:3], ["billing", "bug", "how-to"])]

ROWS = 1_000_000
variants = {"labels only": tok(json.dumps(labels)),
            "+ descriptions": tok(json.dumps(described)),
            "+ descriptions + 3 examples": tok(json.dumps(described)) + tok(json.dumps(examples))}
print(f"average ticket: {avg_ticket:.0f} tokens")
for name, extra in variants.items():
    per_row = avg_ticket + extra
    print(f"{name:<28} {per_row:6.0f} tokens/row  {per_row * ROWS / 1e6:7.1f} M input tokens  ({per_row / avg_ticket:.1f}x the tickets alone)")

average ticket: 17 tokens
labels only                      27 tokens/row     26.9 M input tokens  (1.6x the tickets alone)
+ descriptions                  107 tokens/row    106.9 M input tokens  (6.2x the tickets alone)
+ descriptions + 3 examples     222 tokens/row    222.1 M input tokens  (13.0x the tickets alone)

With short tickets, the category definitions dominate: descriptions multiply input tokens about six times, and three few-shot examples about thirteen times, before the function's own prompt is counted. Descriptions and examples often improve accuracy, so the answer isn't to drop them. Measure accuracy with and without them on a labelled sample, and pay for the version that earns it. Then cut the volume:

  • Classify each ticket once. Run the function from a stream-driven task (Level 2 · 06–07) and store the result, so dashboards read a column instead of calling a model.
  • Filter with SQL first. A WHERE on date, language or product before AI_FILTER sends fewer rows to the model.
  • Measure tokens before scaling. AI_COUNT_TOKENS returns the token count for a function and input, at warehouse cost only.

Track actual spend in ACCOUNT_USAGE (with its usual latency, Level 3 · 09):

SELECT function_name, model_name, SUM(tokens) AS tokens, SUM(token_credits) AS credits
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.CORTEX_FUNCTIONS_QUERY_USAGE_HISTORY
GROUP BY function_name, model_name
ORDER BY credits DESC;

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: An AI function call is part of an ordinary query. The warehouse reads and filters the rows, and for each input that reaches the function, Snowflake builds a request (your text plus the function's prompt, labels or schema) and sends it to the model-serving service, which Snowflake optimizes for throughput. Results come back as values in the query's output. That's why the documentation recommends batch use over interactive calls, why a larger warehouse doesn't help (the model service is the bottleneck), and why billing has two parts: warehouse time for the query, and tokens for the model. Access checks happen at both ends. Privileges decide whether the role may call the function and use the model, and the usual table privileges and policies decide which rows and values can be read and sent at all.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Leaving the default PUBLIC grants without deciding to. Every user can send any table they can read to a model.
  • Recomputing model outputs in dashboards. Classify once, store the result.
  • Ignoring NULL results. Errors are silent by default. Count them.
  • Long label descriptions and many examples on large tables without measuring their value. They're billed per row.
  • Large warehouses for AI queries. Medium or smaller, per the documentation.
  • Assuming in-region processing. Check CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION.
  • Treating outputs as deterministic facts. Evaluate against a labelled sample, and re-evaluate when a model changes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. In a trial account, check who can call AI functions (SHOW GRANTS OF DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER) and what CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION is set to. Write down whether either should change for your organization.
  2. Label 50 synthetic tickets by hand. Run AI_CLASSIFY with labels only, with descriptions, and with examples, and record accuracy and TOKENS from the usage view for each. Which version would you pay for?
  3. Build the "classify once" pipeline: a stream on tickets, a task that inserts AI_CLASSIFY results for new rows into ticket_labels, and a check that re-running the task classifies nothing.
  4. Use AI_COUNT_TOKENS on your ticket sample and compare it with classify_tokens.py's four-characters estimate.

docs.title: 05 · Cost Management: Monitors, Budgets & Attribution
docs.text: Level 1 explained how Snowflake bills: credits per second while warehouses run, plus serverless features, cloud services and storage. This lesson is about managing that bill: seeing where credits go, charging them back to the teams that spent them, and stopping runaway spend before it happens. Each tool has a documented blind spot, and knowing those blind spots is the difference between a cost dashboard and a cost dashboard you can trust.

docs.title: Where the credits go
docs.text:
METERING_DAILY_HISTORY breaks credits down by service type. Per the documentation, that includes warehouses, serverless tasks, Snowpipe Streaming, automatic clustering, materialized views, search optimization, query acceleration, replication, AI services and more:

SELECT service_type,
       SUM(credits_used_compute)              AS compute,
       SUM(credits_used_cloud_services)       AS cloud_services,
       SUM(credits_adjustment_cloud_services) AS cs_adjustment,
       SUM(credits_billed)                    AS billed
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.METERING_DAILY_HISTORY
WHERE usage_date >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_DATE())
GROUP BY service_type
ORDER BY billed DESC;

credits_billed already includes the cloud services adjustment: cloud services usage is billed only above 10% of the day's warehouse compute (Level 1 · 04). Start every cost review here. A team obsessing over warehouse sizes is wasting effort if search optimization or a forgotten serverless task is the biggest line.

docs.title: Attribution: which query spent it?
docs.text:
QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY gives the warehouse credits attributed to each query (credits_attributed_compute), with its user, warehouse, query tag and a parameterized hash for grouping repeated queries. Its documented limits:

  • It excludes warehouse idle time: credits for a warehouse running with nothing to do aren't attributed to any query.
  • Very short queries (about 100 ms or less) aren't included.
  • Latency is up to eight hours.

The first limit matters most, because idle time can be most of a bill. A model of one shared X-Small warehouse for a day, with BI dashboards refreshing every 15 minutes, one nightly job and two ad-hoc sessions:

# Model (not Snowflake output): one shared X-Small warehouse (1 credit/hour) for a day, billed per second with a 60 s
# minimum per resume. Assumptions: the warehouse resumes at a query's start and suspends AUTO_SUSPEND seconds after the
# last query ends; a second shared by n running queries is attributed 1/n to each (Snowflake's exact split isn't modelled).
import random
random.seed(42)
queries = []                                                    # (team, start_s, duration_s)
for minute in range(8 * 60, 18 * 60, 15):                       # BI dashboard refreshes every 15 min, 08:00-18:00
    for _ in range(random.randint(1, 4)):
        queries.append(("bi", minute * 60 + random.randint(0, 30), random.randint(2, 20)))
queries.append(("etl", 2 * 3600, 40 * 60))                       # nightly ELT: one 40-minute job at 02:00
for h in (10, 14):                                              # ad-hoc data science twice a day
    queries.append(("ds", h * 3600 + 600, random.randint(300, 900)))

def day(auto_suspend):
    active = {}                                                 # second -> teams running
    for team, s, d in queries:
        for t in range(s, s + d):
            active.setdefault(t, []).append(team)
    running, t_end = set(), None
    for t in sorted(active):                                    # build running intervals
        if t_end is None or t > t_end + auto_suspend:
            if t_end is not None:
                running |= set(range(start, max(t_end + auto_suspend, start + 60)))
            start = t
        t_end = t + 1
    running |= set(range(start, max(t_end + auto_suspend, start + 60)))
    rate = 1 / 3600
    metered = len(running) * rate
    attributed = {}
    for t, teams in active.items():
        for team in teams:
            attributed[team] = attributed.get(team, 0) + rate / len(teams)
    return metered, attributed

print(f"queries: {len(queries)}")
for s in (600, 60):
    metered, attr = day(s)
    total = sum(attr.values())
    print(f"\nAUTO_SUSPEND = {s}")
    print(f"  metered (WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY-like): {metered:6.3f} credits")
    for team in sorted(attr):
        print(f"  attributed to {team:<4}{attr[team]:24.3f} credits")
    print(f"  idle, attributed to nobody: {metered - total:15.3f} credits ({(metered - total) / metered:.0%} of the bill)")

queries: 96

AUTO_SUSPEND = 600
  metered (WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY-like):  7.967 credits
  attributed to bi                     0.209 credits
  attributed to ds                     0.261 credits
  attributed to etl                    0.667 credits
  idle, attributed to nobody:           6.829 credits (86% of the bill)

AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  metered (WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY-like):  1.850 credits
  attributed to bi                     0.209 credits
  attributed to ds                     0.261 credits
  attributed to etl                    0.667 credits
  idle, attributed to nobody:           0.712 credits (39% of the bill)

The teams' attributed credits are identical in both runs, because the queries didn't change. The bill differs by a factor of four, and with a 10-minute auto-suspend, 86% of it is attributed to nobody. A chargeback report that sums credits_attributed_compute by team would show about 1.1 credits for a warehouse that cost 8. The numbers come from a model with stated assumptions, but the shape doesn't: bursty, frequent, short queries with a long auto-suspend produce mostly idle time.

Snowflake exposes the gap directly. WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY has both the compute credits and the part attributed to queries:

SELECT warehouse_name,
       SUM(credits_used_compute)                                            AS compute,
       SUM(credits_attributed_compute_queries)                              AS attributed,
       SUM(credits_used_compute) - SUM(credits_attributed_compute_queries)  AS idle,
       ROUND(100 * idle / NULLIF(compute, 0), 1)                            AS idle_pct
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
GROUP BY warehouse_name
ORDER BY idle DESC;

A high idle_pct is a tuning signal (shorter AUTO_SUSPEND, fewer refreshes, consolidated schedules) and a chargeback decision: idle credits must be allocated to someone, typically in proportion to each team's attributed usage on that warehouse, which is also the approach in Snowflake's own cost-attribution examples. The capstone (lesson 10) builds that allocator with tests.

docs.title: Chargeback with tags
docs.text:
Attribution needs an owner for every credit. Two documented mechanisms:

  • Object tags on warehouses (and other objects): with a dedicated warehouse per team, tag it with cost_center, and its whole metered cost (idle included) belongs to that team. Join WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY to TAG_REFERENCES.
  • Query tags for shared warehouses: set QUERY_TAG per session (tools and pipelines can set it), and group QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY by it.
CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS governance.tags.cost_center ALLOWED_VALUES 'sales', 'hr', 'data-platform', 'data-science';
ALTER WAREHOUSE sales_bi_wh SET TAG governance.tags.cost_center = 'sales';
ALTER WAREHOUSE sales_etl_wh SET TAG governance.tags.cost_center = 'sales';

-- in a pipeline's session
ALTER SESSION SET QUERY_TAG = 'team=data-science;job=churn-features';

SELECT t.tag_value AS cost_center, SUM(m.credits_used) AS credits
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY m
JOIN SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.TAG_REFERENCES t
  ON t.domain = 'WAREHOUSE' AND t.object_name = m.warehouse_name AND t.tag_name = 'COST_CENTER'
WHERE m.start_time >= DATE_TRUNC(month, CURRENT_DATE())
GROUP BY cost_center
ORDER BY credits DESC;

docs.title: Resource monitors: hard stops for warehouses
docs.text:
A resource monitor counts credits against a quota and acts at thresholds:

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE OR REPLACE RESOURCE MONITOR sales_bi_monthly WITH
  CREDIT_QUOTA = 100
  FREQUENCY = MONTHLY
  START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY
           ON 90 PERCENT DO SUSPEND
           ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE;

ALTER WAREHOUSE sales_bi_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = sales_bi_monthly;

From the documentation:

  • They work for warehouses only. Serverless features, AI services and storage aren't covered.
  • Only ACCOUNTADMIN can create them. A warehouse can belong to one monitor, and an account has at most one account-level monitor.
  • SUSPEND lets running statements finish. SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE cancels them.
  • Quotas count all cloud services credits for the warehouses, ignoring the 10% adjustment, so a monitor can trip before the bill shows that spend.
  • Usage resets at 12:00 AM UTC on the schedule's day. For strict limits, Snowflake recommends buffers (act at 90%, not 100%) and one warehouse per monitor, so one warehouse's spend can't suspend another.

Use them as circuit breakers for things that must never run away: reader-account warehouses (Level 3 · 07), sandbox warehouses, and anything that runs unattended.

docs.title: Budgets: forecasts and alerts for everything
docs.text:
A budget sets a monthly spending limit and notifies when spend is projected to exceed it. It covers serverless features and AI services as well as warehouses. There's one account budget, and custom budgets for groups of objects, which can be selected by tag:

CALL SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.ACCOUNT_ROOT_BUDGET!ACTIVATE();
CALL SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.ACCOUNT_ROOT_BUDGET!SET_SPENDING_LIMIT(1000);
CALL SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.ACCOUNT_ROOT_BUDGET!SET_EMAIL_NOTIFICATIONS('costadmin@example.com, finance@example.com');

CREATE SNOWFLAKE.CORE.BUDGET governance.budgets.sales_budget();
CALL governance.budgets.sales_budget!SET_SPENDING_LIMIT(300);
CALL governance.budgets.sales_budget!ADD_RESOURCE_TAG(
  SELECT SYSTEM$REFERENCE('TAG', 'governance.tags.cost_center', 'SESSION', 'applybudget'), 'sales');

Budgets differ from monitors in the ways that matter:

Resource monitor Budget Covers warehouses only warehouses, serverless features, AI services, … Period daily, weekly, monthly, yearly or never calendar month Acts notifies, suspends warehouses notifies (email, cloud queue, webhook); can call your stored procedures Timing thresholds on actual usage projections, refreshed up to every 6.5 hours by default

Per the documentation, a low-latency budget refreshes hourly, at 12 times the budget's own compute cost. A custom budget whose objects are added individually isn't backfilled for the current month, while objects added by tag are. Prefer tags.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Every credit Snowflake meters is recorded against a service and, where there is one, an object: warehouse seconds per warehouse, serverless seconds per task, pipe or table, tokens per AI call. Account Usage views are periodically refreshed copies of those records, which is why they lag. Attribution is a second calculation on top of metering. For each warehouse interval, Snowflake attributes the credits to the queries running in it, by a weighted average of their resource consumption (per the documentation; the model above simply splits equally), and what no query used is idle time. Resource monitors read the warehouse meters frequently and act on warehouses directly, which is why they can stop spend. Budgets read the consolidated metering data on a slower schedule and project to month end, which is why they can cover every service but only warn (or call your procedure). A complete setup uses all three: metering for the truth, attribution plus allocation for chargeback, monitors as circuit breakers, and budgets as the early warning.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Chargeback from QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY alone. It leaves out idle time, which can be most of the bill.
  • Relying on resource monitors to cap total spend. They cover warehouses only.
  • Thresholds at exactly 100% when the limit is a hard one. Monitors aren't instantaneous. Use buffers.
  • One monitor for many warehouses when one team's burst shouldn't suspend another team's warehouse.
  • Untagged warehouses. Every warehouse needs a cost owner from day one.
  • Custom budgets built object by object. Use tags, so new objects are covered and history is backfilled.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the service-type query on a trial account. Which three lines are largest, and which of them could a resource monitor stop?
  2. Run the idle query for your warehouses. Pick the one with the highest idle_pct, change its AUTO_SUSPEND, and compare a week before and after.
  3. Change attribution_gap.py so the BI refreshes run every 5 minutes, then every 60. Predict the idle share first.
  4. Create a monitor for a sandbox warehouse with a tiny quota (1 credit, daily), run queries until it fires, and record what happened to a running query at each trigger.

docs.title: 06 · Warehouse Scaling: Up, Out & Adaptive
docs.text: A warehouse that's too small makes people wait. One that's too big burns credits. Snowflake gives you several levers, and they solve different problems: a bigger size makes individual queries faster, more clusters let more queries run at once, query acceleration helps the odd huge scan, and newer warehouse types change the trade-offs altogether. This lesson shows which lever fits which symptom, with a model that makes the main trade-off visible and states the assumption it hinges on.

docs.title: Two symptoms, two levers
docs.text:
From the Query Profile and QUERY_HISTORY (Level 2 · 03), slow queries come in two kinds:

Symptom Evidence Lever Each query is slow, even alone long execution time, spilling to local or remote storage scale up (a bigger size) Queries wait for their turn high queued_overload_time, fine execution time scale out (more clusters) 
SELECT warehouse_name,
       COUNT(*)                                          AS queries,
       ROUND(AVG(queued_overload_time) / 1000, 1)        AS avg_queued_s,
       ROUND(AVG(execution_time) / 1000, 1)              AS avg_exec_s,
       SUM(IFF(bytes_spilled_to_remote_storage > 0, 1, 0)) AS remote_spills
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_HISTORY
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
  AND warehouse_name IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY warehouse_name
ORDER BY avg_queued_s DESC;

docs.title: Scale up or scale out? A model
docs.text:
Eighty dashboard queries arrive within 20 seconds at 09:00, a typical Monday-morning burst. Each takes 32 seconds of work on a Small warehouse. The deciding question is how much faster a query gets on a bigger warehouse, and that depends on the query, so the model runs twice: once with perfect scaling, once with the poor scaling typical of small queries:

# Model (not Snowflake): 80 dashboard queries arrive in the first 20 s of 09:00, each 32 s of work on a Small warehouse.
# Assumptions, stated because they decide the answer:
#  - a cluster runs at most 8 queries at once (the default MAX_CONCURRENCY_LEVEL) with no slowdown below that;
#  - doubling the size multiplies a query's duration by SPEEDUP: 0.5 is perfect scaling, 0.8 is what small
#    queries that can't use the extra nodes look like (both are assumptions; measure your own);
#  - an extra cluster starts as soon as a query queues and is usable after 0 s; idle clusters stop when empty;
#  - credits: Small = 2/h, Medium = 4/h, Large = 8/h per cluster, per second, 60 s minimum per cluster start.
import statistics
arrivals = [i * 0.25 for i in range(80)]

def simulate(credits_per_h, duration, max_clusters):
    clusters = []                                          # each: list of slot-free times, start time, last end
    finish = []
    for t in arrivals:
        best = None
        for c in clusters:                                 # earliest free slot on running clusters
            slot = min(range(8), key=lambda i: c["slots"][i])
            if best is None or c["slots"][slot] < best[0]:
                best = (c["slots"][slot], c, slot)
        if best is None or (best[0] > t and len(clusters) < max_clusters):
            c = {"slots": [t] * 8, "start": t, "end": t}   # queued (or first query): start a cluster
            clusters.append(c); best = (t, c, 0)
        begin, c, slot = max(best[0], t), best[1], best[2]
        end = begin + duration
        c["slots"][slot] = end; c["end"] = max(c["end"], end)
        finish.append(end - t)
    credits = sum(max(c["end"] - c["start"], 60) for c in clusters) * credits_per_h / 3600
    return len(clusters), statistics.median(finish), sorted(finish)[int(0.95 * len(finish)) - 1], max(finish), credits

for speedup in (0.5, 0.8):
    print(f"\nSPEEDUP per size doubling = {speedup}")
    print(f"{'configuration':<36}{'clusters':>9}{'p50 s':>8}{'p95 s':>8}{'credits':>9}")
    for name, cph, dur, mx in [("Small, 1 cluster", 2, 32, 1),
                               ("Medium, 1 cluster (scale up)", 4, 32 * speedup, 1),
                               ("Large, 1 cluster (scale up)", 8, 32 * speedup ** 2, 1),
                               ("Small, up to 4 clusters (scale out)", 2, 32, 4)]:
        n, p50, p95, _, cr = simulate(cph, dur, mx)
        print(f"{name:<36}{n:>9}{p50:>8.0f}{p95:>8.0f}{cr:>9.3f}")

SPEEDUP per size doubling = 0.5
configuration                        clusters   p50 s   p95 s  credits
Small, 1 cluster                            1     167     302    0.179
Medium, 1 cluster (scale up)                1      79     142    0.180
Large, 1 cluster (scale up)                 1      35      62    0.182
Small, up to 4 clusters (scale out)         4      56      80    0.182

SPEEDUP per size doubling = 0.8
configuration                        clusters   p50 s   p95 s  credits
Small, 1 cluster                            1     167     302    0.179
Medium, 1 cluster (scale up)                1     132     238    0.286
Large, 1 cluster (scale up)                 1     104     187    0.459
Small, up to 4 clusters (scale out)         4      56      80    0.182

With perfect scaling, all options cost about the same, because twice the credits per hour for half the time is the same money, and a Large warehouse gives the best latency. With poor scaling, scaling up costs up to 2.5 times more and still leaves queries waiting, while four Small clusters cut p95 latency from 302 to 80 seconds for the same credits as one. Real queries sit somewhere between, and the model ignores cluster start-up time, so treat the numbers as a shape, not a forecast. The rule it supports: scale out for concurrency; scale up only for queries that get faster when they get more compute. Test that by running the same query on two sizes with the result cache off.

docs.title: Multi-cluster warehouses
docs.text:
Multi-cluster warehouses need Enterprise Edition. Set a range of clusters, and Snowflake starts and stops clusters within it:

CREATE OR REPLACE WAREHOUSE bi_wh
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL'
  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1
  MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 4
  SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD'
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE;
  • Auto-scale mode (MIN < MAX) starts and stops clusters with demand. Maximized mode (MIN = MAX) runs them all whenever the warehouse runs.
  • STANDARD (the default) favours starting clusters to avoid queuing. It adds a cluster when a query queues or Snowflake estimates the running clusters can't take more, and removes the least-loaded clusters after a sustained period of low load.
  • ECONOMY favours full clusters over speed. It adds a cluster only if Snowflake estimates enough load to keep it busy for at least 6 minutes, and marks one for shutdown when it has less than 6 minutes of work left. Queries may queue longer.

Each running cluster bills like a separate warehouse of that size. Per the documentation's example, a Medium warehouse with up to 3 clusters can consume at most 12 credits per hour. Use ECONOMY for batch-ish workloads that can tolerate some queuing, and STANDARD for interactive dashboards.

docs.title: Query acceleration
docs.text:
The Query Acceleration Service (QAS) offloads parts of eligible queries to shared serverless compute. Per the documentation, it targets large scans with selective filters and large inserts, copies, updates and deletes. Results depend on server availability, so gains can vary over time. It's billed as its own service type. QUERY_ACCELERATION_MAX_SCALE_FACTOR caps how much it can lease: per the documentation, a scale factor of 5 on a Medium warehouse (4 credits per hour) allows up to 20 extra credits per hour. The default is 2.

-- which past queries would have benefited?
SELECT query_id, warehouse_name, upper_limit_scale_factor, eligible_query_acceleration_time
FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_ACCELERATION_ELIGIBLE
WHERE start_time >= DATEADD(day, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
ORDER BY eligible_query_acceleration_time DESC
LIMIT 20;

ALTER WAREHOUSE reporting_wh SET ENABLE_QUERY_ACCELERATION = TRUE QUERY_ACCELERATION_MAX_SCALE_FACTOR = 4;

Per the documentation, QAS is enabled by default on Gen2 standard warehouses and multi-cluster warehouses, so check SHOW WAREHOUSES before assuming it's off, and watch the QUERY_ACCELERATION line in your metering.

docs.title: Warehouse types
docs.text:
Type What it is When Standard Gen1 (RESOURCE_CONSTRAINT = STANDARD_GEN_1) the original hardware existing workloads, sizes up to 6X-Large Standard Gen2 (GENERATION = '2' / STANDARD_GEN_2) newer hardware and faster DML and scans; per the docs, the default for new standard warehouses where available most new workloads; not available for 5X- and 6X-Large Snowpark-optimized (WAREHOUSE_TYPE = 'SNOWPARK-OPTIMIZED') much more memory per node, optional x86 (MEMORY_16X_x86) memory-hungry Python: ML training, large UDF libraries Adaptive (CREATE ADAPTIVE WAREHOUSE) a shared, account-dedicated compute pool that sizes, scales and routes each query itself workloads where you'd rather set limits than sizes (Enterprise+, select regions)

Gen2 credit rates differ from Gen1. They're in the Service Consumption Table, so compare cost per job, not per hour.

Adaptive Warehouses are the biggest change. Per the documentation (GA in select regions as of October 2026), you no longer choose a size, cluster counts, QAS settings or suspend behaviour. You set two limits instead: MAX_QUERY_PERFORMANCE_LEVEL (the most compute any single query may get, expressed as a size, default XLARGE) and QUERY_THROUGHPUT_MULTIPLIER (how much total concurrent work it may run, relative to a system baseline, default 2). Billing is per query, visible in QUERY_METERING_HISTORY, and budgets and resource monitors still apply.

CREATE ADAPTIVE WAREHOUSE analytics_awh
  WITH MAX_QUERY_PERFORMANCE_LEVEL = LARGE
       QUERY_THROUGHPUT_MULTIPLIER = 2;

The trade-off is control. The model above, and most of this lesson, is about choices an Adaptive Warehouse makes for you. Try one alongside a standard warehouse on a copy of a real workload, and compare cost per job and p95 latency before moving anything.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A standard warehouse cluster is a fixed set of compute nodes. Size sets the number of nodes, and each size doubles them.
