A query is split across the cluster's nodes, so a bigger size helps only if the query has enough work to divide: large scans, joins and sorts benefit, small lookups don't. Up to MAX_CONCURRENCY_LEVEL queries (8 by default) share a cluster. When it's saturated, new queries queue. A multi-cluster warehouse adds whole clusters, each with its own nodes and local cache, and the services layer routes new queries to clusters with capacity. That's why scale-out fixes queuing without making any single query faster, and why caches warm separately on each cluster. QAS lends extra workers for the scan-heavy fragments of one query. An Adaptive Warehouse drops fixed clusters altogether and gives each query an allocation from a shared pool, within your limits. The same principle runs underneath, matching compute to the parallelism a query can actually use, but it's decided per query instead of per warehouse.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Scaling up to fix queuing. It costs more per hour and leaves queries waiting if they don't speed up. Add clusters.
  • Scaling out to fix spilling. More clusters of the same size spill the same way. Scale up.
  • ECONOMY for interactive dashboards. Users wait for clusters that start only when there are 6 minutes of work.
  • Maximized mode by accident (MIN = MAX), paying for all clusters whenever the warehouse runs.
  • Comparing Gen1 and Gen2 on credits per hour. Compare credits per job.
  • Assuming QAS is off. It's on by default for Gen2 and multi-cluster warehouses.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the queue and spill query for your warehouses. Classify each as healthy, needs scale-up or needs scale-out.
  2. Run one heavy query (an aggregation over SNOWFLAKE_SAMPLE_DATA.TPCH_SF100.LINEITEM) on Small, Medium and Large with USE_CACHED_RESULT = FALSE. Compute its SPEEDUP and its credits for each size, then rerun scaling_model.py with that value.
  3. Fire 50 concurrent copies of a dashboard query (for example with a small Python script and the connector) at a Small warehouse with MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1, then 4. Compare queued time.
  4. If Adaptive Warehouses are available in your region, run the same workload on one and compare cost per job from QUERY_METERING_HISTORY with your standard warehouse's WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY.

docs.title: 07 · Replication, Failover & Business Continuity
docs.text:
Snowflake is built to survive the loss of a data centre within a region. Losing a whole region (or a cloud provider's region-wide outage) is a different event, and surviving it is your design decision: replicate to an account in another region, decide how much data you can afford to lose, and practise switching over. This lesson covers the objects that do the replication, the refresh options, what a schedule actually means for data loss, and redirecting clients.

What was run

Replication needs at least two accounts (and Business Critical Edition for failover), so nothing here was run. The data-loss figures come from a small model with stated assumptions, and the SQL was checked against Snowflake's October 2026 documentation, including features that are new in 2026 (Optimized Refresh and RPO Assurance).

docs.title: What can be replicated, on which edition
docs.text:
Capability Edition, per the documentation Database and share replication all editions Replication groups with other account objects (users, roles, warehouses, integrations, policies, …) Business Critical or higher Failover groups (promote a replica to primary) Business Critical or higher Client Redirect (connection URLs that follow the primary) Business Critical or higher

A replication group is a set of objects replicated together to one or more target accounts, read-only there. A failover group is a replication group that can also be promoted: the secondary becomes the read-write primary. Both give point-in-time consistency across everything in the group, so a role and the tables it's granted on arrive together.

Not everything is replicated. Per the documentation, temporary tables, external tables and hybrid tables are skipped (and won't exist after a failover). Dynamic tables and clustering are replicated. Snowflake-managed Iceberg tables need their external volume replicated too. Warehouses arrive suspended. Read the "replication considerations" page for each object type you depend on. A failover that brings back tables but not the stage integration your pipelines need is only half a recovery.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
On the source account:

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg
  OBJECT_TYPES = USERS, ROLES, WAREHOUSES, RESOURCE MONITORS, DATABASES, INTEGRATIONS, NETWORK POLICIES, ACCOUNT PARAMETERS
  ALLOWED_DATABASES = sales, hr, governance
  ALLOWED_INTEGRATION_TYPES = SECURITY INTEGRATIONS, STORAGE INTEGRATIONS
  ALLOWED_ACCOUNTS = myorg.prod_dr
  REPLICATION_SCHEDULE = '10 MINUTE'
  OPTIMIZED_REFRESH = TRUE;

On the target account (in another region):

USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg AS REPLICA OF myorg.prod.prod_fg;
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg REFRESH;                -- the first, full refresh; afterwards the schedule takes over
SHOW FAILOVER GROUPS;

docs.title: Three refresh modes
docs.text:
The documentation now describes three modes for failover groups:

Mode How refreshes happen Billing (besides data transfer) Replication Classic (the default for existing groups) on REPLICATION_SCHEDULE or manual REFRESH Snowflake-provided compute, service type REPLICATION Optimized Refresh (OPTIMIZED_REFRESH = TRUE) on a schedule of at most 6 hours (10 minutes or less recommended); processes only metadata changes since the last refresh, so duration follows your rate of change rather than your object count based on replicated data volume and object changes RPO Assurance (RPO_ASSURANCE = TRUE, no schedule) continuous, managed by Snowflake, with an RPO target that is backed by an SLA for covered account pairs as Optimized Refresh

Table data is replicated incrementally in every mode. Optimized Refresh makes the metadata pass incremental too, which matters most for accounts with many databases, tables, roles and grants. RPO Assurance currently needs a request to your account team. In all modes, data transfer between regions is billed on the target account, at the source region's rate, plus the target's storage for secondary databases. Per the documentation, charges apply even when a refresh fails.

docs.title: What a schedule means for data loss
docs.text:
The recovery point objective (RPO) is how much committed data you may lose. With a schedule, it isn't the schedule interval. A refresh copies the primary as it was when the refresh started, and the copy is usable only when the refresh finishes:

# Model (not Snowflake): how much committed data a failover can lose with a scheduled refresh.
# Assumptions: a refresh replicates the primary as of the moment it starts and becomes visible on the secondary
# when it finishes; refreshes start every SCHEDULE minutes, or as soon as the previous one finishes if it overran.
# Failure moment is uniform over a day. Data loss = failure time - snapshot time of the last completed refresh.
def rpo(schedule, duration, horizon=24 * 60, step=0.1):
    refreshes, t = [], 0.0                                   # (snapshot_time, visible_time)
    while t < horizon + 1000:
        refreshes.append((t, t + duration))
        t = max(t + schedule, t + duration)
    losses = []
    f = 120.0                                                # start measuring after a warm-up
    while f < horizon:
        snapshot = max(s for s, v in refreshes if v <= f)
        losses.append(f - snapshot)
        f += step
    return sum(losses) / len(losses), max(losses)

print(f"{'schedule':>9} {'refresh takes':>14} {'avg loss':>9} {'worst loss':>11}")
for schedule, duration in [(60, 5), (60, 30), (10, 2), (10, 8), (10, 25)]:
    avg, worst = rpo(schedule, duration)
    print(f"{schedule:>6} min {duration:>10} min {avg:>6.1f} min {worst:>8.1f} min")

 schedule  refresh takes  avg loss  worst loss
    60 min          5 min   35.0 min     65.0 min
    60 min         30 min   60.0 min     90.0 min
    10 min          2 min    7.0 min     12.0 min
    10 min          8 min   13.0 min     18.0 min
    10 min         25 min   37.5 min     50.0 min

The worst case is the interval plus the refresh duration (65 minutes on an hourly schedule with 5-minute refreshes, not 60). And when refreshes take longer than the interval (the last row), refreshes run back to back and the worst case becomes twice the refresh time. That's the case Optimized Refresh addresses by making refresh time depend on change rather than size, and the one RPO Assurance takes off your hands. Measure your real refresh durations:

SELECT phase_name, start_time, end_time, DATEDIFF(second, start_time, end_time) AS seconds
FROM TABLE(INFORMATION_SCHEMA.REPLICATION_GROUP_REFRESH_PROGRESS('prod_fg'));

docs.title: Client Redirect
docs.text:
After a failover, every tool's connection string would still point at the old account. A connection object gives clients a stable URL (<organization>-<connection>.snowflakecomputing.com) that Snowflake resolves to whichever account is primary:

-- source account
CREATE CONNECTION prod_conn;
ALTER CONNECTION prod_conn ENABLE FAILOVER TO ACCOUNTS myorg.prod_dr;

-- target account
CREATE CONNECTION prod_conn AS REPLICA OF myorg.prod.prod_conn;

Point BI tools, drivers and pipelines at the connection URL from the start. Changing every client during an outage is exactly the work you don't want to do then.

docs.title: The failover runbook
docs.text:
Promotion happens in the target account, which is reachable while the source region is down:

-- in the target account
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg SUSPEND IMMEDIATE;      -- only if a scheduled refresh is in progress and blocks promotion
ALTER FAILOVER GROUP prod_fg PRIMARY;                -- the replicas become read-write
ALTER CONNECTION prod_conn PRIMARY;                  -- clients now resolve to this account

-- resume what doesn't move by itself
ALTER WAREHOUSE etl_wh RESUME;
ALTER TASK sales.mart.merge_orders RESUME;

Per the documentation, promotion fails while a refresh is in progress. SUSPEND waits for it, and SUSPEND IMMEDIATE cancels a scheduled one, with a warning that cancelling during the data-download phases can leave an inconsistent state, so know which phase you're in before choosing. A runbook also needs the parts SQL doesn't cover: who decides to fail over, how pipelines that write to the old primary are stopped, how you'll fail back (the old primary becomes a secondary and must be refreshed first), and a scheduled drill that proves all of it works.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A refresh starts by taking a consistent snapshot of the primary group: the metadata for every object in it, and the list of micro-partitions each table version references. Because micro-partitions are immutable (Level 1 · 01), the target only needs files it doesn't already have, so table data is naturally incremental. Snowflake copies those files across regions, applies the metadata, and switches the secondary to the new snapshot atomically, which is what gives point-in-time consistency. Promotion flips the group's role. The secondary's objects become writable, and the old primary, when it's back, becomes a secondary that can only receive refreshes. Client Redirect is a DNS-level indirection: the connection URL resolves to whichever account currently holds the primary connection.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Replicating databases but not roles, users and integrations. The data arrives, and nobody can use it.
  • Equating the schedule with the RPO. Add the refresh duration, and watch for refreshes that overrun.
  • Relying on temporary, external or hybrid tables without a plan to recreate them.
  • Hard-coded account URLs in clients. Use a connection URL.
  • Never testing failover. A drill is the only proof that the runbook, the grants and the pipelines all work.
  • Forgetting that warehouses and tasks need resuming on the new primary.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. List every object your most important pipeline needs (databases, roles, integrations, stages, network policies, tasks), and mark which a failover group would bring across and which it wouldn't.
  2. With two accounts, replicate one database with a replication group, refresh it twice, and query the refresh history. How long did each refresh take, and how much did it transfer?
  3. Rerun rpo_model.py with your measured durations and a 5-minute schedule. What's your worst-case data loss?
  4. Write your failover runbook as a checklist with owners, including fail-back, and schedule a drill.

docs.title: 08 · dbt & CI/CD for Snowflake
docs.text:
Level 2's pipelines were SQL objects created by hand. In a team, transformation code needs what application code has: version control, review, automated tests and repeatable deployment. dbt is the most common way to get that for SQL. Snowflake adds pieces that make it cheaper than elsewhere: zero-copy clones give every pull request a full production-shaped environment for free, and dbt Projects on Snowflake run dbt inside the account. This lesson builds a small dbt project, shows a bug that survived every standard test, and wires it into CI.

What was run

The dbt project was run for real with dbt-core 1.12.5 against DuckDB 1.5.6 (dbt-duckdb 1.11.0) locally, not Snowflake, through three batches of data. Its compiled SQL was checked to parse as Snowflake SQL, and dbt parse ran against the Snowflake targets (dbt-snowflake 1.12.2, which needs no connection to parse). The CI workflow and Snowflake CLI commands were checked for syntax and against snow dbt --help (Snowflake CLI 3.29.0), but not run.

docs.title: The project
docs.text:
A staging model that keeps the latest version of each order, and an incremental mart of daily revenue by the day each order was created. profiles.yml has a local DuckDB target for development and Snowflake targets for CI and production:

sales:
  target: local
  outputs:
    local:                                   # DuckDB file, for development without an account
      type: duckdb
      path: dev.duckdb
      threads: 4
    ci:                                      # a per-pull-request clone in Snowflake (key-pair auth from env vars)
      type: snowflake
      ...

models/staging/stg_orders.sql:

-- one row per order: the latest version the feed sent, plus when the order was first seen
select order_id, customer_id, region, amount, status,
       min(updated_at) over (partition by order_id) as created_at,
       updated_at
from {{ source('raw', 'orders') }}
qualify row_number() over (partition by order_id order by updated_at desc) = 1

models/marts/fct_daily_revenue.sql, first version. On incremental runs it reprocesses only days from the latest day already loaded:

{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key=['order_date', 'region']) }}

select cast(created_at as date) as order_date, region,
       count(*) as orders, sum(amount) as revenue,
       max(updated_at) as last_change
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where status <> 'cancelled'
{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- reprocess from the latest day already loaded
  and cast(created_at as date) >= (select max(order_date) from {{ this }})
{% endif %}
group by 1, 2

The tests: unique, not_null and accepted_values on staging, a uniqueness test on the mart's key, and a dbt unit test that feeds four hand-written rows into the mart and checks the exact output:

version: 2
models:
  - name: stg_orders
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        data_tests: [unique, not_null]
      - name: status
        data_tests:
          - accepted_values:
              arguments:
                values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'cancelled']
  - name: fct_daily_revenue
    data_tests:
      - unique_combination:
          arguments:
            columns: [order_date, region]

unit_tests:
  - name: latest_version_wins_and_cancelled_orders_drop_out
    model: fct_daily_revenue
    overrides:
      macros:
        is_incremental: false
    given:
      - input: ref('stg_orders')
        rows:
          - {order_id: 1, customer_id: 101, region: EU, amount: 120.0, status: placed,    created_at: "2026-10-14 09:00:00", updated_at: "2026-10-14 11:00:00"}
          - {order_id: 2, customer_id: 101, region: EU, amount: 30.0,  status: placed,    created_at: "2026-10-14 10:00:00", updated_at: "2026-10-14 10:00:00"}
          - {order_id: 3, customer_id: 102, region: EU, amount: 50.0,  status: cancelled, created_at: "2026-10-14 09:00:00", updated_at: "2026-10-14 12:00:00"}
          - {order_id: 4, customer_id: 201, region: US, amount: 80.0,  status: placed,    created_at: "2026-10-14 09:00:00", updated_at: "2026-10-14 09:00:00"}
    expect:
      rows:
        - {order_date: 2026-10-14, region: EU, orders: 2, revenue: 150.0, last_change: "2026-10-14 11:00:00"}
        - {order_date: 2026-10-14, region: US, orders: 1, revenue: 80.0, last_change: "2026-10-14 09:00:00"}

docs.title: A bug that passed every test
docs.text:
Three batches arrive. The third contains a late cancellation: order 3, created on 13 October, is cancelled on the 15th. After each batch, dbt build ran the models and all tests, and then a script compared the incremental table with recomputing it from scratch:

$ python load_raw.py 1
batch 1 landed; raw.orders has 5 rows
$ dbt build --target local
Done. PASS=7 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=7
$ python load_raw.py 2
batch 2 landed; raw.orders has 7 rows
$ dbt build --target local
Done. PASS=7 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=7
$ python load_raw.py 3
batch 3 landed; raw.orders has 9 rows
$ dbt build --target local
Done. PASS=7 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=7
$ python compare.py
incremental: [('2026-10-13', 'EU', 3, 200.0), ('2026-10-13', 'US', 1, 80.0), ('2026-10-14', 'EU', 1, 40.0), ('2026-10-14', 'US', 1, 25.0), ('2026-10-15', 'EU', 1, 60.0)]
full build : [('2026-10-13', 'EU', 2, 150.0), ('2026-10-13', 'US', 1, 80.0), ('2026-10-14', 'EU', 1, 40.0), ('2026-10-14', 'US', 1, 25.0), ('2026-10-15', 'EU', 1, 60.0)]
MISMATCH: [(datetime.date(2026, 10, 13), 'EU', 2, 150.0), (datetime.date(2026, 10, 13), 'EU', 3, 200.0)]

Every test passed, and 13 October still shows three EU orders and 200 in revenue, including the cancelled order. The incremental filter only reprocessed days from 14 October onwards, so a change to an older day never reached the mart. None of the standard tests can see this: each row is unique, non-null and well-formed. It's simply stale. The unit test passed too, because it runs the model in full mode (is_incremental: false), which is correct.

The test that catches it compares the incremental table with a rebuild, inside dbt. tests/assert_incremental_matches_full_rebuild.sql:

-- fails (returns rows) if the incremental table differs from recomputing it from scratch
with rebuilt as (
    select cast(created_at as date) as order_date, region, count(*) as orders, sum(amount) as revenue
    from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
    where status <> 'cancelled'
    group by 1, 2
),
loaded as (
    select order_date, region, orders, revenue from {{ ref('fct_daily_revenue') }}
)
select 'missing or wrong' as problem, * from (select * from rebuilt except select * from loaded)
union all
select 'unexpected' as problem, * from (select * from loaded except select * from rebuilt)

(The first version named its CTE full, which failed to parse: FULL is a reserved word in DuckDB and in Snowflake.) With it, the same three batches fail where they should:

$ python load_raw.py 3
batch 3 landed; raw.orders has 9 rows
$ dbt build --target local
7 of 8 FAIL 2 assert_incremental_matches_full_rebuild … [FAIL 2]
Done. PASS=7 WARN=0 ERROR=1 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=8
Got 2 results, configured to fail if != 0
[ERROR]: in test assert_incremental_matches_full_rebuild (tests/assert_incremental_matches_full_rebuild.sql)

| problem          | order_date | region | orders | revenue |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ------ | ------ | ------- |
| missing or wrong | 2026-10-13 | EU     |      2 |     150 |
| unexpected       | 2026-10-13 | EU     |      3 |     200 |

The fix is to reprocess every day that has an order changed since the last load, however old the day is. The table records last_change per row, so the model knows where it left off:

{{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key=['order_date', 'region']) }}

select cast(created_at as date) as order_date, region,
       count(*) as orders, sum(amount) as revenue,
       max(updated_at) as last_change
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
where status <> 'cancelled'
{% if is_incremental() %}
  -- reprocess every day that has an order changed since the last load, however old the day is
  and cast(created_at as date) in (
      select distinct cast(created_at as date)
      from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
      where updated_at > (select max(last_change) from {{ this }})
  )
{% endif %}
group by 1, 2

The same three batches from an empty database:

$ python load_raw.py 1
batch 1 landed; raw.orders has 5 rows
$ dbt build --target local
Done. PASS=8 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=8
$ python load_raw.py 2
batch 2 landed; raw.orders has 7 rows
$ dbt build --target local
Done. PASS=8 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=8
$ python load_raw.py 3
batch 3 landed; raw.orders has 9 rows
$ dbt build --target local
Done. PASS=8 WARN=0 ERROR=0 SKIP=0 NO-OP=0 REUSED=0 TOTAL=8
$ python compare.py
incremental: [('2026-10-13', 'EU', 2, 150.0), ('2026-10-13', 'US', 1, 80.0), ('2026-10-14', 'EU', 1, 40.0), ('2026-10-14', 'US', 1, 25.0), ('2026-10-15', 'EU', 1, 60.0)]
full build : [('2026-10-13', 'EU', 2, 150.0), ('2026-10-13', 'US', 1, 80.0), ('2026-10-14', 'EU', 1, 40.0), ('2026-10-14', 'US', 1, 25.0), ('2026-10-15', 'EU', 1, 60.0)]
MATCH

And the portability check for the Snowflake targets:

7 compiled files (2 models, 5 data tests) parse as Snowflake SQL with sqlglot 30.22.0

Two lessons here. Incremental models need a test against a full rebuild, run in CI on realistic data, because their bugs are staleness, which row-level tests can't see. And the incremental filter must be driven by what changed (a watermark on change time), not by the business date you group by. One gap remains, deliberately left for the exercise: if every order of a day and region is cancelled, the new run produces no row for it, and a merge on unique_key doesn't delete the old one.

docs.title: CI with zero-copy clones
docs.text:
The expensive part of testing data code is a realistic environment. In Snowflake, CREATE DATABASE … CLONE copies only metadata (Level 1 · 09), so every pull request can get its own full copy of production in seconds, at no storage cost until it diverges. A GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/dbt-ci.yml):

{{.github/workflows/dbt-ci.yml}}

The pull-request job authenticates with a key pair from repository secrets (a SERVICE user, Level 3 · 02), clones production, runs dbt build in the clone (models, data tests, unit tests and the rebuild comparison), and always drops the clone, even when the build fails. Two refinements for larger projects:

  • Slim CI. dbt build --select state:modified+ --defer --state <production artifacts> builds only changed models and their dependents, and reads unchanged parents from production. Per Snowflake's documentation, dbt Projects on Snowflake can provide the production state directly.
  • A dedicated CI warehouse with a resource monitor (lesson 05), so a runaway test can't spend more than you've decided.

docs.title: Deploying: dbt Projects on Snowflake
docs.text: The deploy job uses dbt Projects on Snowflake: snow dbt deploy uploads the project as a dbt project object in the account, and snow dbt execute runs a dbt command on it inside Snowflake, using a warehouse. Per the documentation, Snowflake provides managed dbt Core (and dbt Fusion) runtimes, runs can be scheduled with tasks, and run history and logs are kept in the account. Executions cost warehouse time, with no separate licence fee. Note the argument order in the workflow: everything after the project name is passed to dbt itself, so Snowflake CLI options go before it.

docs.title: Beyond dbt: declarative DDL and Git
docs.text:
Not everything is a dbt model: roles, warehouses, policies, tasks. Two Snowflake features help manage those in Git too:

  • CREATE OR ALTER: you state the full desired definition, and Snowflake works out the change, preserving data, grants, tags and policies. Re-running it is idempotent, which makes it safe in a deploy script. Per the documentation, a change that drops a column still drops its data (recoverable with Time Travel), so review the diff as carefully as any migration.
  • Git repository objects and EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM: Snowflake can fetch a Git repository and run a SQL file from it (with optional Jinja templating), so the deploy step is EXECUTE IMMEDIATE FROM @repo/branches/main/deploy/roles.sql.
CREATE OR ALTER TABLE sales.mart.customers (
  customer_id NUMBER NOT NULL,
  email       VARCHAR,
  region      VARCHAR,
  created_at  TIMESTAMP_NTZ
);

CREATE OR ALTER WAREHOUSE transform_wh WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60;

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text:
dbt is a compiler and a scheduler. It reads models (SQL with Jinja) and YAML, builds a dependency graph from ref() and source(), renders each model into plain SQL for the target adapter, and runs them in dependency order, wrapping each in the DDL its materialization needs: a view, CREATE TABLE AS, or for incremental models, a temporary result followed by a MERGE (Snowflake's default) or delete-and-insert. Tests are just queries that must return zero rows. Unit tests render a model with fixed inputs in place of its parents. Nothing in dbt knows whether your incremental filter is complete, which is why the rebuild comparison has to be written by you.

The CI pattern works because of how Snowflake stores data. A clone is a new set of metadata pointing at the same immutable micro-partitions, so it's instant and free. Writes in the clone create new partitions that only the clone references, and dropping the clone discards them without touching production.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Incremental models tested only with row-level tests. Compare with a full rebuild.
  • Filtering increments by business date instead of change time. Late changes to old dates are lost.
  • CI against a shared dev database, where runs collide and data drifts. Clone per pull request and drop afterwards.
  • Personal credentials in CI. Use a SERVICE user with a key pair and a narrow role.
  • No resource monitor on the CI warehouse.
  • Unreviewed CREATE OR ALTER diffs. Dropping a column drops its data.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the project locally with dbt-duckdb (copy the files, run load_raw.py with batches 1–3, then dbt build). Then switch back to the first version of fct_daily_revenue and confirm the rebuild test fails.
  2. Add batch 4: cancel order 6, the only EU order on 14 October. Does the fixed model leave a stale row? Change the model (for example, with incremental_strategy and a delete step, or by emitting zero rows for emptied days) until the rebuild test passes.
  3. With a trial account, set up the pull-request job against a clone and check the time the clone took and its storage after the build in TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS.
  4. Deploy the project with snow dbt deploy and schedule snow dbt execute … build as a Snowflake task. Where do you see the run's logs?

docs.title: 09 · Migrating to Snowflake
docs.text: Most Snowflake estates start as a migration from somewhere: Teradata, SQL Server, Oracle, Redshift, BigQuery, a Hadoop cluster. The hard part is rarely moving bytes. It's proving that the new system gives the same answers. This lesson walks through the phases, shows automated SQL translation producing code that runs but means something different, and builds the reconciliation that catches what translation and export get wrong.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text:
1. Inventory. List objects (tables, views, procedures, jobs) and, more usefully, the queries actually run, from the old system's query logs. Unused objects don't need migrating, and the most-run queries are your test suite.
  2. Translate DDL, views, procedures and ETL code into Snowflake SQL.
  3. Move data: a one-off historical load, then the ongoing pipeline.
  4. Validate: reconcile the same questions on both systems, for every table and the top queries.
  5. Run in parallel, then cut over consumers (BI tools, applications, downstream exports) one at a time, with a rollback plan.

Snowflake's own tooling covers phase 2: SnowConvert AI converts SQL from, per the documentation, Teradata, Oracle, SQL Server, Redshift, Azure Synapse, Sybase IQ, Spark SQL, Databricks SQL, BigQuery, PostgreSQL and others, and the Snowpark Migration Accelerator handles Spark code. Neither was run for this course. Whatever converts the code, phases 4 and 5 are yours.

docs.title: Translation runs, but does it mean the same?
docs.text:
Open-source sqlglot (30.22, run locally) transpiles between dialects. Eight typical source queries, translated to Snowflake:

import sqlglot
cases = [
    ("tsql", "SELECT TOP 10 customer_id, ISNULL(region, 'n/a') AS region, DATEADD(day, -7, GETDATE()) AS since FROM dbo.orders WITH (NOLOCK) ORDER BY amount DESC"),
    ("tsql", "SELECT customer_id, total_items / order_count AS avg_items FROM dbo.customer_stats"),
    ("tsql", "SELECT first_name + ' ' + last_name AS full_name FROM dbo.customers"),
    ("redshift", "SELECT order_id, NVL(amount, 0) AS amount, GETDATE() AS loaded_at FROM sales.orders WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE)"),
    ("redshift", "SELECT LISTAGG(sku, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY sku) FROM sales.order_lines GROUP BY order_id"),
    ("bigquery", "SELECT user_id, ARRAY_AGG(event ORDER BY ts LIMIT 5) AS last_events FROM `proj.web.events` GROUP BY user_id"),
    ("bigquery", "SELECT * FROM `proj.web.events` WHERE DATE(ts) = CURRENT_DATE() AND SAFE_CAST(value AS INT64) > 10"),
    ("bigquery", "SELECT EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM ts) AS dow, COUNT(*) FROM `proj.web.events` GROUP BY dow"),
]
for dialect, sql in cases:
    print(f"-- {dialect}: {sql}")
    try:
        print(sqlglot.transpile(sql, read=dialect, write="snowflake", pretty=False)[0])
    except Exception as e:
        print("!! ", type(e).__name__, e)
    print()

-- tsql: SELECT TOP 10 customer_id, ISNULL(region, 'n/a') AS region, DATEADD(day, -7, GETDATE()) AS since FROM dbo.orders WITH (NOLOCK) ORDER BY amount DESC
SELECT customer_id, COALESCE(region, 'n/a') AS region, DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()) AS since FROM dbo.orders ORDER BY amount DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10

-- tsql: SELECT customer_id, total_items / order_count AS avg_items FROM dbo.customer_stats
SELECT customer_id, total_items / order_count AS avg_items FROM dbo.customer_stats

-- tsql: SELECT first_name + ' ' + last_name AS full_name FROM dbo.customers
SELECT first_name + ' ' + last_name AS full_name FROM dbo.customers

-- redshift: SELECT order_id, NVL(amount, 0) AS amount, GETDATE() AS loaded_at FROM sales.orders WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE)
SELECT order_id, COALESCE(amount, 0) AS amount, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() AS loaded_at FROM sales.orders WHERE order_date >= DATEADD(MONTH, -1, CAST(CURRENT_DATE AS TIMESTAMP))

-- redshift: SELECT LISTAGG(sku, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY sku) FROM sales.order_lines GROUP BY order_id
SELECT LISTAGG(sku, ',') WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY sku) FROM sales.order_lines GROUP BY order_id

-- bigquery: SELECT user_id, ARRAY_AGG(event ORDER BY ts LIMIT 5) AS last_events FROM `proj.web.events` GROUP BY user_id
SELECT user_id, ARRAY_AGG(event ORDER BY ts NULLS FIRST LIMIT 5) AS last_events FROM "proj"."web"."events" GROUP BY user_id

-- bigquery: SELECT * FROM `proj.web.events` WHERE DATE(ts) = CURRENT_DATE() AND SAFE_CAST(value AS INT64) > 10
SELECT * FROM "proj"."web"."events" WHERE DATE(ts) = CURRENT_DATE AND CAST(value AS BIGINT) > 10

-- bigquery: SELECT EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM ts) AS dow, COUNT(*) FROM `proj.web.events` GROUP BY dow
SELECT DATE_PART(DAYOFWEEK, ts) AS dow, COUNT(*) FROM "proj"."web"."events" GROUP BY dow

Every output parses, and several are subtly wrong. Each problem below is confirmed against Snowflake's documentation:

Query What changed silently T-SQL total_items / order_count In SQL Server, integer ÷ integer is integer division (7 / 2 = 3). In Snowflake, division of integers returns a decimal (3.5). Averages change. T-SQL first_name + ' ' + last_name + concatenates strings in SQL Server. In Snowflake, + is arithmetic, so this fails at run time. Use \|\| or CONCAT. T-SQL TOP 10 … ORDER BY amount DESC Handled correctly: the translator added NULLS LAST, because the two systems order NULLs differently. Good translators know these rules. Your hand-written code may not. BigQuery SAFE_CAST(value AS INT64) Became CAST, which errors on bad values instead of returning NULL. The Snowflake equivalent is TRY_CAST. BigQuery `proj.web.events` Became "proj"."web"."events": quoted, therefore case-sensitive lowercase. Snowflake stores unquoted names in upper case, so this won't find a table created as events. BigQuery EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK …) BigQuery numbers days 1 (Sunday) to 7. Snowflake's DAYOFWEEK with the default WEEK_START = 0 returns 0 (Sunday) to 6. Every value is off by one. BigQuery ARRAY_AGG(… LIMIT 5) Snowflake's ARRAY_AGG syntax has no LIMIT. This fails to compile in Snowflake, so at least it fails loudly. Redshift NVL, GETDATE(), LISTAGG Translated correctly.

The pattern: translation tools are good at syntax, but they can't know your column types or your intent, so semantic differences slip through code that compiles. The only defence is running the translated query on both systems and comparing the results, which is why the inventory's top queries become the test suite.

docs.title: Moving the data
docs.text:
The standard path for historical data is: export from the old system to Parquet in cloud storage, then load with COPY (Level 1 · 05):

CREATE STAGE migration.raw.legacy_export
  URL = 's3://my-company-migration/legacy/'
  STORAGE_INTEGRATION = s3_migration_int
  FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = PARQUET);

COPY INTO sales.raw.orders
  FROM @migration.raw.legacy_export/orders/
  MATCH_BY_COLUMN_NAME = CASE_INSENSITIVE
  ON_ERROR = ABORT_STATEMENT;

Parquet carries types, which is both its strength and the risk. The export tool decides how decimals and timestamps are written, and it doesn't always decide well.

docs.title: Reconciliation finds what exports get wrong
docs.text:
A local experiment (DuckDB 1.5.6, not Snowflake) on the course's 200,000 orders. The "legacy" table has DECIMAL(10,2) prices and timestamps without a time zone, recorded in Berlin local time. Three export jobs are reconciled per day against the source:

# DuckDB 1.5.6 locally, not Snowflake. The "legacy warehouse" is the course's orders table: DECIMAL(10,2) prices and
# TIMESTAMP (no time zone) order times recorded in Europe/Berlin local time. Three export jobs write Parquet for loading:
#   faithful : types unchanged
#   double   : prices written as DOUBLE (a common export-tool default)
#   utc      : timestamps reinterpreted as Berlin time and converted to UTC (a common "normalise to UTC" step)
# Reconciliation compares source and export per day: row count, revenue rounded to cents, and exact revenue.
import duckdb, sys
con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute(f"attach '{sys.argv[1]}' as legacy (read_only)")
con.execute("set TimeZone = 'Europe/Berlin'")
exports = {
    "faithful": "select * from legacy.orders",
    "double":   "select * replace (cast(unit_price as double) as unit_price) from legacy.orders",
    "utc":      "select * replace (timezone('UTC', ordered_at::timestamptz) as ordered_at) from legacy.orders",
}
for name, q in exports.items():
    con.execute(f"copy ({q}) to 'export_{name}.parquet' (format parquet)")

print(f"{'export':<10}{'days':>6}{'count differs':>15}{'cents differ':>14}{'exact differs':>15}")
for name in exports:
    days, n, cents, exact = con.execute(f"""
        with src as (select cast(ordered_at as date) d, count(*) n, sum(quantity * unit_price) r
                     from legacy.orders group by 1),
             tgt as (select cast(ordered_at as date) d, count(*) n, sum(quantity * unit_price) r
                     from 'export_{name}.parquet' group by 1)
        select count(*),
               count_if(src.n is distinct from tgt.n),
               count_if(round(src.r, 2) is distinct from round(tgt.r, 2)),
               count_if(src.r::double is distinct from tgt.r::double)
        from src full join tgt using (d)""").fetchone()
    print(f"{name:<10}{days:>6}{n:>15}{cents:>14}{exact:>15}")

export      days  count differs  cents differ  exact differs
faithful     270              0             0              0
double       270              0             0            247
utc          271            263           271            271
  • faithful: identical on every measure. That's the baseline a correct pipeline produces.
  • double: counts and revenue rounded to cents match every day, but exact sums differ on 247 of 270 days. Floating-point prices accumulate tiny errors. Here they vanished at cent precision, but they won't always (large sums, ratios, = comparisons in joins). Keep money in NUMBER, and make the reconciliation compare exactly so you see the drift and decide on purpose.
  • utc: the "normalise to UTC" step moved every order by one or two hours, so orders near midnight moved to a different day. Row counts differ on 263 days, and a day appears that didn't exist. Nothing failed, and the total row count is still 200,000. Only a per-day reconciliation shows it.

The Snowflake side of the same checks:

-- per-day profile, to compare with the same query on the legacy system
SELECT CAST(ordered_at AS DATE) AS d, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS revenue
FROM sales.raw.orders
GROUP BY d
ORDER BY d;

-- a whole-table fingerprint, for tables copied between Snowflake accounts or schemas
SELECT HASH_AGG(*) FROM sales.raw.orders;
SELECT HASH_AGG(*) FROM sales_migrated.raw.orders;

HASH_AGG is fast and order-independent, but it can only compare Snowflake to Snowflake, since the legacy system computes different hashes. Across systems, compare profiles: counts, sums, min and max per key period and per important column, and distinct counts for keys.

docs.title: Cutting over
docs.text: Run both systems in parallel long enough to cover your business cycles (month end at least), with the daily reconciliation running automatically and failing loudly. Move consumers one by one, starting with the least critical, and keep the old system read-only until the last consumer has moved and a full cycle has passed. Then decommission it, and write down which of the differences you accepted on purpose. Someone will ask in a year.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A SQL translator parses source code into a syntax tree, rewrites nodes whose syntax differs (TOP → LIMIT, ISNULL → COALESCE) using rules for each dialect pair, and prints the tree in the target dialect. It sees text, not data. It usually doesn't know column types (is a / b integer division?), session settings (WEEK_START) or which objects exist, and that's exactly where the semantic traps above live. Reconciliation works one level down: it compares results computed independently on each system, so it catches translation errors, export errors and loading errors alike, whatever their cause. That's why it's the part of a migration you can't skip or automate away.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Migrating everything. Use query logs to find what's actually used.
  • Trusting code that compiles. Integer division, string +, CAST vs TRY_CAST, week numbering and NULL ordering all compile.
  • Exporting money as floating point and timestamps through an unreviewed time-zone conversion.
  • Reconciling only total row counts. Compare per key period, and compare values exactly.
  • Quoted lower-case identifiers from translated code, creating a mixture of case-sensitive and normal names.
  • Cutting over all consumers at once with no parallel run.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Pick five queries your team runs often on another database. Translate them with sqlglot (sqlglot.transpile(sql, read=…, write="snowflake")) and review each against the table above.
  2. Run reconcile.py on your machine, then add a fourth export that writes quantity as a string. What does the reconciliation show?
  3. Write the per-day profile query for the legacy system you know best, and a script that diffs its output against Snowflake's.
  4. In a trial account, load the export_utc.parquet file from the experiment and find the shifted orders with SQL alone.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone — A Cost-Aware Data Platform
docs.text:
The final project brings Level 4 together around the question every growing Snowflake account eventually faces: who is spending what, and is it worth it? You'll set up a platform where every credit has an owner, runaway spend is stopped or flagged, and a monthly chargeback assigns all compute, including the idle time that per-query attribution leaves out (lesson 05). The chargeback is the component everything else depends on, so it's tested, and the tests themselves are tested.

What was run

The chargeback query was run in DuckDB 1.5.6 locally (not Snowflake) against synthetic tables shaped like the ACCOUNT_USAGE views, with seven pytest tests and a mutation check. The platform SQL, which embeds the same query, was syntax-checked and checked against Snowflake's October 2026 documentation, but not executed.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. Every warehouse has a cost owner: a team for dedicated warehouses, and a team per query for shared ones.
  2. Sandbox spend is capped daily. Shared spend is flagged before it gets out of hand. The whole account has a forecast with alerts.
  3. A monthly chargeback assigns 100% of warehouse compute, with idle time shared in proportion to usage, and makes unowned spend visible instead of hiding it.
  4. Platform health is one number: the share of credits nobody owns.

docs.title: The platform
docs.text:
platform.sql: ownership, workload warehouses, monitors, budget, and the chargeback as a scheduled task:

-- 1. ownership vocabulary and the FinOps schema
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS governance;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS governance.finops;
CREATE TAG IF NOT EXISTS governance.finops.cost_center
  ALLOWED_VALUES 'sales', 'finance', 'marketing', 'data-science', 'data-platform';
CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS finops_admin;                         -- runs the chargeback; not an administrator
GRANT ROLE finops_admin TO ROLE SYSADMIN;
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.USAGE_VIEWER TO ROLE finops_admin;       -- WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY, QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY
GRANT DATABASE ROLE SNOWFLAKE.GOVERNANCE_VIEWER TO ROLE finops_admin;  -- TAG_REFERENCES
GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE governance TO ROLE finops_admin;
GRANT ALL ON SCHEMA governance.finops TO ROLE finops_admin;
GRANT EXECUTE TASK ON ACCOUNT TO ROLE finops_admin;

-- 2. warehouses by workload, each with an owner or a shared purpose
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS transform_wh WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'MEDIUM' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE WITH TAG (governance.finops.cost_center = 'data-platform');
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS sales_bi_wh WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  MIN_CLUSTER_COUNT = 1 MAX_CLUSTER_COUNT = 3 SCALING_POLICY = 'STANDARD'
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE WITH TAG (governance.finops.cost_center = 'sales');
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS shared_wh WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'SMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE COMMENT = 'Shared: charged by QUERY_TAG team=<cost center>';
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS sandbox_wh WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL' AUTO_SUSPEND = 60 AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;

-- shared-warehouse users and services identify their team by default
ALTER USER etl_service SET QUERY_TAG = 'team=data-platform';
ALTER USER ana SET QUERY_TAG = 'team=sales';

-- 3. circuit breakers (warehouses only) and forecasts (everything)
CREATE OR REPLACE RESOURCE MONITOR sandbox_daily WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 5 FREQUENCY = DAILY START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 80 PERCENT DO NOTIFY ON 100 PERCENT DO SUSPEND_IMMEDIATE;
ALTER WAREHOUSE sandbox_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = sandbox_daily;
CREATE OR REPLACE RESOURCE MONITOR shared_monthly WITH CREDIT_QUOTA = 300 FREQUENCY = MONTHLY START_TIMESTAMP = IMMEDIATELY
  TRIGGERS ON 75 PERCENT DO NOTIFY ON 90 PERCENT DO NOTIFY ON 110 PERCENT DO SUSPEND;
ALTER WAREHOUSE shared_wh SET RESOURCE_MONITOR = shared_monthly;

CALL SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.ACCOUNT_ROOT_BUDGET!ACTIVATE();
CALL SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.ACCOUNT_ROOT_BUDGET!SET_SPENDING_LIMIT(2000);
CALL SNOWFLAKE.LOCAL.ACCOUNT_ROOT_BUDGET!SET_EMAIL_NOTIFICATIONS('finops@example.com');

-- 4. the monthly chargeback, materialised on the 2nd (attribution data can lag by up to eight hours)
USE ROLE SYSADMIN;
GRANT USAGE ON WAREHOUSE transform_wh TO ROLE finops_admin;
USE ROLE finops_admin;
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS governance.finops.chargeback (
  month DATE, warehouse_name VARCHAR, cost_center VARCHAR, credits NUMBER(38, 6), basis VARCHAR);

CREATE OR REPLACE TASK governance.finops.monthly_chargeback
  WAREHOUSE = transform_wh
  SCHEDULE = 'USING CRON 0 6 2 * * UTC'
AS
INSERT INTO governance.finops.chargeback
with metered as (
    select warehouse_name,
           sum(credits_used_compute) as compute,
           sum(credits_attributed_compute_queries) as attributed
    from SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY
    where start_time >= DATE_TRUNC(month, DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE())) and start_time < DATE_TRUNC(month, CURRENT_DATE())
    group by warehouse_name
),
owner as (                                            -- dedicated warehouses carry a cost_center tag
    select object_name as warehouse_name, tag_value as cost_center
    from SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.TAG_REFERENCES
    where domain = 'WAREHOUSE' and tag_name = 'COST_CENTER' and tag_database = 'GOVERNANCE'
),
by_team as (                                          -- shared warehouses: queries carry 'team=<name>;...'
    select warehouse_name,
           coalesce(nullif(split_part(split_part(query_tag, 'team=', 2), ';', 1), ''), 'untagged') as cost_center,
           sum(credits_attributed_compute) as team_attributed
    from SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY
    where start_time >= DATE_TRUNC(month, DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE())) and start_time < DATE_TRUNC(month, CURRENT_DATE())
    group by 1, 2
),
team_share as (
    select warehouse_name, cost_center,
           team_attributed / sum(team_attributed) over (partition by warehouse_name) as share
    from by_team
)
select DATE_TRUNC(month, DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE())), m.warehouse_name, o.cost_center, m.compute as credits, 'dedicated' as basis
from metered m join owner o using (warehouse_name)
union all
select DATE_TRUNC(month, DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE())), m.warehouse_name, s.cost_center, m.compute * s.share, 'shared: usage plus proportional idle'
from metered m join team_share s using (warehouse_name)
where m.warehouse_name not in (select warehouse_name from owner)
union all
select DATE_TRUNC(month, DATEADD(month, -1, CURRENT_DATE())), m.warehouse_name, 'unallocated', m.compute, 'no owner tag and no attributed queries'
from metered m
where m.warehouse_name not in (select warehouse_name from owner)
  and m.warehouse_name not in (select warehouse_name from team_share);

ALTER TASK governance.finops.monthly_chargeback RESUME;

-- 5. a month is healthy when almost nothing is unowned
SELECT month,
       SUM(IFF(cost_center IN ('untagged', 'unallocated'), credits, 0)) / SUM(credits) AS unowned_share
FROM governance.finops.chargeback
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month DESC;

Design choices, with the lessons behind them:

  • Warehouses by workload, not by person (lessons 05–06): transformation, BI (multi-cluster STANDARD for Monday-morning bursts), a shared warehouse for small teams, and a capped sandbox. All have AUTO_SUSPEND = 60, because idle time was 86% of the bill in lesson 05's model with a 10-minute setting.
  • Two ownership mechanisms: an object tag on dedicated warehouses, and QUERY_TAG defaults on users for the shared one. Pipelines can override the tag per job.
  • Monitors where you must stop spend, the budget for everything else. The sandbox monitor suspends immediately at its daily quota. The shared warehouse's notifies at 75% and 90% and suspends only at 110%, because stopping a shared warehouse stops several teams. The account budget covers serverless and AI services, which monitors can't.
  • A dedicated, non-admin role runs the chargeback, with exactly the SNOWFLAKE database roles its views need (USAGE_VIEWER, GOVERNANCE_VIEWER), per the documentation.
  • The task runs on the 2nd, because QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY can lag by up to eight hours. A chargeback run at midnight on the 1st would compute shares from incomplete data.

docs.title: The chargeback, tested
docs.text:
The allocation logic as one SQL statement (chargeback.sql), written to run unchanged on DuckDB for testing, with parameters for the month:

-- Monthly chargeback: every compute credit of every warehouse assigned to exactly one cost center.
-- Inputs mirror SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE: WAREHOUSE_METERING_HISTORY, QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY, TAG_REFERENCES.
with metered as (
    select warehouse_name,
           sum(credits_used_compute) as compute,
           sum(credits_attributed_compute_queries) as attributed
    from warehouse_metering_history
    where start_time >= :month_start and start_time < :month_end
    group by warehouse_name
),
owner as (                                            -- dedicated warehouses carry a cost_center tag
    select object_name as warehouse_name, tag_value as cost_center
    from tag_references
    where domain = 'WAREHOUSE' and tag_name = 'COST_CENTER'
),
by_team as (                                          -- shared warehouses: queries carry 'team=<name>;...'
    select warehouse_name,
           coalesce(nullif(split_part(split_part(query_tag, 'team=', 2), ';', 1), ''), 'untagged') as cost_center,
           sum(credits_attributed_compute) as team_attributed
    from query_attribution_history
    where start_time >= :month_start and start_time < :month_end
    group by 1, 2
),
team_share as (
    select warehouse_name, cost_center,
           team_attributed / sum(team_attributed) over (partition by warehouse_name) as share
    from by_team
)
select m.warehouse_name, o.cost_center, m.compute as credits, 'dedicated' as basis
from metered m join owner o using (warehouse_name)
union all
select m.warehouse_name, s.cost_center, m.compute * s.share, 'shared: usage plus proportional idle'
from metered m join team_share s using (warehouse_name)
where m.warehouse_name not in (select warehouse_name from owner)
union all
select m.warehouse_name, 'unallocated', m.compute, 'no owner tag and no attributed queries'
from metered m
where m.warehouse_name not in (select warehouse_name from owner)
  and m.warehouse_name not in (select warehouse_name from team_share)

The test data (fixtures.py) covers each case the logic must handle: a dedicated warehouse that also has tagged queries (it must not be counted twice), a shared warehouse with three teams and one untagged query, a dedicated warehouse fully used, an idle sandbox with no owner, and rows from the previous month that must be ignored:

        ) t(domain, object_name, tag_name, tag_value)""")

test_chargeback.py states the invariants:

"""Invariants the chargeback must satisfy, run against chargeback.sql in DuckDB (local, not Snowflake)."""
import duckdb, pytest
from fixtures import load

SQL = open("chargeback.sql").read()

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def rows():
    con = duckdb.connect(); load(con)
    sql = SQL.replace(":month_start", "timestamp '2026-10-01'").replace(":month_end", "timestamp '2026-11-01'")
    return con.execute(sql).fetchall()      # (warehouse, cost_center, credits, basis)

def total(rows, **match):
    return sum(r[2] for r in rows if all(r[i] == v for i, v in ((0, match.get("wh")), (1, match.get("cc"))) if v))

def test_every_credit_is_allocated_exactly_once(rows):
    assert total(rows) == pytest.approx(30 + 10 + 40 + 20 + 25 + 3)        # October compute, nothing more

def test_each_warehouse_sums_to_its_meter(rows):
    for wh, metered in {"SALES_BI_WH": 40, "SHARED_WH": 60, "DS_WH": 25, "SANDBOX_WH": 3}.items():
        assert total(rows, wh=wh) == pytest.approx(metered)

def test_dedicated_warehouse_goes_to_its_owner_including_idle(rows):
    assert [(r[1], r[2]) for r in rows if r[0] == "SALES_BI_WH"] == [("sales", 40)]

def test_shared_idle_is_split_in_proportion_to_usage(rows):
    # October attributed on SHARED_WH: finance 21, marketing 6, untagged 3 (of 30); compute 60
    assert total(rows, wh="SHARED_WH", cc="finance") == pytest.approx(60 * 21 / 30)
    assert total(rows, wh="SHARED_WH", cc="marketing") == pytest.approx(60 * 6 / 30)

def test_queries_without_a_team_are_visible_not_hidden(rows):
    assert total(rows, wh="SHARED_WH", cc="untagged") == pytest.approx(60 * 3 / 30)

def test_idle_warehouse_without_owner_is_reported_as_unallocated(rows):
    assert [(r[1], r[2]) for r in rows if r[0] == "SANDBOX_WH"] == [("unallocated", 3)]

def test_no_negative_or_null_allocations(rows):
    assert all(r[1] is not None and r[2] is not None and r[2] >= 0 for r in rows)

docs.title: Testing the tests
docs.text:
All seven tests passed on the first run, which proves less than it seems: tests that can't fail prove nothing. So the suite was run against three deliberately wrong versions of the query, each a mistake a real chargeback could make (mutants.py):

# Runs the test suite against deliberately wrong versions of chargeback.sql: does it catch each mistake?
import pathlib, shutil, subprocess, sys
MUTANTS = {
    "charge shared warehouses only for attributed usage (no idle)":
        ("m.compute * s.share", "m.attributed * s.share"),
    "forget the month filter on query attribution":
        ("from query_attribution_history\n    where start_time >= :month_start and start_time < :month_end",
         "from query_attribution_history\n    where true"),
    "drop queries without a team tag":
        ("coalesce(nullif(split_part(split_part(query_tag, 'team=', 2), ';', 1), ''), 'untagged')",
         "nullif(split_part(split_part(query_tag, 'team=', 2), ';', 1), '')"),
}
original = pathlib.Path("chargeback.sql").read_text()
shutil.copy("chargeback.sql", "chargeback.sql.orig")
try:
    for name, (old, new) in MUTANTS.items():
        assert old in original, name
        pathlib.Path("chargeback.sql").write_text(original.replace(old, new))
        r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "pytest", "-q", "-p", "no:cacheprovider", "test_chargeback.py"],
                           capture_output=True, text=True)
        failed = [l.split("::")[1].split(" ")[0] for l in r.stdout.splitlines() if l.startswith("FAILED")]
        print(f"{name}:\n  {'CAUGHT by ' + ', '.join(failed) if failed else 'NOT CAUGHT'}")
finally:
    shutil.move("chargeback.sql.orig", "chargeback.sql")

charge shared warehouses only for attributed usage (no idle):
  CAUGHT by test_every_credit_is_allocated_exactly_once, test_each_warehouse_sums_to_its_meter, test_shared_idle_is_split_in_proportion_to_usage, test_queries_without_a_team_are_visible_not_hidden
forget the month filter on query attribution:
  CAUGHT by test_shared_idle_is_split_in_proportion_to_usage, test_queries_without_a_team_are_visible_not_hidden
drop queries without a team tag:
  CAUGHT by test_queries_without_a_team_are_visible_not_hidden, test_no_negative_or_null_allocations

Each mistake is caught, and the second result is the instructive one. Forgetting the month filter on attribution still allocates exactly the metered total, so both "sums to the meter" tests pass. It's caught only because a test checks the proportions, which September's queries distort. A suite of invariants alone would have shipped that bug. Exact expected values for a hand-checked case are what caught it.

docs.title: From tested SQL to the deployed task
docs.text: The task in platform.sql was generated from chargeback.sql by four mechanical substitutions: the three table names become the SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE views, the month parameters become "last calendar month", the tag lookup is restricted to the governance database's tag, and the month is added as the first column. Generating it, rather than editing a copy, keeps the deployed logic identical to the tested logic.

docs.title: Running the platform
docs.text:
A monthly FinOps review, an hour a month:

  1. Unowned share (the last query in platform.sql). Above a few percent, fix tags and default query tags first, because every other number depends on ownership.
  2. Idle share per warehouse (lesson 05's query). High idle points to AUTO_SUSPEND, refresh schedules or consolidation.
  3. Top repeated queries by query_parameterized_hash in QUERY_ATTRIBUTION_HISTORY. One dashboard query run 10,000 times a month is usually the cheapest big win: cache it, materialize it, or refresh it less often.
  4. Service-type lines in METERING_DAILY_HISTORY (serverless, AI services, replication), against the budget forecast.
  5. Queuing vs spilling per warehouse (lesson 06), to choose scale-out or scale-up, or neither.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The platform works because each piece reads the same underlying meter at a different speed and for a different purpose. Resource monitors watch warehouse credits close to real time and can act, so they're the brakes. Budgets read consolidated metering for all services every few hours and project to month end, so they're the early warning. Account Usage views are the complete, lagging record, so the chargeback reads them once the month is settled. Tags and query tags are the join keys that turn that record into owners. The chargeback is a closed allocation: for each warehouse, metered compute is split among owners by shares that sum to one. That's why "every credit allocated exactly once" holds whatever the shares are, and why correctness lives in the shares, which is where the tests have to look.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Chargeback from attribution alone, leaving idle time (often most of the bill) on nobody's books.
  • Running the chargeback before the data settles. Wait for the documented latency.
  • Monitors that suspend shared warehouses at 100%, stopping several teams for one team's spike.
  • Untagged warehouses and missing default query tags. Ownership has to be set up first.
  • Tests that check only totals. Totals hide shifted proportions. Pin hand-checked values too.
  • Editing a copy of tested SQL for production. Generate the deployed version from the tested one.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run the tests locally (pip install duckdb pytest, then pytest test_chargeback.py), then python mutants.py. Add a fourth mutant (for example, splitting idle equally between teams instead of by usage) and make sure a test catches it.
  2. Extend the chargeback to serverless costs: assign SERVERLESS_TASK credits from METERING_HISTORY to the task's database owner tag. Write the tests first.
  3. In a trial account, run platform.sql (adjusting users and emails), run some tagged and untagged queries on shared_wh, and two days later run the chargeback query by hand for the current month. What's your unowned share?
  4. Write the one-page FinOps review for that month, using the five checks above, with one recommended change and its expected saving.
